1. Introduction**

A B S T R A C T

Colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) are a major indication for liver surgery in Europe, highlighting the need for
standardized knowledge and training in surgical oncology. The European Society of Surgical Oncology (ESSO)
has updated its core curriculum to provide a structured framework for education. Previous publications have
addressed pancreatic, hepatocellular, and biliary tract cancers to support candidates preparing for the European
Board of Surgery Qualification (EBSQ) exams in Surgical Oncology and Hepato-Pancreato-Biliary Surgery.
However, a dedicated guide for CRLM remains absent.
This article aims to fill that gap by offering a structured reference on CRLM, covering epidemiology, staging,
genetics, and diagnosis of metastatic colorectal cancer. It also outlines multidisciplinary treatment strategies,
including systemic, surgical, interventional, and palliative approaches. A structured literature review was con­
ducted using PubMed to identify the most updated (inter)national management guidelines, prioritizing recent
multicentre studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published from January 2020 to January 2025.
By bridging the gap between the ESSO core curriculum and detailed subspecialty training, this guide provides
an essential resource for hepatobiliary surgeons and surgical oncologists. It serves as a valuable tool for those
preparing for board examinations while promoting a standardized approach to CRLM education and manage­
ment across Europe.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
3. Epidemiology and staging of colorectal cancer**

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a significant health concern, being the

third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer death
worldwide [5]. At the time of diagnosis, between 15 and 30 % of pa­
tients will have metastatic disease, and a further 20–50 % of patients
with initially localized disease will develop metastases down the line.
The liver is the most frequent site of metastatic spread, with 70–80 % of
patients presenting with liver only disease, followed by lung, perito­
neum and distant lymph nodes [6,7]. The staging of CRC has evolved,
with the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition
providing detailed categorisations. The TNM system remains the
cornerstone of staging, with recent updates emphasising the importance
of tumour deposits and lymph node involvement. Cellular heterogene­
ity, plasticity and the tumour microenvironment play an important role
in metastatic spread and therapy resistance [8].
Resection of CRLM provides a clear survival benefit, yet resection
rates vary significantly across countries. In the UK, rates are notably
lower (4–5%) compared to MD Anderson in North America (10 %) and
Norwegian registry data (20 %) [9]. These differences may stem from
population-based versus institutional referral patterns. However, un­
derutilization of liver surgery is also linked to limited awareness of
multimodal treatment options and inadequate referral to multidisci­
plinary teams (MDTs) that include hepatobiliary surgeons, which is not
mandatory in all healthcare settings. Improving access to MDT evalua­
tion is crucial, as it optimizes treatment strategies and improves out­
comes [10].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
4. Genetics of colorectal cancer**

Colorectal cancer shows distinct genetic differences based on age of
onset, histological type ((mucinous) adenocarcinoma, signet-ring cell
carcinoma), and on tumour location (right colon, left colon, and
rectum). While common adenocarcinomas most frequently metastasize
to the liver and lung, mucinous adenocarcinoma and signet-ring cells
carcinoma more often spread to the peritoneum, distant lymph nodes,
bone and other extra-hepatic sites [11]. Tumour location, also called
“sidedness”, reflects tumour biology and mutational status and can
therefore influence metastatic potential and overall oncological prog­
nosis [12] (see Fig. 1). Accordingly, routine mismatch repair
(MMR)/microsatellite instability (MSI) testing is recommended, with
additional molecular testing in the presence of metastatic disease (rat
sarcoma (RAS) and v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homolog B1
(BRAF) mutations; human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)
amplifications; mostly as part of a broad molecular profiling) [13].

_4.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
1. Tumour location_

Right-Sided Colon Cancers often have higher rates of MSI and mu­
tations in genes such as BRAF and phosphatidylinositol-4,5bisphosphate 3-kinase catalytic subunit alpha (PIK3CA), which are
linked to a poorer prognosis. They also exhibit a higher tumour muta­
tional burden (TMB), which may contribute to their distinct clinical
behaviour [12]. Patients undergoing liver resection for metastases from
right-sided CRC also have worse survival, indicating that sidedness is a
simple yet effective factor in predicting outcomes [14].
Left-Sided Colon Cancers are more likely to have chromosomal
instability and mutations in TP53. They tend to have fewer BRAF mu­
tations compared to right-sided tumours [12].
Rectal Cancers show unique molecular characteristics, such as higher
Her2/neu amplification. Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog
(KRAS) and neuroblastoma ras viral oncogene homolog (NRAS) muta­
tions are more common in rectal cancer and seem to be associated with
distinct metastatic patterns such as lung metastases, which are more
frequent in rectal cancers than in colon cancers [12].

_4.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
2. Age of onset_

Early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC), defined as CRC occurring in
patients under 50 years of age, is characterized by distinct molecular and
clinical profiles. EOCRC exhibits a higher prevalence of MSI-high status,
a lower incidence of BRAF mutations, are predominantly located in the
distal colon or rectum and are more frequently associated with syn­
chronous metastatic disease [15]. In contrast, late-onset CRC, occurring
in patients aged 50 years and older, demonstrates varying characteristics
based on tumour location. Right-sided tumours are often linked to
sporadic MSI, whereas left-sided tumours are more likely to exhibit fa­
milial predisposition and higher levels of chromosomal instability [12].
These genetic differences underscore the importance of considering
both tumour location and patient age when evaluating CRC, as they can
significantly impact prognosis and treatment strategies. Molecular
profiling is crucial for tailoring personalised treatment approaches in
CRC patients [13].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
5. Diagnosis of metastatic colorectal cancer**

Almost half of all liver metastasis are detected at the time of diag­
nosis of the primary cancer (synchronous CRLM) and the remaining
during follow-up for treated primary CRC (metachronous CRLM).
Different imaging modalities are available for the diagnosis and
treatment planning of patients with metastatic (m)CRC. Most European
and non-European guidelines agree on the need of computedtomography (CT) and magnetic-resonance imaging (MRI) as an inte­
gral part of the diagnostic algorithm, although the choice of imaging

modality may vary based on resource availability and clinical context
[6,13,16–18].

 - CT scan chest-abdomen-pelvis: is the standard for initial staging,
allowing assessment of both hepatic and extrahepatic disease. The
sensitivity and specificity of a contrast-enhanced CT for detecting
liver metastases ranges from 51.8 to 84.6 % and 77.2–98.0 %,
respectively [19].
 - Liver MRI: particularly with hepatospecific contrast agents, is rec­
ommended to better evaluate liver metastases, especially when CT
findings are equivocal. MRI offers superior sensitivity and specificity
(86.9–100.0 % and 80.2–98.0 %, respectively) for small liver lesions
and can lead to changes in treatment plan in about 31 % of patients,
when compared to CT scan alone [19,20].
 - Positron emission tomography (PET)/CT: useful for detecting
extrahepatic metastases and assessing the extent of disease, partic­
ularly in candidates for attempted curative-intent surgery, for pa­
tients with a high disease burden or extrahepatic disease [13].
Several studies have not been able to show a gain in the routine use of
PET-CT in the work-up of all patients with CRLM, hence, a select use
may be warranted. PET/MRI has now emerged as a more sensitive
and specific imaging, but the data on its applicability and use is
limited [21].
 - Contrast-enhanced ultrasound can be an alternative for evaluating
liver metastases, especially in settings where MRI is not available
and, in particular, as an intraoperative supportive tool for smaller
lesions, unclear/indeterminate lesions.
 - Tumour markers: biochemical testing of carcinoembryonic antigen
(CEA) and, optionally, carbohydrate antigen (CA 19-9) levels is
recommended [6]. Reduction in CEA levels (“biochemical response”)
after systemic chemotherapy has been associated with radiological
response, longer progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival
(OS) in mCRC patients. Thus, tumour biomarkers may provide
valuable prognostic and predictive information that can potentially
guide treatment decisions [22].
 - Biopsy of the primary tumour or metastatic sites is recommended for
histological confirmation and for molecular testing (RAS/BRAF/
MMR status) in order to guide targeted therapies, especially in syn­
chronous metastatic disease [6].
 - Clinical risk scores (CRS): Several CRS were developed to predict
survival in mCRC, many of them in cohorts of patients undergoing
liver resection without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, which questions
their applicability in the era of multimodal management of these
patients [23]. The Fong CRS (CEA level _>_ 200 ng/mL, disease-free
interval from primary to metastases _<_ 12 months, number of hepat­
ic tumours _>_ 1, largest hepatic tumour _>_ 5 cm, node-positive primary
tumour) [24], and the modified CRS, which includes RAS status [25],
are commonly used.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
6. Defining a treatment strategy**

Before assessing technical resectability, a comprehensive treatment
strategy should be defined (Fig. 2). This usually requires a case manager
to present all relevant details to an MDT comprising all relevant spe­
cialists in cancer treatment. Key considerations include patient perfor­
mance status, comorbidities, and the stage and location of the primary
tumour, which may require specific multimodal treatment. Extrahepatic
metastases are not necessarily a contraindication to liver resection but
influence the strategy based on their extent, timing, response to systemic
therapy, and available local treatments, including surgery, radio­
therapy, and interventional techniques. Regarding hepatic metastases,
biological resectability must also be evaluated, considering factors such
as molecular profile (e.g., BRAF mutation, microsatellite status) and
disease dynamics (synchronous vs. metachronous, progression vs.
response to systemic therapy). Concepts like “oligometastatic disease”
and “oligometastatic progress,” increasingly recognized in guidelines

such as those from the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO),
should be integrated into decision-making [6].
The specific surgical assessment of CRLM resectability includes
technical aspects and the functional capacity of the future liver remnant
(FLR). The management of CRLM is highly dependent on the initial
resectability status, with a focus on achieving resectability through a
combination of systemic and locoregional therapies, guided by MDT
discussions. The aim of CRLM resection should be curative, as debulking
surgery in this context does not have a clearly defined role [26]. Taking
this into consideration, we can classify CRLM as:

 - Upfront resectable: those that can be directly removed with clear
margins while preserving adequate liver function.
 - Borderline resectable: those that are technically challenging to resect
but may become resectable after downsizing with neoadjuvant
chemotherapy.
 - Initially unresectable: those that cannot be surgically removed at the
time of diagnosis due to extensive liver involvement (FLR _<_ 20–30 %)
or unfavourable anatomical considerations.

Patient fitness is crucial for decision-making. The ESMO guidelines
classify fit CRLM patients into four groups based on resectability, with
the revised version simplifying the algorithm to prioritize fitness [6]. In
fit patients, the presence of symptoms will decide the initial treatment
strategy (Fig. 3).

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
7. Systemic chemotherapy**

Perioperative chemotherapy is often used to downsize tumours and
improve resectability, which is key in patients with borderline resect­
able or initially unresectable CRLM. The total recommended duration is
6 months, considering both preoperative and postoperative phases [27],
although the number of preoperative cycles will depend on the resect­
ability of the CRLM and should be kept as short as possible to avoid
chemotherapy-associated liver injury. The use of folinic
acid-5-fluorouracil-oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) is considered as a standard of
care. Using irinotecan instead of oxaliplatin (FOLFIRI) is a valid alter­
native. Triplet chemotherapy combining these three drugs (FOFLFOX­
IRI) is also used in selected patients to improve tumour response,
particularly in initially unresectable liver metastases [13]. The combi­
nation with targeted agents such as bevacizumab or cetuximab, is

recommended for borderline or initially unresectable CRLM, based on
molecular testing.

 - Anti-epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) (i.e. Cetuximab): in
RAS-wt patients with left-sided primary
 - Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (i.e. Bevacizumab):
In RAS-mutant or BRAF-mutant disease or right-sided primary

In patients with resectable metastases and with favourable prog­
nostic criteria (i.e. metachronous lesions, unilobar disease, no extrahe­
patic disease), perioperative systemic treatment may not be needed [6],
although its use is still commonplace due to benefits beyond OS [37].

**

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
8. Synchronous CRLM**

The management of CRC with synchronous CRLM involves a multi­
disciplinary approach, integrating surgery, systemic treatment and local
therapies. Current guidelines for the management of CRC are provided
by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) [13] and
ESMO [6] in addition to other organizations/societies [28].
Multidisciplinary Team discussion involving a specialist liver sur­
geon from the time of diagnosis, as well as medical oncologists, pa­
thologists, (interventional) radiologists, radiation oncologists,
colorectal surgeons and gastroenterologists, is crucial to tailor treatment
plans and optimize outcomes [6,7,10,28]. Fig. 4 exemplarily depicts a
multimodal treatment strategy plan in a patient with synchronous oli­
gometastatic disease.
Surgery remains the cornerstone for resectable liver metastases,
aiming for long-term disease-free survival. In borderline resectable or
initially unresectable CRLM, surgery should be performed as soon as
technically feasible, planned at least 4 weeks after the last chemo­
therapy cycle (±anti-EGFR) and 5 weeks after bevacizumab to prevent
medication-related complications [6]. The timing of resection of the
primary tumour and liver metastases determines the surgical approach:


- Simultaneous: involves resecting the primary tumour and liver me­
tastases in a single operation. It is associated with a shorter hospital
stay but may have a higher risk of perioperative mortality, especially
in high-risk patients (combining complex liver and colorectal pro­
cedures). However, in well-selected patients, it offers equivalent

 - Primary first: Resection of the primary tumour followed by liver

is particularly beneficial for patients with rectal primary tumours
requiring preoperative long-course chemo-radiotherapy, as liver
surgery can be performed during the 8-week waiting period before

an indication for short-course radiotherapy for the primary tumour.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
9. Metachronous CRLM**

Metachronous CRLM are defined as those detected after the initial
diagnosis of colorectal cancer [28]. The majority of them occur within
the first 3 years after curative-intent treatment, hence, the follow-up
strategies are focused on this period. Early metachronous metastases
are most commonly defined as those detected _<_ 12 months after diag­
nosis or surgery of the primary tumour [7,28]. Metastases detected
during or immediately after adjuvant therapy may represent unfav­
ourable disease biology (clonal selection) or radiologically occult,
typically small lesions, which were already present at the time of diag­
nosis. Late metachronous metastases are those detected _>_ 12 months
after the diagnosis of the colorectal cancer [7,28]. Advanced disease
(T3-T4 stage), lymph node metastasis and vascular invasion of the pri­
mary tumour as well as KRAS and BRAF mutations and raised CEA (in
CEA-expressing tumours) are recognized risk factors for developing
metachronous metastases [34]. Surgical options might be restricted by
the extent of the tumour burden and the impact of adjuvant chemo­
therapy on the liver function, sometimes enabling only limited re­
sections. In that case, a combination of parenchyma sparing resections
with locoregional treatments is desirable. Systemic treatment can be
administered preoperatively as a biological test to assess disease dy­
namics or with the aim to convert unresectable disease. In the case of
regression or stable disease on restaging imaging after 2–3 months,

resection or local treatment is recommended. Even patients progressing
on first-line chemotherapy, though responsive to the second-line, should
be considered for surgery. In the case of favourable prognostic criteria
and no concerns about technical resectability, perioperative systemic
treatment (e.g. FOLFOX) may not be required [6]. Adjuvant chemo­
therapy should be reserved for high-risk patients with an expected short
relapse-free interval, high CEA level, multiple CRLMs, or lesions _>_ 5 cm
[35].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
1. Assessment of liver function before liver resection_

The assessment of liver function before liver resection is crucial to
minimise the risk of post-hepatectomy liver failure (PHLF) [36]. Euro­
pean consensus guidelines highlight the limitations of routine CT volu­
metry assessment alone, particularly in patients with compromised liver
parenchyma (i.e. prolonged preoperative chemotherapy, steatosis or
steatohepatitis). Dynamic quantitative liver function tests, such as the
indocyanine green (ICG) clearance test and the LiMAx 13C-methacetin
breath test, can provide valuable additional information on global
liver function [36]. Also, tools such as the blood-parameter based
APRI/ALBI score can predict the risk of PHLF before operation [37]. The
use of (99m)Tc-mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy SPECT/CT and
gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI facilitates combined volume and function
assessment before liver resection [36]. Currently, no universal standard
for volumetry or FLR function assessment is available, and institutio­
nal/regional practice is guided by experience, preference and avail­
ability of modalities to evaluate the FLR.

_10.

Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
2. Surgical strategies for borderline (or initially un-)resectable CRLM_

Different strategies for advanced (bilobar, multiple) CRLM have been
proposed to overcome the limitations of an expected low-volume FLR
(Fig. 5). These should also consider functional challenges such as
impaired liver parenchyma quality. One major difference between
possible surgical option lies in the utilization of major anatomical re­
sections versus parenchymal-sparing non-anatomical resections for he­
patic tumour clearance. To date, the value of strict anatomical resection
vs. non-anatomical parenchymal-sparing hepatectomy (PSH] for CRLM

Also, although an R0 resection with a ≥1 mm margin still remains
the intended gold standard in liver resection for CRLM, more recent
studies have shown that a positive R1 status at the parenchymal resec­

(such as KRAS [mut ] vs. KRAS [wt] ) on the prognostic importance of a safety
margin between metastatic lesion border and the resection surface [40,

All these factors must be carefully evaluated during resectability
assessment and surgical planning, particularly in patients at high risk for
hepatic recurrence, where there is a significant likelihood of requiring
subsequent local treatments. Recently developed clinical risk scores can
support identification of high-risk cases [42]. Ensuring adequate resid­
ual liver parenchyma is essential in these patients to support potential
future interventions.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
3. Combined ablation and resection (CARe)_

Several groups have described the combination of hepatic resection
for CRLM supplemented by thermal ablation of deeply located or chal­
lenging lesions. Surgical thermal ablation, usually with microwave or
radiofrequency technology, is performed with intraoperative ultrasound
guidance [43,44]. Other ablative strategies at pre- or postoperative
timepoints utilize percutaneous techniques with computed or magnetic
resonance tomography-guided single- or (stereotactic) multineedle ap­
proaches [45–47].

_10.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
4. Parenchyma-sparing vessel-guided surgery (intended R1vascular)_

This strategy has been driven by the increasing knowledge around
advanced parenchymal-sparing resection techniques, intraoperative ul­
trasound, and an improved understanding of pathological differences in
subgroups of R1 resection margin status (R1 [vasc ] vs. R1 [par] ). Some groups
have demonstrated good oncological outcomes utilizing this approach as
an alternative to conventional volume-augmentation-based major
anatomical surgery [48], and the strategy has now been successfully
adopted by other units [49].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
5. Volume augmentation techniques_

Portal vein embolization (PVE) or ligation (PVL) are well-established
techniques to induce hypertrophy of the FLR before major hepatectomy,
with limitations in cirrhosis or extensive liver disease. PVE/PVL re­
directs blood flow to non-embolized segments, promoting hypertrophy
over several weeks [50,51].
The ALPPS (Associating Liver Partition and Portal vein Ligation for
Staged hepatectomy) procedure, described in 2012 by Schnitzbauer
et al., accelerates liver regeneration and reduces waiting time. ALPPS
involves two stages: liver partition and portal vein ligation in the first,
followed by resection in the second. It results in greater FLR volume
increase and higher resection rates compared to traditional two-stage
hepatectomy (TSH) and PVE, but has higher morbidity and mortality,
requiring careful patient selection [52–54].
The Scandinavian LIGRO RCT comparing ALPPS to TSH for CRLM in
patients with insufficient FLR showed superior resection rates for ALPPS
with comparable R0 rates and complications, though 90-day mortality
was 8.4 % for ALPPS vs. 6.1 % for TSH [55]. A long-term analysis
showed a median OS of 45 months vs. 27 months, but this was not
statistically significant (p = 0.057). Rectal cancer as the primary tumour
was a positive prognostic factor, while extrahepatic disease correlated
with reduced survival [56].
Simultaneous portal and hepatic vein embolization, also known as
liver venous deprivation (LVD), a newer minimally invasive technique,
induces rapid liver growth without requiring two surgeries [57]. LVD
results in greater FLR volume increase and faster kinetic growth than
PVE, offering benefits for patients with compromised liver function, as it
induces more robust hypertrophy. It shows higher resection rates and
lower incidence of post-hepatectomy liver failure (PHLF) [58,59]. The
DRAGON 1 trial, a worldwide multicentre prospective single-arm study,
reported a substantial kinetic growth rate post-LVD, achieving a 90 %
resection rate [60]. The upcoming DRAGON-2 trial will compare LVD to
PVE alone in a multicentre RCT [61].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
6. Disappearing metastases after systemic therapy_

The management of disappearing colorectal liver metastases (DLM)
presents an ongoing challenge. Systemic chemotherapy has increased
the incidence of DLM, where metastases become undetectable on im­
aging. However, this radiologic disappearance often does not indicate a
complete pathological or durable clinical response, which occurs in 20
%–40 % of patients treated with systemic chemotherapy [65]. Magnetic
resonance imaging with intravenous, hepatobiliary-specific contrast is
the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting DLM preoperatively
[66–68].
Some studies indicate that residual microscopic disease is often
found in a significant proportion of resected DLM sites, suggesting the
need for an aggressive surgical approach to reduce recurrence risk [66].
As an alternative to resection of these sites, fusion of pre-chemotherapy
MRI with post-treatment CT for image-guided percutaneous ablation
represents a potential therapeutic option [69].
In many cases, surgical resection or percutaneous ablation of the
original sites of DLM is not feasible or advisable when considering the
risk/benefit balance. For those patients, close surveillance with regular
imaging is essential, as local recurrence rates are elevated [66]. The
decision to monitor versus intervene should be tailored to the patient’s
clinical context, with consideration for the feasibility of future surgical
or ablative options [70].

**11. Minimally-invasive surgery (MIS) and oncological outcome**
**for CRLM**

Recent RCTs have highlighted the potential benefits of a minimallyinvasive approach in the resection of CRLM, particularly for short-term
perioperative outcomes. The OSLO-COMET trial from Norway

confirmed significantly fewer postoperative complications (Grades 1–2)
with laparoscopic access compared to open surgery (19 % vs. 31 %, p =
0.021). The study also found a reduced inflammatory response and
similar R0 resection margin rates [71,72]. In a secondary study of the
same cohort, there was no difference in OS at a median follow-up of 70
months [73]. However, the study was not designed to detect differences
in secondary endpoints, nor was it powered to assess non-inferiority in
survival.
Similarly, the 2019 LapOpHuva RCT from Spain reported compara­
ble benefits of laparoscopy in terms of reduced overall complications
and shorter hospital stays, with similar oncological outcomes [74]. A
subsequent patient-level data meta-analysis of these RCTs, alongside
propensity-score-matched studies, even suggested a long-term survival
benefit for laparoscopic resections over open surgeries in CRLM [75].
While these results have been critically debated, they at least suggest a
non-inferiority of MIS in terms of oncological safety. Given the results
from recent RCTs on MIS for both primary and secondary liver malig­
nancies — which not only confirm positive short-term outcomes but also
demonstrate improved quality of life, faster recovery, and quicker
initiation of adjuvant systemic therapy - a minimally invasive
approach should now be considered the new standard for patients un­
dergoing CRLM resection, provided it is technically feasible [76,77]. A
detailed publication on MIS for HPB cancers is also planned within the
ESSO core curriculum paper series.

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
12. Liver transplantation for CLRM**

Liver transplantation (LT) has recently been considered a potential
treatment for CRLM in highly selected patients with isolated, unresect­
able CRLM who respond to chemotherapy for extended periods, often
over 12 months. However, "rescue" transplants for CRLM have shown
poor outcomes. The first successful series of LT for CRLM in extensively
pre-selected patients was reported by the Oslo group in 2010 [78]. A
proof-of-concept study published in 2013 showed promising results with
a 60 % 5-year survival rate in 21 consecutive patients [79]. From this
study, the Oslo score was developed, identifying four negative predictors
of OS: maximum size _>_ 5.5 cm, progressive disease on chemotherapy,
interval from primary tumour resection to LT _<_ 24 months, and
pre-transplant carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) _>_ 80mcg/mL.
An update from the same group in 2020, including 61 patients,
showed a median follow-up of 91.6 months, with a 50 % 5-year overall
survival (OS) and a median disease-free survival of 11.8 months. Addi­
tional negative factors beyond the Oslo score included metabolic liver
tumours on PET scans _>_ 70 cm [3], primary tumours in the ascending
colon, tumour burden score of 9 or higher, and nine or more liver le­
sions. Patients with an Oslo score of 0 had a 10-year survival rate of 88.9
% [80]. Interestingly, patients with recurrence following LT frequently
develop pulmonary metastases, which however are often amenable to
surgical resection. Interestingly, several patients demonstrate prolonged
survival despite persistent pulmonary disease, even in the absence of
achieving constant, long-term disease-free state.
The strict selection criteria for patients who may benefit from LT are
still under debate. Consequently, the 2021 International HepatoPancreato-Biliary Association consensus guideline proposed a clinical
management algorithm [81]. As LT is only an option for a very small
subset of patients with unresectable CRLM, refining patient selection,
donor criteria, and understanding the biological mechanisms behind
successful LT could improve outcomes for these patients.
Different randomised trials currently compare transplantation to
chemotherapy (SECA-III study; NCT03494946; and COLT study,
NCT03803436). The most promising results comes from the TransMet
Study, a multicentre, open-label, prospective RCT conducted between
2016 and 2021 in 20 European centres. The study assigned 94 highly
selected patients to receive either LT plus chemotherapy (n = 47) or
chemotherapy alone (n = 47). After a median follow-up of 59 months,
the 5-year survival rate was 56 % in the LT group compared to 12.6 % in

the chemotherapy-only group, offering the potential to significantly
change clinical practice [82].
Given the critical shortage of deceased donor liver allografts, case
series primarily from North America [83], have demonstrated that living
donor LT may be a viable alternative for this indication. Additionally,
the RAPID (Resection and Partial Liver Transplantation with Delayed
Total Hepatectomy) technique has shown promising results, with Eu­
ropean experience reported in 2023 [84]. Another encouraging devel­
opment is the hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) technique,
which could use livers otherwise discarded for CRLM. Since these pa­
tients do not suffer from liver failure, they may tolerate lower-quality
grafts better than typical transplant patients [85].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
13. Loco-regional therapies for CRLM**

In clinical practice, alternative locoregional interventions for liver
metastases are commonly used alongside surgery. Thermal ablation
techniques, such as cryoablation and radiofrequency ablation, were
initially popular but have progressively been replaced by microwave
ablation due to its more effective and consistent energy delivery [86].
These techniques are used in various clinical settings, ranging from
curative treatments to palliative care [87].
Thermal ablation was introduced as an alternative to surgery and has
been shown to provide survival benefits over chemotherapy alone in
palliative care, and for small lesions, it can be a viable alternative to
surgery for curative intent [88]. Conversely, for larger tumours, its
oncological outcomes have traditionally been inferior to surgery [89].
The recent COLLISION trial demonstrated that thermal ablation is
non-inferior to surgery for lesions under 3 cm in size, with better safety,
leading to early trial termination [47]. For tumours over 3 cm, evidence
for ablation remains limited, although it is still considered feasible [87].
Other newer locoregional therapies, such as irreversible electropo­
ration (IRE), are emerging but lack extensive long-term data. IRE uses
high-voltage pulses to induce apoptosis without thermal heat, poten­
tially preserving biliary and vascular structures [90]. Electro­
chemotherapy (ECT), which uses electric pulses to enhance drug uptake,
showed promising results in a Phase II trial with a 75 % objective
response rate and median overall survival (OS) of 29 months, particu­
larly for smaller tumours [91].
Intravascular therapies are evolving as well. While transarterial
chemoembolization has not shown significant benefits for CRLM, its
combination with drug-eluting beads and transarterial chemosaturation
is yielding promising long-term results in unresectable cases [92].
However, conclusions are difficult due to the varied clinical scenarios
(palliative versus curative intent).
Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been effective for
palliative treatment of large metastases, with positive results in many
series, but it has not demonstrated superior long-term outcomes
compared to ablative techniques [87].
Hepatic artery infusion (HAI) therapy has been extensively studied at
Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) and has been asso­
ciated with improved survival outcomes in the adjuvant setting for pa­
tients with resected CRLM [93]. An ongoing Dutch trial is evaluating the
safety and feasibility of adjuvant HAI chemotherapy, with early results
showing minimal severe postoperative complications [94].

**14. Management of CRLM in the presence of extra-hepatic**
**disease**

Liver resection for CRLM with extrahepatic disease (EHD) remains
controversial, though selected patients may benefit, particularly those
with good response to systemic therapy and the potential for R0 resec­
tion. This is especially true for isolated lung metastases [6]. The Liver­
MetSurvey registry reported a 5-year survival rate of 44.5 % for patients
undergoing resection of both liver and lung metastases, comparable to
those with isolated liver metastases (51.5 %) [95]. Even with

unresectable lung metastases, liver resection improves survival
compared to non-surgical management (2.6 vs. 1.5 years) [96].
For patients with limited peritoneal metastases, cytoreductive sur­
gery (CRS) combined with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy
(HIPEC) may provide prolonged survival [97]. However, no RCTs sup­
port this as standard care, and the phase III PRODIGE-7 trial found no
added benefit of oxaliplatin-based HIPEC after CRS [98]. Ongoing trials
are evaluating alternative HIPEC regimens using mitomycin and
different procedures [99].

Title: Liver metastases from colorectal cancer: A joint ESSO –EAHPBA –UEMS core curriculum collaboration
Author: Carrion-Alvarez
Content:
15. Inoperable disease and palliative care**

Management of patients with inoperable CRLM focuses on systemic
therapies and locoregional treatments to control disease progression and
improve quality of life. Resection of an asymptomatic primary with
unresectable metastases offers no survival benefit and is not recom­
mended [100]. The Dutch ORCHESTRA trial (NCT01792934) is evalu­
ating the OS benefit of cytoreductive surgery alongside chemotherapy in
multiorgan mCRC, with initial data from 100 patients confirming
feasibility [26].
When disease control is unattainable, palliative care prioritizes
symptom management, including pain relief, nutritional support and
psychosocial care. Multidisciplinary team involvement is essential to
address the complex needs of these patients.

**Data sources and search strategy**
All potentially eligible publications were retrieved
from PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, and Web of Science

from database inception until July 14, 2023. The search,
employing the keywords “colorectal liver metastases”,
“surgery”, “early”, and “recurrence”, was carried out by two
investigators (YT, SFW). Supplementary File 1 included
detailed information on the search strategy. Additionally, the bibliographies of included articles and relevant
reviews were manually scrutinized to identify additional
research and explore potentially relevant studies.

**Eligibility criteria and study selection**
Subjects were eligible for inclusion if the following criteria were met: (1) Prospective or retrospective studies
including patients with CRLM who received liver resection; (2) Articles presenting ER rates categorized by a
prognostic factor; (3) Articles reporting a relative ratio
(RR) or an odds ratio (OR) (with a 95% confidence interval [CI]) or offering adequate data for RR/OR estimation;
(4) No language restrictions.
Studies were excluded according to the following criteria: (1) Articles on palliative surgery; (2) Articles without
sufficient data for analysis; (3) Experimental animal studies; (4) Reviews, commentaries, conference proceedings,
letters, case reports, editorials, and meta-analysis.
Article screening and study selection were independently performed by two reviewers (SFW, YQW).
In instances of discordance, resolution was achieved
through collaborative deliberation within the research
team, culminating in a final consensus.

**Data extraction**
The following data were extracted from each included
study, and missing data were noted: (1) first author, publication year, country, period of recruitment, study type,
patient count, follow-up period, overall recurrence rate,
ER definition, ER rate, 5-year OS in the ER group, and
inclusion/exclusion criteria (Table 1); (2) Prognostic factors, including patient characteristics (continuous variables: age, carcinoembryonic antigen [CEA], carbohydrate
antigen 19–9 [CA199], binary variables: gender), primary
tumor characteristics (binary variables: tumor differentiation [poor vs moderate/good], lymph node metastases
[LNM], tumor stage [T3-4 vs T1-2], tumor location [rectum vs colon]), liver metastases characteristics (binary
variables: number [more vs less], diameter [> 5 cm
vs ≤ 5 cm], synchronous metastases, bilobar distribution, extrahepatic metastases), and therapeutic factors
(binary variables: laparoscopic resection,simultaneous
resection, major hepatectomy,surgical margins [positive
vs negative],preoperative chemotherapy, postoperative

RRs or ORs and corresponding 95% CIs for association

Continuous variables were summarized using median
and interquartile range values, while categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages. In cases
where RR was unavailable, we either convert OR to RR or
employed the events and patients counts in both exposed
and non-exposed groups to calculate RR. By using standardized forms, two authors (YT, YQW) independently
extracted the data from each eligible study. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or discussion with the
third person (NYW).

**Risk‑of‑bias assessment**
To evaluate the risk-of-bias (RoB) at the study level, the
Quality in Prognostic Factor Studies (QUIPS) tool was
employed. This tool has six domains, with each domain
assigned a RoB rating categorized as high, moderate,
or low [38]. Studies were deemed to have low RoB if
all domains were rated as low RoB or only one domain
scored moderate RoB. Conversely, studies were classified as high RoB if at least one domain scored high RoB
or if three or more domains scored moderate RoB. The
remaining studies were attributed a moderate RoB rating.

**Statistical analysis**
The primary outcomes of the study focused on the RRs
depicting the association between ER and prognostic factors. When available, preference was given to the most
adjusted effect estimate, specifically opting for the Cox
multivariable coefficient over the univariable estimate.
Subsequently, all pooled outcomes were derived utilizing
a random-effects model (Mantel–Haenszel method). The
magnitude of the summary effects was graphically represented through forest plots.
Between-study heterogeneity was assessed utilizing the
­I [2] statistical estimate, with an ­I [2] value > 50% regarded as
severe heterogeneity [39]. Consequently, subgroup analyses were executed to identify potential sources of heterogeneity. Assessment of reporting bias was undertaken
through funnel plots and the Egger’s test, specifically for
prognostic factors identified in over 10 studies. A _P_ value
below 0.1 was deemed indicative of significant publication bias, prompting the execution of Trim and Fill analysis in such instances. Additionally, sensitivity analysis was
performed by switching to fixed-effects models to test
the robustness of the conclusions.
All statistical analyses were conducted using Review
Manager software (Version 5.4) and Stata software (version 14.1). A significant two-way _P_ value for comparison
was defined as _P_ < 0.

The grading of evidence strength for the identified associations in observational studies was based on the following criteria: Egger’s test _P_ value > 0.1, a cumulative

assigned for each of the following: LNM of the primary
tumor, the interval < 1 year from primary tumor resection to the detection of liver metastasis, preoperative
CEA > 200 ng/ml, more than one liver tumor, and largest
tumor > 5 cm [41]. The combination of RRs in three studies showed that CRS > 2 had the potential to increase the

**Reporting bias**
Reporting bias was evaluated by funnel plot and Egger’s
test. Our results comparing the ER rates between groups
with and without LNM of primary tumor revealed an
asymmetric funnel, with a _P_ value of 0.035 for the Egger’s
test (Fig. 6). By filling 4 studies using the Trim and Fill
method, the recalculated pooled RR was 1.20, 95% CI
(1.06, 1.37) (Fig. 7), which was not significantly changed
from the initial estimate (RR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.17–1.48).
Therefore, the presence of publication bias has little significant effect on the overall finding.

rated as Class IV. High-quality (Class I) evidence showed
that poor differentiation of CRC, larger and bilobar-distributed liver metastases, major hepatectomy, positive
surgical margins, and postoperative complications were
factors linked to an elevated hazard of ER. Among other

**Subgroup analyses**
Among the prognostic factors analyzed, an elevated
number of metastases was reported of having high heterogeneity ­(I [2] - 50%). Subgroup analyses were conducted,
employing diverse thresholds for defining an increased
number of metastases, categorized as multiple, > 3,
and > 4 metastases. As shown in Fig. 8, all subgroup
analyses showed significant differences in the ER rate
between cases with more and fewer metastases. Notably,
the subgroup of multiple metastases showed great heterogeneity ­(I [2] = 79%), whereas the other two groups did
not. Therefore, we found that the divergent definitions
of “multiple” across different articles constituted the primary source of heterogeneity.

**Sensitivity analyses**
We performed sensitivity analysis by switching to fixedeffects models on all variables. The results were consistent across all variables except in the case of preoperative
chemotherapy, wherein a fixed-effects model revealed an
association with diminished risk of ER (RR, 1.11; 95% CI,
1.02–1.21; ­I [2] = 58%) (Fig. S3). However, this result was
deemed unreliable and excluded.

This is the first-ever published meta-analysis summarizing prognostic factors associated with ER following LR
for CRLM. Specifically, most of the studies used a postoperative interval of 6 months to define ER, which is earlier than the ER definition for other tumors in the liver.

CRLM is more common but the prognosis is relatively
better, compared with other intrahepatic tumors. Furthermore, with the development of surgical techniques
and minimally invasive local treatment strategies, CRLM
patient is more likely to undergo re-resection and/or
ablation after recurrence, and the 5-year OS after repeat
hepatectomy is as high as 50% [46].
After pooling data from 21 studies involving 5791
patients, this meta-analysis identified ten prognostic
factors that could play a crucial role in ER across four
domains: patient-related factors, primary tumor characteristics, liver metastases attributes, and therapeutic
factors.
As patient-related factors, elevated levels of preoperative CEA and CA199 were identified as potential risk
factors for ER. However, the evidence was classified as
level II due to high heterogeneity, which was attributed
to varying cutoff values in different studies. Studies indicated that postoperative serum molecular markers had
stronger predictive potential. Even within the normal
limits, higher levels of postoperative CA199 were effective in predicting ER [15, 47, 48].
For primary tumor factors, the analysis of aggregated
RR values indicated a heightened risk of ER associated
with poor differentiation and LNM, both indicative of
a more advanced tumor stage. The impact of LNM on
ER was categorized as class II evidence due to reporting bias, but the Trim and Fill analysis indicated that the
presence of publication bias had no substantial influence on the overall findings. Besides, previous investigations have validated that individuals with LNM in
primary tumors exhibit an adverse OS and progressionfree survival (PFS) [49–51]. This reveals the significance
of pathological characteristics of primary colorectal
tumors in the prognosis assessment following LR. Particularly for metachronous liver metastases, defined as
liver metastases discovered after primary tumor surgery, these primary tumor factors may assist surgeons in
identifying patients who would derive greater benefits
from LR [52, 53].
Characteristics of liver metastases, such as increased
size, number, and bilobar distribution, have been recognized as potential risk factors associated with ER. Tumor

variables, with varying cutoff values, leading to heterogeneity across studies. However, these two variables

as the resection of three or more liver segments [59].
Indeed, the presence of more and larger, and bilobar-distributed metastases mentioned above not only represents
worse tumor behavior but also increases the probability
of occult intrahepatic spread and affects the radicality
of the treatment. Consequently, to ensure the complete
removal of all lesions, more extensive liver resection
may be performed, leaving little room for salvageability
[60]. Besides, R1 resection has been identified as a risk
factor, implying that overlooked lesions and residual
microscopic tumor cells left after surgery contribute to
ER. However, it remains uncertain whether recurrence
at the surgical margin or the emergence of new metastases are the primary contributors to ER in patients with

positive surgical margins. Severe postoperative complications could potentially extend the immunosuppression
induced by major surgeries and delay the initiation of
adjuvant chemotherapy [14].
The current study failed to demonstrate the benefit of preoperative or postoperative chemotherapy in
preventing ER. The reason is that, on the one hand,
patients with more advanced tumors and R1 resection
have a greater tendency to receive adjuvant therapy, on
the other hand, the effects of different regimens and
cycles of adjuvant treatment are combined. But a study
revealed that > 1 chemotherapy line and progression
of disease during last-line chemotherapy, were identified as independent predictors of ER, suggesting that
the response to chemotherapy was more important
than the chemotherapy itself [22]. Therefore, the cooperation between surgeons and oncologists is essential,
especially when aggressive indications are present.
In addition to individual prognostic factors, the CRS
combines tumor markers, primary tumor factors, and
liver metastasis factors and was widely adopted for the
prognosis of CRLM patients. In this study, class I evidence demonstrated that a CRS > 2 increase the risk of
ER. Furthermore, several studies have utilized multiple
prognostic factors to develop nomograms to better predict ER of CRLM [15, 19, 20]. However, the generalizability of these nomograms requires further research,
and there is an urgent need to develop a universal ER
risk prediction score.
When liver recurrence occurs, salvage resection had
the potential to extend long-term survival [22]. However, it was noteworthy that the secondary resection
rate was notably diminished in individuals with ER
compared to those experiencing late recurrence, due
to worsened condition status and potential surgical
complications [26]. Additionally, studies indicated that
the survival benefit associated with salvage resection
disappeared within the subgroup of patients exhibiting more than two risk factors for ER [29]. For these
patients, salvage treatment may accelerate disease
progression and postoperative complications, thereby
mitigating survival benefits rather than effectively controlling local recurrence. Therefore, the indications for
salvage resection in patients with ER should be strictly
controlled.
There are several limitations in this review. Initially,
all the included studies are non-randomized control
trials, introducing the possibility of confounding bias.
Moreover, the combination of various ER definitions,
ranging from 6 to 24 months, and amalgamation of
diverse cutoff values for prognostic factors contributed

**Conclusion**
This review offers a consolidated summary of the prognostic factors associated with ER subsequent to LR for
CRLM. These findings have the potential to enhance
the efficacy of surveillance strategies, refine prognostic
assessments, and guide judicious treatment decisions for
CRLM patients with high risk of ER. Additionally, it is
essential to undertake well-designed prospective investigations to examine additional prognostic factors and
develop salvage therapeutic approaches for ER of CRLM.

# A Comprehensive Prognostic Model for Colorectal Cancer Liver Metastasis Recurrence After Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy

Zhenyuan Zhou [1][†], Xin Han [2][†], Diandian Sun [1], Zhiying Liang [1], Wei Wu [3][*] and Haixing Ju [3][*]

Background: For patients with colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRLMs), it is important
to stratify patients according to the risk of recurrence. This study aimed to validate the
predictive value of some clinical, imaging, and pathology biomarkers and develop an
operational prognostic model for patients with CRLMs with neoadjuvant chemotherapy
(NACT) before the liver resection.

Methods: Patients with CRLMs accompanied with primary lesion and liver metastases
lesion resection were enrolled into this study. A nomogram based on independent risk
factors was identified by Kaplan–Meier analysis and multivariate Cox proportional hazard
analysis. The predictive ability was evaluated by receiver operating characteristic (ROC)
curves and decision curve analysis (DCA). Calibration plot were also used to explore the
consistency between prediction and reality.

Results: A total of 118 patients were enrolled into the study. Multivariable Cox analysis
found that histopathological growth patterns (HGPs) [Hazard Rate (HR) = 2.130],
radiology response (stable disease vs. partial response, HR = 2.207; progressive
disease vs. partial response, HR = 3.824), lymph node status (HR = 1.442), and age
(HR = 0.576) were independent risk factors for disease-free survival (DFS) (p < 0.05).
Corresponding nomogram was constructed on the basis of the above factors,
demonstrating that scores ranging from 5 to 11 presented better prognosis than the
scores of 0–4 (median DFS = 14.3 vs. 4.9 months, p < 0.0001). The area under ROC
curves of the model for 1-, 2-, and 3-year DFS were 0.754, 0.705, and 0.666, respectively,
and DCA confirmed that the risk model showed more clinical benefits than clinical risk
score. Calibration plot for the probability of DFS at 1 or 3 years verified an optimal
agreement between prediction and actual observation. In the course of our research,
compared with pure NACT, a higher proportion of desmoplastic HGP (dHGP) was
detected in patients treated with NACT plus cetuximab (p = 0.030), and the use of

Conclusion: Our model is concise, comprehensive, and high efficient, which may
contribute to better predicting the prognosis of patients with CRLMs with NACT before

INTRODUCTION

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third commonest malignancy,
leading to about 0.9 million deaths in 2020 globally (1). The
prognosis of colorectal cancer is closely relating to the stage; 5year survival rate of stage I is more than 90%, whereas that of
stage IV with distant metastasis is less than 14% (2).
Accumulating evidence has revealed that liver is the most
frequent site of CRC metastasis, 15%–25% of patients with
CRC having liver metastasis at initial diagnosis and another
18%–25% developing liver metastasis within 5 years of early
diagnosis (3, 4). The traditional sandwich approach of
neoadjuvant therapy–surgical excision–adjuvant chemotherapy
is considered the standard treatment for these patients, but the 5year survival rate is less than 60% (5–7). Clinical risk score (CRS)
is a mature biomarker that was used to predict the risk of
recurrence in patients with colorectal cancer liver metastasis
(CRLMs) after surgery and direct the preoperative treatment (8).
However, CRS focuses on clinical traits of tumor and pays little
attention to genetic, pathological, and imaging data of tumor. In
addition, CRS assigns one point to all risk factors, without
considering the weight of these factors. Furthermore,
chemotherapy and follow-up after surgery are an important
part of the treatment of CRLMs, but CRS does not seem to
focus on this. Therefore, we urgently need a novel,
comprehensive, and high-efficient recurrence risk prediction
model in clinical practice to guide the postoperative treatment.
For patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT)
before liver resection, the response evaluation criteria in solid
tumors (RECIST) are commonly used to estimate the curative
effect of NACT and patients’ prognosis, which relies on magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) or computerized tomography (CT) or
both (9–11). After hepatectomy, tumor regression grade (TRG),
a pathological assessment approach, is utilized to assess the
chemotherapy efficacy and outcome (12–14). Recently,
histopathological growth patterns (HGPs), new pathology
evaluation criteria, have been gradually introduced. Several
studies have shown that CRLMs are present in one of three
common HGPs referred to as desmoplastic HGP (dHGP),
replacement HGP (rHGP), and pushing HGP (pHGP) (15, 16).
dHGP presents as the metastatic cancer cells separated with
hepatocytes by a margin of fibrous tissue; but in rHGP, cancer
cells directly contact with hepatocytes and are in continuity with
liver cell; finally, pHGP is the hepatocytes that surround the
metastasis, which are pushed away and compressed (15, 17, 18).
In terms of prognosis, dHGP is the best, followed by pHGP, and

rHGP is the worst (15). Boris et al. further pointed out that
patients with non-100% dHGP at liver–tumor interface had
significantly lower survival than those with 100% dHGP (19).
Here, we investigated the value of some biomarkers to predict
the prognosis of patients with CRLMs accepting NACT before
liver resection. Then, we constructed an operational prognostic
model for predicting recurrence and stratifying patients. In
addition, we compared the purely predictive ability between
our model and CRS.

MATERIALS AND METHODS

Patients
Specimens were obtained from patients treated at the Zhejiang
Cancer Hospital from May 2009 to December 2019 diagnosed
with synchronous or metachronous CRLMs. All lesions
presented in the liver before the first chemotherapy. Patients
with insufficient basic information, without genetic test results,
non-simultaneous radical liver metastases resection, and
interventional treatment like radiofrequency ablation or
selective hepatic arterial embolization before liver resection
were excluded. Patients with extrahepatic metastases before
liver resection were excluded from the study. Patients who died
within 1 month of hepatectomy were also excluded. The
characteristics like age, gender, NACT regimen, targeted drugs,
number of metastases, diameter of maximum liver metastasis,
time of liver metastasis, invasion depth and lymph node status,
RAS and BRAF genes status (RAS gene includes KRAS and
NRAS gene), and serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels
were recorded. Follow-up was done via outpatient and telephone
visits. Regular liver and lung imaging and serum tumor marker
levels were used to monitor tumor recurrence.

Pathological Assessment of
Liver Metastases
All participants gave written informed consent. Liver resection
specimens were fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin, and
stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). The slices were
independently and blindly evaluated by two experienced
pathologists. In case of inconsistent conclusions, the HGPs and
TRG results were reviewed by two experts. Positive surgical
margins (R1/R2) were defined as residual tumor cells present
at or within 1 cm of the resection margins, such patients were
excluded. According to the National Comprehensive Cancer
Network (NCCN) guideline–recommended evaluation criteria

(20–22), TRGs 0 to 2 indicate major response, whereas TRG 3
indicates minor response. HGP analyses were done as the report
quoted from the study by Boris et al. (19), with 100% dHGP at
tumor–liver interface indicating dHGP and any proportion of
rHGP or pHGP at tumor–liver interface indicating non-dHGP.

Evaluation Criterion of Other Biomarkers
Radiologic evaluation was done on the basis of RECIST version
1.1 (23). We evaluated all measurable lesions and pathological
lymph nodes by CT or MRI. A sum of the diameters of longest
tumor lesions and short axis for lymph nodes of all target lesions
was calculated as baseline sum diameters. The response
evaluation of NACT was implemented within 2 weeks after
treatment. Next, the sum of shrunken or enlarged diameters of
target lesions was determined. Finally, the therapeutic response
of the target lesions was obtained by comparing the guideline,
including complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable
disease (SD), and progressive disease (PD).
CRS for each patient was determined the report from Fong
et al. (8); each of the following criteria assigned 1 point: serum
CEA level > 200 ng/ml, diameter of the largest hepatic tumor
- 5 cm, number of metastases > 1, and positive lymph nodes and
disease-free interval from primary lesion excision to liver
metastases < 12 months. The first three clinical data were
obtained from the first visit. The total score for each patient
was then calculated; scores of 0 to 2 indicated low risk, whereas
scores of 3 to 5 indicated high risk.

Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were performed using R and SPSS version 26.0.
Ordinal and unordered categorical variables were compared using
the Chi-square or Fisher exact test, as appropriate. Survival was
evaluated by Kaplan–Meier (K-M) analysis and compared using the
log-rank or Breslow test. Disease-free survival (DFS) is defined as
the time from liver and primary tumor resection to tumor
recurrence. Cox proportional hazard analysis was used to identify
independent DFS prognostic factors. Multivariate analysis was
completed for factors with p ≤ 0.200 after univariate analysis;
p ≤ 0.05 was statistical significance. The Cox regression
consequence was adjusted for confounding bias, checking for
multicollinearity, and setting up disordered multi-category
variable as dummy variable.

RESULTS

Clinical Patient Characteristics
From May 2009 to December 2019, a total of 118 patients with
CRLMs who underwent NACT before liver resection were
recruited into the study after meeting inclusion criteria. The
cohort’s characteristics were summarized on Table 1. Most
patients were male (66.9%), and 66.9% were < 60 when they
first came to the hospital due to colorectal cancer. In addition,
87.3% were in stage T3 or T4, 70.3% have positive lymph nodes,
and 63.6% of patients had multiple metastases. Of these, 24.6%
had resected lesions with maximum diameters of >5 cm, and

22% were metachronous metastases. Positive serum CEA levels
of > 5ng/ml were detected in 72.9% of patients. RAS or BRAF
mutations were observed in 50% of patients. With regard to
NACT, 69.5% of patients received oxaliplatin-based regimens,
16.1% received irinotecan-based regimens, 17 patients received
more than one regimen, and more than half of patients did not
receive targeted drugs (61.9%).
According to radiology response, we found that none of patient
achieved CR after several cycles of chemotherapy and more than
half got SD (50.8%), whereas PD occurred in 14.4% of the patients.
Patients with larger tumors tended to have a better regression.
Only one (3.4%) patient with > 5-cm lesion progressed, whereas 16
(18.0%) patients with a < 5-cm metastasis progressed after
chemotherapy (p = 0.001). Moreover, CRS low-risk and highrisk patients were approximately evenly distributed (46.6%
vs. 53.4%).
In terms of pathological assessment, 19 (16.1%) patients had a
dHGP. Considering the TRG score, patients with TRG 3
accounted for the vast majority (71.2%). Meanwhile, a high
correlation between HGPs and TRG was observed, which
found that non-dHGP accounted for 95.2% of TRG 3 (p <
0.001). Negative lymph node was more common in dHGP
(52.6% vs. 25.3%, p = 0.017). Moreover, all patients with PD
were non-dHGP (p = 0.009), and 91% of primary tumor had
penetrated the muscularis propria in non-dHGP (p = 0.024).

Disease-Free Survival and
Prognostic Factors
The median follow-up was 7.2 months, and the 1-, 2-, and 3-year
DFS rates after liver resection were 38.0%, 18.5%, and 13.5%,
respectively. A total of 39 (33.1%) patients had not recurrence at
the last follow-up.
Results of univariate and multivariate analysis of DFS
prognostic factors are shown in Table 2. Univariate analysis
showed that HGPs (p = 0.014, Figure 1A) and radiology
response (p = 0.001, Figure 1B) correlated with prognosis. In
the multivariate one, HGPs was confirmed as an independent
prognostic factor for DFS (HR = 2.130, p = 0.048). The median
DFS of patients with dHGP was 14 months [interquartile range
(IQR): 3–26 months] compared with 7 months (IQR: 6–8
months) in patients with non-dHGP. Additional independent
prognostic factors were age (HR = 0.576, p = 0.024), lymph node
status (HR = 1.442, p = 0.015), and radiology response (SD vs.
PR, HR = 2.207, p = 0.007; PD vs. PR, HR = 3.842, p < 0.001).
Radiology response was set as a dummy variable in data
processing. No multicollinearity was found.

The DFS nomogram showed in Figure 2A based on biomarkers
including age, lymph node status, radiology response, and HGPs.

then performed a K-M analysis and found that patients’ outcome
was improved significantly in score ≥5. Therefore, we classified
patients with a score of 5 to 11 as low risk and those with a score
of 0 to 4 as high risk. We found DFS to be markedly higher in

Cetuximab Led to a Low rHGP Proportion
In our study, we found a strong correlation between HGPs and
cetuximab. rHGP was rare in patients who used cetuximab in
NACT before lesion excision. We added a cohort (27 patients)
that did not accept NACT before liver resection (control group);
thereby, the study cohort was extended to 145 patients. Then,
HGP was obtained from every patient in light of the latest
international consensus guidelines (15): Taking 50% as the
cutoff value, rHGP < 50% rim of liver–tumor interface is nonrHGP and rHGP ≥ 50% rim of liver–tumor interface is rHGP. In
univariate analysis, compared with control group, patients who
accepted pure NACT without targeted drugs had a lower
proportion of rHGP (51.9% vs. 38.4%, p = 0.225, Table 3). The
addition of bevacizumab or cetuximab plus chemotherapy

chemotherapy as the one and only independent factor

was observed with bevacizumab (38.4% vs. 30.4%, p = 0.491).
Transforming patients who treated with pure NACT as control
group, cetuximab plus chemotherapy still significantly reduced
rHGP incidence (38.4% vs. 13.6%, p = 0.030). In addition,
cetuximab plus chemotherapy was not an independent factor
(HR = 0.267, p =0.055). After ruled out patients who had a more
than 50% pHGP or mixture HGP in non-rHGP subgroup, a
separate multivariate analysis was calculated. In this further
analysis, we also discovered low rHGPs level in cetuximab plus
chemotherapy subgroup [HR = 0.176, p = 0.025 (vs. non-NACT
patients); HR = 0.256, p = 0.049 (vs. pure NACT patients)].

DISCUSSION

The novel recurrence risk prediction model has shown great
effectiveness for patients who received NACT before radical
primary tumor and liver metastases resection. All the
indicators of this model are from the routine preoperative and
postoperative examinations of patients, which does not require
additional unnecessary medical examinations and will not
increase the economic burden of patients. Patient who
underwent chemotherapy would evaluate the suitability for
surgery using imaging tests before lesions resection, so it is
very convenient to acquire every patient’s radiology response.
Lymph node status and HGPs assessment are available to
perform via pathological evaluations on surgical specimens.
Compared with other examinations, postoperative pathological
examination can more directly reflect the characteristics and the
response to preoperative chemotherapy of the tumor and
may provide guidance for the selection of postoperative
chemotherapy regimens.

CRS system, a basis for the formulation of treatment
strategies, provides reliable stratification of patients and is now
widely used in clinical practice (24–26). Previous studies have
shown no difference in DFS between patients in the low-CRS
group who underwent direct surgery and those who received
NACT before surgery, but patients in the high-CRS group who
received NACT pre-operation had significantly better DFS than
those who underwent direct surgery (27). Furthermore, the
NCCN guidelines have recommended CRS as the standard
stratification for the patients with CRLMs to determine
whether patients receive preoperative chemotherapy (20, 21).
In clinical practice, there are more patients with high CRS.
However, a part of low-CRS patients who have some high-risk
factors such as local progression of the primary lesion, the large
metastases, or hepatic vascular invasion will also receive NACT.
Our model was designed for patients with high CRS and some
low CRS who received NACT before surgery. Five criteria of CRS
are from the preoperative, focusing on the preoperative
personalized treatment of patients with CRLMs. Our model
includes both preoperative and postoperative indicators, which
can more accurately predict patients’ DFS and provide a
reference for clinicians to formulate personalized follow-up
and treatment plans for patients after surgery. Nomogram has
the inherent advantage of providing different coefficient for
different risk factors. Our model and CRS can be used together
to demonstrate the precision treatment of cancer, which is in line
with the direction of modern cancer treatment. Our model
outperforms CRS if it only predicts the prognosis of patients
receiving NACT before surgery.

study; this is an emerging biomarker and is also the focus of this
study. It is also being studied by more and more oncologist and

Title: Clinical Usefulness of Postoperative Serum Carcinoembryonic Antigen in Patients with Colorectal Cancer with Liver Metastases
Author: Yoshino
Content:
ABSTRACT
Background. Colorectal cancer with liver metastasis
(CLM) has high postoperative recurrence rates; therefore,
optimizing perioperative treatment is imperative. Postoperative carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) can aid in
detecting minimal residual disease in colon cancer following curative resection. This study aimed to identify the
potential role of serum CEA following liver resection in
patients with CLM.
Methods. This retrospective study was conducted at the

Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most common
types of cancer worldwide. [1] There were an estimated 18.1
million new cancer cases and 9.6 million cancer deaths in
2018. [1] In addition, the number of CRC deaths in Japan is
continuously increasing, with the number of CRC deaths
exceeding 50,000 annually. [2] Although the prognosis of
patients with metastatic CRC is especially poor, the prognosis has improved in recent years because of
developments and advancements in diagnostic techniques
and treatment methods, including surgery and chemotherapy. [3] In particular, as 25% of patients with CRC have liver
metastases, [4] a treatment strategy for colorectal cancer with
liver metastasis (CLM) is necessary to improve the prognosis of CRC. Resection of CLM contributes to the

radical resection of CLM was reportedly 35–58%). [5][–][7]
However, the recurrence rate after resection of CLM is also
high, ranging from 52 to 72%, with residual liver recurrence accounting for more than 25% of cases. [8][–][10]
Therefore, biomarkers for predicting postoperative recurrence may be useful for optimizing perioperative
treatments for CLM. Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was
first reported in 1965 by Gold et al. as a common fetal
antigen for CRC. [11] CEA is a well-known, low-cost, biological tumor marker for CRC. [12] It is widely used in CRC
follow-up for detecting postoperative recurrence as well as
one of the predictors of the response to chemotherapy,
recommended by several clinical treatment guidelines for
CRC. [12][,][13] Several reports have indicated that the preoperative CEA level is useful as a predictor of prognosis and
recurrence after curative resection of CRC. [14][,][15] On the
other hand, Konishi et al. reported that the postoperative
CEA level is more important than the preoperative CEA
level for predicting recurrence after curative surgery and
prognosis in CRC. [16] However, it remains unclear whether
the postoperative CEA level is useful for predicting
recurrence in patients with CLM after curative surgery. [17]
In the present study, we comprehensively investigated the
usefulness of perioperative CEA levels in patients with
CLM, which has a higher recurrence rate than CRC.

PATIENTS AND METHODS

Patients

Patients who underwent R0 resection for both primary
tumors and CLM at the Cancer Institute Hospital of the
Japanese Foundation for Cancer Research from 2004 to
2018 were enrolled retrospectively. Patients who had
extrahepatic metastases, had unmeasured CEA levels, and
were treated with repeat metastasectomy for CLM were
excluded from this study. This study was approved by the
Institutional Review Board of the Japanese Foundation for
Cancer Research in Tokyo, Japan (registry number
2020-1263). The protocol was described on the hospital
website, and the participants were provided with the
opportunity to opt out; therefore, no additional consent was
required from the patients. All methods were performed in
accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Study Endpoints

To assess the value of CEA as a predictor of recurrence
after resection of CLM, we analyzed the association
between perioperative CEA levels and characteristics of
recurrence after resection of CLM. We collected data on

the characteristics of the primary tumor and liver metastases, perioperative chemotherapy, recurrence, and
survival, as well as the preoperative and postoperative CEA
levels, which were defined as CEA levels measured within
8 weeks before and after perioperative chemotherapy, 8
weeks before liver resection, and 8–12 weeks after liver
resection. The CEA level at time of recurrence was also
measured.

We explored the possible roles of perioperative CEA
levels in patients with CLM who were treated with curative
surgery.
Postoperative CEA is considered to be useful for the
prediction of recurrence in patients with CRC as it was
independently associated with disease-free survival (DFS)

can detect recurrence more sensitively than preoperative
CEA, which has been considered important for predicting
recurrence in CRC. In contrast, there are few reports on the
prediction of recurrence in CLM. Generally, predictive
factors for recurrence and survival in patients after resection of CLM include high preoperative CEA levels as well
as: (1) liver metastases factors: number of liver metastases,
tumor diameter, and histology (poorly differentiated,
mucinous), positive vascular invasion, and positive hilar
lymph nodes; (2) primary site factors: number of positive
regional lymph nodes and histology; (3) factors after
resection of liver metastases: positive margins and resection marginal distance; and (4) background factors: old age,
preoperative distant metastases positivity, concurrent disease, and disease-free period \ 1 year. [21][–][26] However, the
role of postoperative CEA is still unclear. Okazaki et al.
investigated the usefulness of perioperative CEA level in
CLM and reported that postoperative CEA level [ 5 ng/ml
was an independent predictor of recurrence; however,
abnormal preoperative CEA level was not a predictor of
recurrence after liver resection of CLM. [17] One of the reasons is that an elevated preoperative CEA level can often
normalize after resection of the CLM. On the other hand, in
this study, the number of CLM ([ 5) was significantly
higher in the postoperative CEA level[5 ng/ml group and
was an independent predictor of recurrence on multivariate
