They observed improved resection rates in the resection +RFA group compared to resection alone group (15.1% vs. 8.5%; P= 0.071) (54). ## 3 Therapies with curative intent 3.1 Ablation +/- systemic chemotherapy Percutaneous thermal ablation is a tumor-destructive technique and is based on exposing the tumor cells to a targeted temperature of > 60 [0] C or < -40 [0] C. Ablation can be accomplished through thermal techniques such as radiofrequency, microwave, cryoablation, laser ablation, and focused ultrasound ablation. The irreversible electroporation (IRE), a nonthermal ablation technique utilizes an electrical field to induce tumor death without damaging the tissue protein architecture of vessels and the bile-ducts (55). Either thermal or non-thermal, ablation techniques have the advantages of being minimally invasive and less morbid than surgical resection and can be delivered as an out-patient treatment. The open or percutaneous approach to thermal ablation has been studied in the literature. Puijk et al., reported significantly improving liver tumor PFS following percutaneous ablation (2010-2013: 37.7%; 2014-2017: 69%; 2018-2021: 86.3%; P< 0.0001) whereas the PFS was stable following open ablations (20102013: 87.1%; 2014-2017: 92.7%; 2018-2021: 90.2%; P= 0.12) (56). The complications were less severe in percutaneous rather than open approach (2010-2013: P=0.69; 2014-2017: P= 0.129; 20182021: P= 0.02) (56). The tissue damage secondary to ablation is low when compared to surgical resection, which is the most important requisite in patients with underlying liver disease or those who already had extensive liver resection (55). RFA is a well-studied and most widely used ablative modality in colorectal metastases. The monopolar or bipolar radiofrequency ablation (RFA) systems produce ionic oscillation by a highfrequency alternating current resulting in frictional heating and tissue damage (57). The level of thermal tissue damage varies depending on the achieved temperature. For instance, a 50-55 [0] C for a period of 4-6 minutes induces irreversible cellular damage, 60100 [0] C leads to irreversible coagulation of the cells and 100-110 [0] C results in vaporization and carbonization of tissue (58). The 1, 3, 5,10-year survival rates of CRLM following RFA are 98%, 69%, 48%, and 18% in a study by Solbiati et al. (59). Local tumor progression (LTP) after RFA, seen in 2-60% of cases, is an important factor to consider while ablating the CRLM. There are many factors that attribute to LTP including tumor size, tumor number, ablation zonal geometry, ablative margin, extrahepatic disease, location adjacent to large vessels and subcapsular tumors (60, 61). Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is usually recommended in patients with ≤ 3-5 metastases of size ≤ 3-3.5 cm, not involving bile ducts or large vessels (≥3 mm), and not located centrally (62, 63). Tumor size is critical in selecting patients for RFA as the commercially available devices can deliver the ablation to about 4-5 cm in one session and the studies reported high success rates of RFA in tumors ≤ 3-4 cm. In a study by Nielsen et al., the local recurrence after ablation was reported in 9%, 26.5%, and 45% of metastases measuring 0-3 cm, 3-5 cm and > 5 cm respectively (64). Compared to surgical resection, RFA has a lower complication rate [Frontiers in Oncology](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology) 06 [frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org) Vulasala et al. [10.3389/fonc.2023.963966](https://doi.org/10.3389/fonc.2023.963966) (9.5%) and minimal risk of death (10, 65). However, it cannot replace surgical resection, especially in tumors > 3 cm size (57). The number of CRLM is also an important criterion when selecting the patients for RFA. Solitary CRLM is associated with high tumor control and survival rates. Kim et al. reported the 5-year survival and disease-free survival rates as 51% and 34% respectively in patients with solitary CRLM of size < 3 cm (66). Similarly, Gillams et al. studied the 5-year survival rate of solitary CRLM of size 2.3 cm to be 54% with a median survival of 63 months (67). Wang et al. studied the emphasis of ablative and tumor margins and reported that the risk of LTP decreases by 46% for every 5-mm increase in ablative margin size and increases by 22% with every 5 mm increase in tumor size (68). The tumor abutting large vessels causes convective heat loss termed as “heat-sink effect”, hence preventing heat accumulation in the tumor (63). A study by Elias et al. reported that 23% of CRLM, close to the large vessels, recured compared to 3% of CRLM located away from the vessels (69). In such situations, percutaneous balloon occlusion of large vessels during RFA has demonstrated improved tumor progression rates (62). Van Tilborg et al. studied that the centrally located CRLM recur more often compared to peripheral CRLM (21.4% vs. 6.5%; P= 0.009) (10). Although no major complications were noticed, approximately 45% of patients had minor complications such as abdominal pain, fever with malaise, nausea, vomiting and elevated serum bilirubin levels (73). Pathak et al. reviewed various studies on RFA and MWA and reported that the local recurrence rates of CRLM after RFA and MWA to be ranging from 10-36% and 5-13% respectively (71). IRE is a non-thermal ablative technique that induces high-voltage electrical pulse waves between the electrodes (75). It is a safer ablation method in case of tumors close to the vascular or biliary structures due to the absence of the heat-sink effect (76, 77). The COLDFIRE-1 is a Phase-I study that demonstrated CRLM death and necrosis when exposed to IRE (78). COLDFIRE-2 is a Phase-II study including the patients with ≤ 5 cm CRLM, and it reported a 1-year PFS of 68%. Around 74% of the patients achieved local tumor control after the repeat IRE procedure (79). In a study by Schicho et al., 67% of patients achieved tumor control after the first IRE and 96% after reintervention (80). Complications during IRE were reported to be observed in 40% of patients, with the most severe being arrhythmias, portal vein thrombosis, and biliary obstruction (79). Laser ablation uses micrometer optical fiber to produce heat by transmitting infrared light. The optical fiber is connected to a generator or diode made of neodymium: yttrium aluminum garnet (ND: YAG), which emits a precise wavelength. The size of the fiber, the wavelength used, conduction and penetration of surrounding tissue, and the power and duration of the ablation are the factors that affect the size of the ablation zone (81). The lesions located within 1 cm of the main biliary duct, untreatable coagulopathy, and ascites interposed along the path of the applicator are considered contraindications to the thermal ablation (82). Patients may experience side effects after the procedure including pain, and post-ablation syndrome. Pain is self-limiting and depends on the size of the ablation zone. Postablation syndrome presents with flu-like illness with low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting and malaise, and can be managed symptomatically (72). Complications of the ablation procedure can be secondary to the injury to surrounding structures or the ablation itself, such as pneumothorax, intraperitoneal bleeding, hemothorax, portal vein thrombosis, gastrointestinal tract perforation, strictures, bile duct injury, cholecystitis, and liver abscess (72, 82). The EORTC-CLOCC trial was a phase-II clinical trial that studied the efficacy of systemic chemotherapy with or without RFA in 119 patients diagnosed with unresectable CRLM (83). The trial randomized patients to receive systemic treatment alone or in combination with RFA. A significant improvement in OS and PFS was reported in the combined modality group rather than the systemic chemotherapy alone group (83). Improved OS in the combined modality group compared to the systemic treatment alone group (HR: 0.58; P=0.01) was observed. The 3-, 5- and 8year OS rates were 56.9%, 43.1%, and 35.9% respectively in the combined modality group, and 55.2%, 30.3%, and 8.9% respectively in the systemic chemotherapy alone group. The median OS was 45.6 months in the combined modality group and 40.5 months in the systemic chemotherapy alone group. There was a prolonged PFS in the combined modality group (HR: 0.57; P=0.05). The liver as the first site of recurrence was noticed in 46.7% of the combined modality group and 78% of the systemic chemotherapy alone group (83). Another study, the ARF2003, included 52 unresectable CRLM treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy and RFA. The study reported complete hepatic response in 75% of patients at their 3-month follow-up. The OS at 1-, and 5-years was 94% and 43% respectively, whereas PFS was 46% and 19% (84). Furthermore, another study reported that the combination of RFA and systemic chemotherapy has shown improved 3-year progression-free survival in comparison to systemic chemotherapy alone (27.6% vs. 10.6%; hazard ratio= 0.63; CI: 0.42-0.95; P=0.025) (85). SBRT delivers the radiation to a specified region of interest with millimetric accuracy and reduces the irradiation to surrounding parenchyma. Unlike RFA and MWA, the SBRT is the better technique to access the perihilar, periampullary, or subcapsular lesions (86). SBRT can be considered, in combination with surgical resection, for oligometastatic liver disease that failed local therapies (87). Candidates with ≤ 5 CRLM involving <700 cc of the liver, an expected survival of > 3 months, curative extrahepatic disease, no chemotherapy received before two weeks of planned SBRT, and ≤ 2 Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status are suitable for SBRT (87). A radiotherapy dose of ≥ 100-110 Gy can achieve local tumor control in 80-90% of the patients, while a higher dose may be required in case of larger tumors to attain similar outcomes (86–88). A study by Petrelli et al. included 656 patients and reported that the SBRT provides an overall survival of 67% and 57% and local tumor control of 67% and 59% at 1 and 2 years, respectively (89, 90). Compared to RFA, SBRT achieves greater 2year local tumor control (84% vs. 60%); however, both the techniques had similar OS rates (91). The OLIVER trial compares the SBRT and chemotherapy alone and may provide further validations for its application (NCT03296839). 3.2 Radiation segmentectomy Radiation segmentectomy (RS) delivers a very high ablative radiation dose (>190 Gray) confined to one or two liver segments, thus limiting the radiation-related complications (92, 93). The dose is based on the available literature for RS in patients with HCC which demonstrated a correlation between the level of tumor necrosis and the radiation exposure (93). The major intent of RS is to achieve cure in patients with CRLM, similar to the ablation or ablative external radiation therapy (94, 95). Diagnostic and therapeutic advancements through proper patient selection, imaging and radiation dosimetry allowed transition of lobar salvage to segmental curative radioembolization, especially in patients with features including (i) solitary tumor of size ≤ 5 cm (ii) primary or secondary liver tumor without other organ involvement and (iii) a tumor that can be targeted angiographically such that ≤ 2 liver segments receive the ablative dose of radiation (92, 96). Kurilova et al. observed that the RS of ≤ 3 hepatic segments can provide a 2-year tumor control rate of 83% in patients with limited therapeutic options and limited metastatic disease (Table 5) (102). They also reported that the tumor progression occurred in 21% of their study population which is similar to the study by Padia et al. (103) who reported tumor progression in 28% (102). In a study by Meiers et al, the authors included 10 patients of which 7 patients had inoperable CRLM confined to ≤ 2 liver segments (104). The procedure was unsuccessful in one among 7 patients due to attenuated hepatic vasculature. Of the remaining 6 patients with CRLM, four had a complete response or stable disease at their follow-up evaluation ranging from 1-14 months. Two of six patients had progressive disease after 7- and 18-months period. There were no reported adverse events. The mean PFS was 7.1 months for the entire cohort (92, 104). Although RS has a promising role in the treatment of HCC that cannot be resected or ablated, the literature on CRLM is limited (93, 105–107). In addition, as the most of the CRLM patients may have been pre-treated with chemotherapeutic regimens, the hepatic vasculature can be altered limiting the ability to perform the super-selective RS. Furthermore, the hypovascular nature of CRLM results in difficulty targeting the tumor. Based on the available data, RS appears to provide local tumor control with acceptable toxicity in patients with CRLM. Further studies on patient selection and tumor response are required to emphasize the application of RS in patients with CRLM. 3.3 Firstline chemotherapy plus TARE Combined therapy with radioembolization and systemic chemotherapy has been studied in the literature. Transarterial therapies utilize the advantage of dual blood supply of the liver and hence the cytotoxic agents infused through the hepatic artery selectively target tumor over normal cells. In addition, the first pass metabolism of the chemotherapeutic agents can be bypassed in the intra-arterial therapies. TACE is a catheter-based infusion of one or more chemotherapeutic medications and embolizing material into the hepatic artery. Embolizing material can be either temporary or permanent. The former includes collagen, gelatin sponge and degradable starch microspheres, while the latter include polyvinyl alcohol particles. Lipiodol has both the vaso-occlusive effect and the ability to enhance the effect of cytotoxic agents (117). TACE procedure was first introduced by Yamada et al. in late 1970s (118). In general, TACE is indicated as a second-line modality of treatment in patients who are refractory to systemic chemotherapy or in inoperable CRLM (119). Conventional TACE (cTACE) represents the injection of lipiodol + chemotherapy and embolizing agents. Recently, the drug-eluting beads are being used as embolic materials termed as DEB-TACE. The efficacy of cTACE and DEB-TACE have been extensively studied in the management of CRLM. 4.1.1 Conventional TACE The chemotherapeutic regimen and embolic materials are variable in the published studies. Albert et al. studied the efficacy of TACE with doxorubicin, cisplatin, mitomycin C and lipiodol mixture followed by embolization material- polyvinyl alcohol particles, in 245 unresectable CRLM in 121 patients who were refractory to systemic chemotherapy (120). Median survival from initial CRLM diagnosis and TACE was 27 months and 9 months, respectively. The study described that the OS was better with TACE after first- or second-line systemic chemotherapy than after three to five lines of systemic chemotherapy (11-12 months vs. 6 months; P= 0.03) (120). Vogl et al. studied 463 patients with unresectable CRLM (117). Patients were divided into three groups with each receiving mitomycin C alone, mitomycin C plus gemcitabine, or mitomycin C plus irinotecan and followed by embolization with starch microspheres. The authors reported that 1-year and 2-year survival rates were 62% and 28% respectively with no significant difference among the patient groups (117). The initial results of a Phase II clinical trial comprising 20 patients reported an 80% response rate with reduction of contrast enhancement of treated tumors following treatment with irinotecan drug-eluting beads [37]. Similarly, Aliberti et al. reported 78% tumor response rate at three months in a phase II study comprising 82 patients (130). All the patients had at least two failed systemic chemotherapy lines. The study also described the OS and PFS as 25 months and 8 months respectively (130). Martin et al. studied the efficacy of DEBIRI in patients refractory to oxaliplatin- and irinotecan-based systemic chemotherapy. The study concluded that DEBIRI was safe with minimal complications and 75% tumor response rate (131). This promising treatment for patients with colorectal metastases merits further study both as a salvage agent and potentially in combination with systemic chemotherapy. Fiorentini et al. compared the efficacy of FOLFIRI and DEBIRI-TACE (132). Median OS was longer for DEBIRI-TACE group (22 vs. 15 months). In addition, DEBIRITACE group had better quality of life (8 vs. 3 months) and objective tumor response (69% vs. 20%) (132). However, the study was limited by the omission of bevacizumab, oxaliplatin, panitumumab or cetuximab in the standard care of treatment (132). Martin et al. overcame this limitation by comparing DEBIRI plus systemic FOLFOX and bevacizumab with systemic FOLFOX plus bevacizumab alone (133). The study observed a significantly greater response rate in DEBIRI-FOLFOX arm compared to FOLFOX/bevacizumab arm at the end of 2 months (78% vs. 54%) and 6 months (76% vs. 60%) (133). Th significant tumor downsizing was observed in DEBIRI-FOLFOX arm than the comparison arm (35% vs. 16%) (133). The median PFS of 15.3 months was reported in DEBIRI-FOLFOX arm and 7.6 months in FOLFOX/bevacizumab arm (133). Nonetheless, the study by Martin et al. did not demonstrate improvement in OS compared to cTACE studies that excluded systemic chemotherapy (Table 8) (133). Recently, a systematic review by Akinwande et al. included 13 studies comprising a total of 850 patients (135). The weighted average PFS and OS were 8.1 months and 16.8 months respectively (135). Narsinh et al. described the importance of hepatopulmonary shunting as a prognostic indicator of survival in their study of 606 patients who underwent Y90-TARE for CRLM. They reported that increased liver shunt fraction (LSF) indicated worse prognosis in CRLM. The LSF > 10% was associated with reduced survival rate compared to LSF < 10% (6.9 months vs. 10 months; HR: 1.60; P<0.001) (153). Dendy et al. studied the survival predictive biomarkers in patients who underwent Y90-TARE for CRLM (140). They described that low tumor burden, sufficient calculated Y90 dose, increased albumin, and low ECOG score are the pre-interventional biomarkers which indicate favorable outcome (140). Likewise, after the procedure, decreased tumor burden, reduced tumor glycolysis, radiological tumor response and reduced expression of surviving, p53, Bcl-2 are indicative of favorable outcome (140). Irrespective of timing of biomarker evaluation, the increased HMGB1(High mobility group box 1), nucleosome expression, increased carcinoembryonic antigen, CA 19-9, CYFRA 21-1 (Cytokeratin 19 fragment), lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate transaminase, choline esterase, gamma glutamyl transferase, alkaline phosphatase, amylase are the indicators of unfavorable response (140). Usually, Y90 radioembolization is safe with minor complications and post-embolization syndrome. Gastric ulceration (<5%), portal hypertension (<1%), radiation induced liver fibrosis (<4%), pancreatitis (<1%), biloma (<1%), cholecystitis (<1%), abscess formation (<1%), and radiation induced pneumonitis (<1%) are the few of reported complications secondary to radioembolization (154). The post-embolization syndrome can be observed in 50% of the patients within 2 weeks of the procedure. In contrast to post-embolic syndrome, it rarely requires patient hospitalization. ## 5 Other hepatic metastases Very few studies have been performed on the interventional management of non-CRLM. In liver metastases secondary to gastric tumors, RFA is proven beneficial only in cases of single metastases limited to a single lobe and without extrahepatic disease (155). Combined systemic chemotherapy is also recommended in addition to RFA to prolong the OS (155). RFA in liver metastases secondary to breast cancer has also been studied to improve OS; however, the extrahepatic metastases (P=0.013) and age >60 years (P=0.025) are considered worse prognostic factors for OS (156). MWA has equal benefits to RFA and can be an alternate therapy in patients with liver metastases originating from ovarian, pancreatic, esophageal, and neuroendocrine neoplasms (157). Further broad studies are required for more data on patient outcomes and efficacy. Arterial [Frontiers in Oncology](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology) 15 [frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org) Vulasala et al. [10.3389/fonc.2023.963966](https://doi.org/10.3389/fonc.2023.963966) interventions such as TACE with raltitrexed eluting beads are studied to be safe and efficient in hepatic metastases due to gastric adenocarcinoma (158). In contrast to CRLM, the focus of arterial interventions in neuroendocrine liver metastases (NELM) is on the controlling the endocrine secretions (159). NELM are hypervascular tumors, and the studies show that the embolization alone has good efficacy on patient outcomes, unlike colorectal metastases, requiring chemotherapeutic embolization (160, 161). Elf et al. demonstrated that the NELM has optimal response rates to embolization therapies compared to SIRT (162). Other than CRLM and NELM, the literature is limited to other hepatic metastases. Saxena et al. studied that SIRT in chemoresistant hepatic metastases due to breast cancer has improved 24-month survival rates to 39% (163). Despite this, prospective trials on optimal patient selection and survival data are necessary for further validation. ## 6 Future directions The combination of immunotherapy and targeted ablation is a new revolutionizing concept based on enhanced exposure of the tumor antigen. Ablated and dead tumor cells release tumor antigens into the bloodstream which augments the T-cell response, enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapy (164). Both the proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, and the anti-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-10, get elevated after the ablation procedure. So far, cryoablation has been proven to induce a higher (4.6 fold) IL10 release compared to heat-based techniques such as RFA (1,7 fold) and MWA (1.2 fold) (165, 166). Shi et al. reported that the PDL1-PD-1 axis inhibits the T-cell response; hence monoclonal antibodies against the PD-1 are used to increase the feasibility of an anti-tumor immune response (167). The stronger T-cell response, robust anti-tumor immunity, and improved survival rates were observed in mice after combining anti-PD1 monoclonal antibodies with an ablation procedure (167). Likely, the TACE procedure triggers tissue hypoxia and the release of vascular endothelial growth factor, which could be used as the target for bevacizumab and tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are responsible for tumor nurture and metastasization by inducing the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and vascular disruption. Current studies are targeting TGF-beta signaling pathway, which is responsible for the EMT. The collagen triple helix repeat containing 1 (CTHRC1) is secreted by the colorectal cancer cells, stabilizing the TGF-beta signaling and activation. Studies show that the monoclonal antibodies against CTHRC1 combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade have led to the shrinkage of CRLM (168). Similarly, strategies targeting the TAMs reprogramming, depletion, and inhibition were studied (169). However, stronger validations are not yet provided due to the heterogenous behavior of the TAMs. ## 7 Conclusion Tremendous evolution has occurred over the last two decades in the locoregional interventional therapies for CRLM. Surgical resection is the curative treatment for patients with CRLM. In case of unresectable tumors or non-surgical candidates, evaluation for ablation is recommended. Transarterial therapies are indicated as a salvage therapy and Y90-TARE is the FDA approved therapy for CRLM. DEBIRI-TACE or cTACE is considered in patients with progressive liver disease after Y90-TARE. ## Author contributions SV, PS, SK, NO and SPK have contributed equally to this work. liver metastasis (CLM), a population with good prognosis,
have been treated with upfront surgery, some patients have

Author: Kobayashi
Content:
Colorectal liver metastases · Liver resection ·
Perioperative chemotherapy · Tumor markers · Prognosis

In the field of colorectal cancer, the multidisciplinary
treatment approach has been proposed for the use of systemic therapies, including various effective chemotherapy
regimens or radiation therapy, to improve the clinical outcomes of patients undergoing surgery. [1][,][2] An aggressive
surgical approach is reportedly associated with improved
survival for patients with colorectal liver metastasis (CLM).

Prognostic Impact of Tumor Markers … 7339

Various perioperative and surgical strategies have been
reported to increase the resectability and curability of
CLM. [3][–][6] However, indications for preoperative chemotherapy (neoadjuvant chemotherapy [NAC]) for patients with
CLM remain controversial. [7][,][8] The oncologic backgrounds
of patients with CLM are considerably heterogeneous in
terms of tumor size, number and location of metastases,
somatic mutations, presence of extrahepatic metastases,
and characteristics of the primary colorectal cancer. The
administration of unnecessary chemotherapy (duration or
indications) is associated with an increased risk of liver
injury, and clinical practice must balance the risks and
benefits of chemotherapy to maximize the opportunity to
cure CLM. [9][–][11]
To establish eligible NAC for CLMs, the resectability of
CLM had been classified as “resectable,” “borderline-resectable” (BR), or “initially unresectable” using an oncologic
perspective. [12][,][13] Since 2010, we have defined BR-CLM as
tumor with a diameter of 5 cm greater, four or more tumors,
or concomitant resectable extrahepatic metastases. Hepatectomy after six cycles of NAC has been the treatment
strategy. [14][,][15] As a result of this strategy, favorable overall
survival (OS) has been achieved. [15] In contrast, resectable
CLMs, stratified by fewer than four tumors, a tumor diameter less than 5 cm, and absence of extrahepatic metastasis
have a relatively good prognosis without NAC. However,
some patients experience early recurrence, resulting in a
poor prognosis for resectable CLMs. Although our resection criteria considered only tumor burden and the presence
of extrahepatic metastases, there are other valuable biologic
factors that influence prognosis, such as tumor markers and
gene mutations. [13][,][16]
This study aimed to assess the long-term outcomes of our
surgical strategy for CLMs and to identify biologic prognostic factors for patients with resectable CLMs, which is
a limited population stratified by the number and size of
tumors treated by liver resection without NAC.

Title: Prognostic Impact of Tumor Markers (CEA and CA19‑9) on Patients with Resectable Colorectal Liver Metastases Stratified by Tumor Number and Size: Potentially Valuable Biologic Markers for Preoperative Treatment
Author: Kobayashi
Content:
_Patient Selection_

This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients who underwent liver resection for initial CLMs
at the Cancer Institute Hospital between January, 2010 and
December, 2020. We used the available data to analyze baseline characteristics and both short- and long-term patient
outcomes. This study was approved by the Institutional
Review Board of the Cancer Institute Hospital (registration
no. 2022-GB-164). The requirement for written informed
consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the
study.

_Definition of Resectability_

Treatment-related decisions were collectively made at a
multidisciplinary conference on liver tumors. Resectability
of CLM was established by reviewing the computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging findings obtained
at the initial visit from an oncologic perspective. Initially,
unresectable CLMs were defined as those with insufficient
future liver remnant volume (< 30%) and/or the presence of
unresectable extrahepatic metastases. Technically, resectable
CLM was divided into “resectable” (with <4 CLMs, tumor
diameter <5 cm, or no extrahepatic metastasis) and “borderline resectable (BR)’’ (with ≥4 CLMs, tumor diameter
≥5cm, or resectable extrahepatic metastasis) (Fig. S1).

_Treatment Strategies and Definition_

The patients with resectable CLMs underwent upfront
liver resection without preoperative NAC. Preoperative
chemotherapy was routinely administered to all patients with
a diagnosis of either BR or unresectable CLMs. Patients
with unresectable CLMs were initially treated with chemotherapy, and the possibility of conversion was periodically
discussed at a multidisciplinary liver tumor conference. Conversion surgery was indicated when chemotherapy allowed
for complete resection (one- or two-stage disease with or
without portal vein embolization) of all CLMs with negative
margins and adequate remnant liver volume. [5] Liver function parameters also were evaluated preoperatively using
the indocyanine green retention test and 99mTc-Galactosyl
sialyl albumin scintigraphy.
Parenchyma-sparing liver resection is the standard procedure for CLMs, even for patients with initially unresectable
CLMs. Major liver resections were performed only when
CLMs were close to the major Glissonean pedicles and in
cases for which R0 resection with the parenchymal-sparing
approach was not feasible. Contrast-enhanced intraoperative
ultrasound was performed in all cases to confirm the tumor
detected by preoperative imaging and search for new occult
lesions. [17] Liver transection was always performed using the
Pringle maneuver, with clamp-crushing in open liver resection and clamp-crushing and/or CUSA in laparoscopic liver
resection. No additional radiologic ablation was performed
in any patient.
Adjuvant chemotherapy was selectively administered
to patients who underwent simultaneous resection of
advanced primary disease and to those evaluated necessarily by a multidisciplinary team. The advanced primary
disease was defined as greater than stage III or stage II with
high-risk factors such as T4, poor differentiation (G3/4),
vascular invasion (venous/lymphatic), perineural invasion,
obstruction/perforation, and fewer than 12 analyzed lymph
nodes. For example, the multidisciplinary team discussed

and administered adjuvant chemotherapy to patients with
metachronous CLMs who had not yet received adjuvant
chemotherapy after resection of the primary disease.
Postoperative complications were graded using the Clavien–Dindo classification. [18] Liver sections/segments were
classified based on the Brisbane 2000 Terminology of Liver
Anatomy and Resections. [19]

_Statistical Analysis_

Categorical variables were expressed as _n_ (%) and compared using Fisher’s exact test or the chi-square test, as
appropriate. Continuous variables were expressed as median
(interquartile range) and compared using Wilcoxon’s ranksum test (two groups) or the Kruskal–Wallis test (three
groups).
The cutoff values for carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) were determined
using the univariable Cox regression model. The value
with the lowest _p_ value (2nd highest hazard ratio [HR])
was regarded as the optimal critical point of classification
(Table S1a and b). Factors with a _p_ value lower than 0.050
in univariable analyses were entered into the Cox regression
model for multivariate analysis. Both HR and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for each factor.
Survival curves were constructed using the Kaplan–Meier
method and compared using the log-rank test. Overall survival was defined as the interval between the date of liver
resection and death. Time to surgical failure (TSF) was
defined as the time until unresectable relapse or death.
Recurrence-free survival (RFS) was defined as the interval between resection and recurrence. Recurrence was
diagnosed on the basis of imaging as well as clinical and/

or histopathologic findings. Mortality cases were excluded
based on RFS and TSF. A _p_ value lower than 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance. Statistical analyses were performed using JMP Pro 15.0.0 software (SAS
Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

Title: Prognostic Impact of Tumor Markers (CEA and CA19‑9) on Patients with Resectable Colorectal Liver Metastases Stratified by Tumor Number and Size: Potentially Valuable Biologic Markers for Preoperative Treatment
Author: Kobayashi
Content:
For the patients with resectable CLMs stratified by tumor
number and size, high TM levels (CEA and CA19-9) had a
strong prognostic impact. The patients with high TM levels
had earlier recurrence and a significantly worse prognosis
than those with low TM levels. In addition, only the patients
in the high-TM group who received adjuvant chemotherapy
had a significantly better prognosis than those who did not.
Many studies have analyzed the impact of perioperative
treatment of CLMs, but the results remain controversial.
In a study of all resectable simultaneous liver metastases,
NAC did not independently affect the prognosis. [20] Another
study showed that patients with high-risk predictive factors,
including TM level and tumor size, benefited from NAC. [21]
To maximize clinical outcomes, oncologic stratification of CLMs and identification of risk factors have been
reported. In the traditional clinical risk score, the significant prognostic factors for patients undergoing hepatectomy for CLM are tumor size, number of nodules, primary

lymph node status, disease-free interval, and preoperative
CEA levels. [22] Another clinical risk score established on
the basis of a nationwide Japanese survey included similar
clinical factors. [23] Additionally, a recent international multicenter study confirmed that the inclusion of RAS status
further improves the predictive power of the conventional
risk score to estimate the survival outcomes of patients
undergoing surgery for CLM. [24] However, the prognostic
impact of RAS status is not evident in all CLMs, especially in the low tumor burden group, for whom no prognostic difference has been observed between patients with
and without RAS mutations. [25] Similarly, in the current
study, RAS status did not affect prognosis in the population stratified by tumor number and size.
Several reports have indicated that the TM levels of CEA
are significant prognostic factors for patients undergoing
hepatectomy for CLM, [13][,][14][,][20] and CA19-9 also is reported
to be a useful predictor of oligometastatic CLM. [26] However,
due to insufficient stratification of the background (tumor
size or number), maximum tumor size also was an independent prognostic factor in a previous study. [26]
Compared with previous reports, our criteria for resectable CLMs were limited in terms of the size and number of
tumors. Therefore, the finding that high TM levels remain a
prognostic factor has a greater impact. In the current study,
the reason for the combination of CEA and CA19-9 in the
definition of the high-TM group was the determination of
previous studies that CEA and CA19-9 are important prognostic factors that cannot be ignored. Although CA19-9 had
a higher hazard ratio than CEA (Table S1), it is considered
more useful in clinical practice to combine CA19-9 and
CEA than to use either of them alone.
In the current study, the recurrence pattern did not differ between the high- and low-TM groups. Similarly, the
resection rates for the first recurrence after the initial liver
resection did not differ significantly. However, the rate of
early recurrence within 1 year was significantly higher and
the TSF was poor in the high-TM group. In other words, high

7346 K. Kobayashi et al.

TM may be a predictor of early recurrence and subsequent
surgical failure.
Currently, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network
guidelines (version 2.2020) for colon and rectal cancers recommend surgery with postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy
or preoperative chemotherapy combined with surgery and
postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy (perioperative chemotherapy and surgery) for patients with resectable CLMs. In
contrast, randomized controlled trials have shown significant
or marginal improvements in RFS in patients who underwent
CLM resection, perioperative chemotherapy, or postoperative chemotherapy. However, no differences in OS were
observed. [27][,][28] One reason for this is the insufficient stratification of the CLMs. Tumor burden, consisting of the number
and size of tumors and proven to be a major prognostic factor in CLMs, is associated with RFS and OS. Therefore, it
should be considered a strong confounder.
In our study, when limited tumor burden and high TM
levels were analyzed, the patients who received adjuvant
chemotherapy exhibited a significantly longer OS than those
who did not. These patients have the potential to benefit
from chemotherapy, which is expected to further prolong
their prognosis jdm when combined with preoperative
chemotherapy. High TM levels in resectable CRLs should
be included in the biologic BR criteria, and a prospective
multicenter clinical trial of NAC for these patients is needed.
Our study had several limitations. First, it was a singlecenter, retrospective study. Nevertheless, it should be noted
that the number of patients in each group was relatively
large for a single center, with 89 patients in the high-TM
group and 220 patients in the low-TM group. These were
relatively pure populations stratified by tumor number and
size, excluding BR-CLMs and initially unresectable CLMs.
Second, historical bias may have influenced the findings
because the multidisciplinary treatment strategy changed
over time. However, the population with resectable CLMs
was a relatively uniform group that did not receive preoperative treatment, and the impact of the historical bias was
likely infinitesimal.
Third, indications for adjuvant chemotherapy were not
established during the study period. Normally, adjuvant
chemotherapy is indicated for patients who undergo simultaneous resection of an advanced primary disease (above
stages III and II with high-risk factors). However, it was not
performed for all the patients with simultaneous primary
cancer and CLM, whereas it was performed for some of the
patients with metachronous cancer who had not yet received
adjuvant chemotherapy after resection of the primary disease (e.g., synchronous [71%] vs metachronous [35%]; _p_
< 0.0001). The multidisciplinary team decided to administer adjuvant chemotherapy, although it will be necessary to
establish a uniform indication for adjuvant chemotherapy in
the future. The multidisciplinary team decided to administer

adjuvant chemotherapy, although it will be necessary to
establish a uniform indication for adjuvant chemotherapy
in the future.
Additionally, in this study, high TM levels, no adjuvant
chemotherapy, and poor prognosis for older adults also were
poor prognostic factors. Pre- and postoperative chemotherapy are expected to improve the outcomes of patients who
have CLM with high TM levels. However, in older patients,
the indication for perioperative chemotherapy should be
carefully considered based on the tolerability for chemotherapy. Notably, adjuvant chemotherapy was a prognostic
factor for the entire cohort, which differs from the results
of previous reports. In the subgroup analysis, the presence
or absence of adjuvant chemotherapy showed a prognostic
difference only in the high-TM group and did not contribute
to prognosis in the low-TM group. Adjuvant chemotherapy
did not contribute to prognosis in the low-TM group because
this study cohort consisted of only patients with resectable
colorectal liver metastases. In particular, the low-TM group
had a relatively good prognosis, with an 81% 5-year OS rate
and a 44% recurrence rate, suggesting a small additional
benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy.
High TM levels (CA19-9 and CEA) had a prognostic
impact for the patients with resectable CLMs stratified
by tumor number and size. Perioperative chemotherapy is
expected to improve long-term outcomes for patients with
CLM and high TM levels.

Title: The Future Liver Remnant: Definition, Evaluation, and Management
Author: Dixon
Content:
The limits of hepatic surgery are constantly expanding.
With improvements in anesthetic techniques, deeper
understanding of hepatic anatomy, and refinements to surgical technique, the boundaries of what is safely possible
to accomplish in the operating room continue to widen.
Furthermore, the indications for a major hepatectomy
have expanded. Liver resections are considered not only
for primary liver malignancies such as hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma but also for metastatic
disease such as colorectal and neuroendocrine hepatic
metastases, among others. This trend has resulted in tremendous benefits to patients. For example, in the case of
colorectal cancer, liver metastases are the most common
site of metastatic disease. Approximately 25% of patients
will develop synchronous liver metastases while up to
50% will develop metachronous liver metastases. [1,2]
Colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) had a historically
poor overall survival. Patients with unresectable liver
metastases have a 5- year overall survival as low as 5.3%. [3]
As hepatic surgery has become safer and more widely
available, liver resections have become a common component of treatment for CRLM, resulting in dramatically
increased 5- year overall survival of up to 58%. [4]
When considering patients for liver resection, both
technical and biological factors need to be taken into
account. [5] Biological factors include the extent of intrahepatic and extrahepatic disease as well as disease- free
interval, tumor histology, and tumor mutational status.
Significant progression of metastatic disease during treatment with optimal preoperative chemotherapy, for

example, should give the surgeon pause before entertaining a major hepatectomy, as this is indicative of a more
aggressive tumor biology. Important technical factors
include the ability to achieve an R0 resection margin and
a reasonable anticipation that the following criteria be
met: (1) the anticipated ability to preserve at least 2 contiguous liver segments; (2) maintenance of adequate vascular inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage; and (3) the
ability to preserve adequate future liver remnant (FLR)
volume. The accurate prediction of the FLR based on volumetric analysis of cross- sectional imaging has become a
crucial component to liver surgery. Furthermore, the ability to manipulate the volume of the liver using portal
venous embolization (PVE) in order to push patients from
an unresectable volume to a resectable status has helped
broaden the application of a major hepatectomy. When a
PVE has been performed, the ability of the FLR to adequately function based on the appropriate regenerative

Author: Dixon
Content:
Matthew Dixon, MD, Division of Surgical Oncology, Department of

Email: mdixon2@ pennstatehealth. psu. edu

response after PVE in patients with marginal FLR volume is also an important consideration when evaluating
patients for resection. This review considers the optimal
volume of the FLR and analyzes the techniques of augmenting this volume as well as various growth parameters to assess adequate growth of the FLR. In cases when
the FLR has not adequately grown despite optimal technique, we review additional measures that can be undertaken to attempt to improve growth in the FLR prior to a
major hepatectomy.

_Calculation of the FLR_
Accurate calculations of the FLR prior to planned liver
resections rely on high- quality cross- sectional imaging to
accurately delineate both the tumors themselves as well
as the anatomic structures within the liver, such as the
inflow vasculature (portal vein and hepatic artery
branches) and the hepatic veins. This is ideally done with
either a computed tomography (CT) scan with images in
the precontrast, arterial, and venous phases, or an magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enhanced with intravenous (IV) contrast such as gadoxetate disodium (Eovist [®] ).
There are 2 accepted techniques for estimating and
computing volumes for the FLR. The first method calculates the FLR as a proportion of the nontumor- bearing
liver:
TLVMeasured = VTotal Liver _−_ VTumor
FLRMeasured = LRV/TLVMeasured _×_ 100%
The measured total liver volume (TLVMeasured) is computed by first calculating the volume of the entire liver
(VTotal Liver) on cross- sectional imaging. This is followed
by measuring the volume of each individual tumor within
the liver (VTumor). Once TLVMeasured is calculated, it is
then used to calculate the FLR volumes. First, the FLR
volume is measured on cross- sectional imaging (liver
remnant volume, LRV) and the FLRMeasured is calculated
as a percentage of the nontumor- containing TLV. While
theoretically this may give the most accurate measurement of FLR volume, disadvantages of this method
include errors in measurement due to partial volume
effect and respiratory phase changes, the tedious work of
measuring all tumor volumes in cases with multiple liver
metastases, as well as high inter- observer variability. [6]
The second method is known as the standardized
future liver remnant (FLRStandard). In an effort to estimate
the hepatic metabolic demands for individual patients,
this method was developed to estimate appropriate TLV
based on patient characteristics in combination with a
measure of LRV measured on CT. [6,7] Vauthey et al examined the relationship between body surface area (BSA)
and liver size, and determined the presence of a linear

The standardized total liver volume (TLVStandard) is therefore estimated as a function of BSA, rather than being
measured as a function of the nontumor- containing liver
parenchyma volume on cross- sectional imaging. Similar
to the calculation of the FLRMeasured, the FLRStandard is
calculated by first measuring on cross- sectional imaging
the LRV and the FLRStandard is calculated based on the
TLVStandard rather than the TLVMeasured. This allows one
to be more nuanced in determination of the FLR by standardizing it to BSA as a way to estimate liver function,
and improves the ability to compare the FLR across different individuals, based on their height and weight. This
has, therefore, emerged as the preferred method of determining the FLR. For this reason, any mention of FLR in
the remainder of this review can be assumed to represent
FLRStandard.

_Defining the Optimal FLR_
Consideration of the postoperative function of the FLR is
important for all patients undergoing a major hepatectomy, which is defined as the removal of at least 3 segments of the liver. Three important considerations should
be made when preoperatively defining whether or not the
FLR is optimized. The first, and perhaps the best studied,
is the FLR volume, expressed as a percentage of the standardized liver volume. Two other parameters can be considered in patients who have undergone PVE in an effort
to induce hypertrophy in the FLR: the degree of hypertrophy of the FLR after PVE, and the kinetic growth rate
(KGR) after PVE. A summary of these parameters can be
found in Table 1, and management strategies are summarized in Figures 1 and 2.

Title: The Future Liver Remnant: Definition, Evaluation, and Management
Author: Dixon
Content:
Summary for evaluation and management of the future liver remnant in patients with colorectal liver metastases that are
resectable with a major hepatectomy. ALPPS indicates associating liver partition and portal vein occlusion for staged hepatectomy;
DOH, degree of hypertrophy; FLRStandard, standardized future liver remnant; KGR, kinetic growth rate. [6,8–11]

The FLR volume can be estimated using 1 of the 2
techniques outlined above. Historically, extensive liver
resections were associated with increased risk of liver
failure and postoperative mortality. Volume cutoffs in a
variety of circumstances have been established in an
effort to reduce the chance of posthepatectomy liver failure. In a retrospective study, Kishi et al looked at a series
of patients undergoing an extended right hepatectomy. [13]
Patients who did undergo a liver volumetric analysis on
CT scans were organized into categories based on the size
of their FLR: ≤20%, 20%-30%, or >30%. Among patients
who had an FLR of ≤20%, the incidence of posthepatectomy liver failure was 34%, while the incidence of death
from liver failure was 11%. This was significantly worse
compared to the patients who had an FLR of 20%-30%,
where the rates of posthepatectomy liver failure and death
from liver failure were 10% ( _P_ < .001) and 3% ( _P_ = .038),

respectively. In patients who had an FLR of >30%, the
incidence of posthepatectomy liver failure and death
from liver failure was 15% ( _P_ = .010) and 2% ( _P_ = .021),
respectively. There was no statistically significant difference in the posthepatectomy liver failure and death from
liver failure rates between the latter 2 groups. Furthermore,
on multivariate analysis in this study, body mass index
(BMI) of 25 mg/m [2], need for intraoperative blood transfusion, and an FLR of ≤20% were independent predictors
of posthepatectomy liver failure. When the FLR was
<20%, the odds ratio for posthepatectomy liver failure
was 3.18 (95% CI 1.34-7.54). [13] Importantly, the administration of preoperative chemotherapy was a statistically
significant predictor of posthepatectomy liver failure on
the univariate analysis, but not on the multivariate
analysis.

Title: The Future Liver Remnant: Definition, Evaluation, and Management
Author: Dixon
Content:
Summary for evaluation and management of the future liver remnant in patients with a primary hepatic malignancy.
ALPPS indicates associating liver partition and portal vein occlusion for staged hepatectomy; C- P, Child- Pugh Classification; DOH,
degree of hypertrophy; FLRStandard, standardized future liver remnant; KGR, kinetic growth rate; PVE, portal vein embolization. [6,8–12]

The FLR volume required to reduce the risk of posthepatectomy liver failure depends primarily on the quality of underlying liver tissue. Often patients with
colorectal liver metastases have undergone preoperative
systemic chemotherapy, which can have varying adverse
effects on the underlying liver tissue. For example,
patients who have had chemotherapy regimens utilizing
oxaliplatin, such as FOLFOX, can develop sinusoidal
obstruction syndrome (“blue liver”). In patients who have
had chemotherapy regimens that utilize irinotecan, the
liver can develop steatohepatitis (“yellow liver”). [14] Both
of these chemotherapeutic agents have a negative effect
on the function of the underlying hepatic parenchyma and
must be taken into account when considering a hepatectomy, such that a higher FLR volume may be more desirable. In a retrospective study, Shindoh et al examined 194
patients who underwent an extended right hepatectomy

after receiving preoperative chemotherapy. [15] All patients
in the study had an FLR greater than 20%, and were
grouped according to whether their FLR was less than or
greater than 30%. Each cohort was defined as having no
preoperative chemotherapy, short- course chemotherapy
(≤12 weeks), or long- course chemotherapy (>12 weeks).
In patients who had an FLR ≤30% but did not have any
preoperative chemotherapy, no patient experienced posthepatectomy liver failure. In patients who had an FLR
<30%, 5.1% of patients undergoing short- course chemotherapy developed posthepatectomy liver failure. This
was not statistically significant over baseline patients.
However, 16.3% of patients undergoing long- course chemotherapy experienced posthepatectomy liver failure
with an FLR <30% (vs short- course chemotherapy, _P_ =
.006). In terms of death from liver failure, 1.3% of
patients who had short- course chemotherapy and 2.3% of

280 _The American Surgeon 87(2)_

patients who had long- course chemotherapy died from
complications from liver failure compared to no deaths in
the >30% FLR group. Furthermore, there were no cases
of posthepatectomy liver failure in patients who had no
chemotherapy or short- course chemotherapy. In patients
who had long- course chemotherapy with an FLR >30%,
10% of patients experienced liver failure ( _P_ = .15). The
authors of this study concluded that in patients who had
long- course chemotherapy and subsequently underwent
an extended right hepatectomy, there is an increased risk
of posthepatectomy liver failure, but ensuring an FLR
>30% reduces the rate of posthepatectomy liver
failure. [15]
Patients with fibrosis and cirrhosis represent another
group of patients that warrant discussion. In these
patients, an FLR cutoff of 40% has generally been
accepted as the minimum FLR value [16,17] with some
authors advocating for an even higher ideal residual volume. [18] When chronic liver disease and cirrhosis are present, there is a temptation to dichotomize patients as
having cirrhosis or not. Instead, chronic liver disease
should be regarded as a disease spectrum. Clinical judgment as well as use of clinical scoring systems such as the
Child- Pugh classification and the model for end- stage
liver disease (MELD) score are important factors in evaluating patients with underlying cirrhosis for liver resection. For example, a patient with Child’s A cirrhosis and a
low MELD score who has a hepatocellular carcinoma
(HCC) outside of the Milan criteria for transplantation [19]
that is otherwise resectable with a partial hepatectomy
may tolerate this procedure well with a low risk of liver
failure and death. However, if signs of portal hypertension are present, or the patient has ascites, abnormal
serum bilirubin, or elevated prothrombin time, [18] the
patient will tolerate hepatic parenchymal loss very poorly
and even a limited partial hepatectomy may result in liver
failure and death.
The first of 2 parameters to consider in patients who
have undergone a PVE looks at the amount of growth of
the FLR. This is defined as the degree of hypertrophy by
Ribero et al, who examined the relationship between FLR
before PVE and the degree of hypertrophy measured after
PVE. [8] Patients were dichotomized into having an FLR
≤20% or >20%. Through a sensitivity analysis of the
receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) curve, an
optimal cutoff value of 5% was determined. Among
patients who had an FLR <20% with a degree of hypertrophy of <5%, all experienced posthepatectomy liver
failure. Among patients who had an FLR >20%, 11%
experienced posthepatectomy liver dysfunction. In
patients with a degree of hypertrophy <5%, 83% experienced posthepatectomy liver dysfunction, while in
patients with a degree of hypertrophy >5%, only 9%
experienced posthepatectomy liver dysfunction ( _P_ <

.001). When patients had an FLR ≤20% and a degree of
hypertrophy <5%, this combination of factors had a sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 94% in predicting posthepatectomy liver failure. [8]
The second parameter in patients who have undergone
PVE looks at the rate of growth of the FLR over time.
This is defined as the kinetic growth rate or KGR by
Shindoh et al. [9] It is important to note, however, that this
rate of growth over time is not uniform as there seems to
be an initial rapid hypertrophy phase in the first weeks
following PVE, which is followed by a plateau phase
characterized by a much slower rate of increase in the
size of the FLR volume. [8] Therefore, the KGR expresses
the degree of hypertrophy averaged over the number of
weeks since PVE. Shindoh et al determined, through a
sensitivity analysis, that a KGR of 2% per week provided
the optimal balance between sensitivity and specificity.
When the KGR was less than 2% per week, the sensitivity was 100% and specificity 71% for predicting posthepatectomy liver failure. When this was applied to their
cohort, the authors found that no patient experienced posthepatectomy liver failure or death from liver failure
when their KGR was >2% per week. If, however, the
KGR was <2% per week, 21.6% of patients experienced
posthepatectomy liver failure ( _P_ = .0001 vs KGR >2%
per week) and 8.1% of patients experienced death from
liver failure ( _P_ = .04 vs KGR >2% per week). The KGR
of 2% per week also proved to be useful in patients who
had an FLR of 20%-30%, where all patients who had a
KGR >2% avoided posthepatectomy liver failure, while
22.6% of patients who had a KGR <2% experienced posthepatectomy liver failure. KGR, therefore, has emerged
as an important predictor of posthepatectomy liver failure
when patients have a KGR <2%. [9]

_Embolization Techniques_
PVE was first described by Kinoshita et al, when they
devised it as a countermeasure to the prevalence of tumor
thrombi within the portal vein with hepatocellular carcinoma, such that the PVE would block the tumor thrombus from continuing to grow. [20] In their original series of
21 patients, they noted a hypertrophy of the remaining
liver with PVE and hypothesized that this may be clinically useful. Makuuchi et al reported their experience
with introducing routine PVE into practice for patients
with cholangiocarcinoma and found no major side effects
from the PVE, and this led to an atrophy of the diseased
lobe with a hypertrophy of the contralateral lobe. [12] Today,
PVE has been extended from cholangiocarcinoma and
HCC to any major hepatectomy where the FLR is found
to be small in size and induction of hypertrophy of the
FLR is desired. This technique is so effective that at 4

_Dixon et al_ 281

weeks after PVE, 85% of patients will undergo the
planned hepatectomy. [21]
There are 3 general approaches described for performing PVE: transileocolic, transhepatic, and transsplenic. The transileocolic approach involves
performing a mini- laparotomy and accessing the portal
vein typically through a branch of the ileocolic vein. [21]
This approach has largely been replaced by the transhepatic approach as this technique avoids the need for
general anesthesia, laparotomy, and risk of postoperative complications [12,21] ; however, it can still be used
when interventional radiologic support is not available.
The transhepatic approach involves percutaneously
accessing branches of the portal vein directly and performing the embolization under venographic guidance.
Transhepatic PVE can be performed by either accessing
the ipsilateral or contralateral portal system from the
side that is to be embolized. Accessing the ipsilateral
side is an attractive option as this avoids instrumentation of the FLR. However, this technique can be technically challenging as the sharp angulation between the
right anterior and posterior pedicles requires the use of
a reverse curved catheter. This can also result in nontarget embolization from displacement of embolization
materials on removal of the catheter. Performing a contralateral transhepatic PVE involves accessing a portal
venous branch within the FLR, which is technically
easier; however this theoretically risks injury to the
FLR by causing vascular injury or risking portal vein
thrombus in the FLR. A meta- analysis by Abdulkhir et
al, however, found no difference in complication rates
between these 2 percutaneous approaches. [21]
A newer approach to PVE is via transsplenic access. [22,23]
This is performed with vascular access into the portal venous
system by direct puncture of the splenic vein through the
splenic parenchyma. This method eliminates the risk of
tumor seeding and nontarget embolization of ipsilateral
access while allowing easy accessibility of the intra- hepatic
portal venous vasculature, offered by contralateral access of
the portal vein through the FLR, without the risk of injuring
the FLR. Procedures via transsplenic access were historically seen as higher risk for bleeding complications, with
some authors reporting bleeding complications as high as
31% in early studies. [24] However, this method of access has
become more accepted, with newer studies demonstrating
88.9% technical success for PVE via transsplenic access
while only reporting 3.8% rate of major complications, and
7.4% for minor complications. [22] A major reason that the
newer studies are demonstrating a significant reduction of
bleeding complications associated with transsplenic access
is due to the use ultrasound guidance during initial access.
Ultrasound guidance allows for targeted access of an intraparenchymal splenic vein branch and also allows visual confirmation of intravascular location of the needle tip, reducing

the number of punctures compared to fluoroscopic
access. [25–27] Effective embolization of the parenchymal
access tract is critical and can reduce the risk of bleeding
complications associated with transsplenic access.
Transsplenic tract embolization has been described using a
variety of materials, including gelatin sponges, coils,
Amplatzer [TM] plugs, and glue, which can be used alone or in
combination. [22–28] These technical advancements have made
PVE via transsplenic access a viable alternative to traditional transhepatic access.
In their original manuscript first describing PVE,
Kinoshita et al used several different embolic agents, including a gelatin sponge cut into 2- mm pieces, a mixture of
thrombin with 50% glucose, and a mixture of fibrin with
Lipiodol. [20] Today, there are several embolic materials available for PVE. Two of the most frequently used agents are
gelfoam and cyanoacrylate. Gelfoam is commonly combined with thrombin and urografin to produce an effective
embolus. This produces an occlusion to small outflow vessels as well; however, a significant disadvantage associated
with gelfoam is that there is frequent recanalization of the
portal vein. [21,29] Cyanoacrylate is often combined with lipiodol during embolization and this leads to reliable hypertrophy of the FLR with effective embolization of the diseased
liver that rarely is recanalized. Cyanoacrylate produces a
90% increase in FLR volume after 30 days compared with a
35% increase in volume after 43 days when gelfoam is
used. [21] A disadvantage of cyanoacrylate, however, is that it
does produce an inflammatory reaction with peribiliary
fibrosis, [21,30,31] which can make subsequent hepatic mobilization and resection more difficult. Other embolic materials
include polyvinyl alcohol, which minimizes the amount of
inflammation and when combined with metal coils produces
a durable portal vein occlusion. However, it does cause
peripheral fibrosis and necrosis and can also cause severe
pain. Furthermore, the risk of damage to the liver parenchyma and bile ducts can potentially increase the risk of subsequent cancers. [21,32] No single agent has been proven to be
consistently superior to another.
The 2 absolute contraindications to PVE are (1)
patients who already have an adequate FLR and can
therefore proceed directly to surgery, and (2) tumor
invasion of the ipsilateral portal vein. Portal hypertension is considered a relative contraindication to performing PVE. For patients with mild subclinical portal
hypertension (10-15 mm Hg), PVE is not always contraindicated. However, PVE may increase PV pressure
and worsen the clinical symptoms associated with portal hypertension. [33]
Overall, PVE is well tolerated by patients. Minor complications are common and these can include abdominal discomfort or pain in 19% of cases, fever in 23%, and nausea or
vomiting in 2.4% of cases. Overflow of embolized material
and coil displacement occur in 0.2% and 0.1% of cases,

282 _The American Surgeon 87(2)_

respectively. Major complications are rare: liver abscess in
0.3% of cases, cholangitis in 0.2%, main or FLR portal vein
thrombus in 0.2%, subcapsular hematoma in 0.2%, portal
hypertension in 0.1%, and septic necrosis from hepatic
artery injury in 0.1%. [21]
In addition to PVE, selective internal radiation therapy (SIRT), also referred to as Y-90 radioembolization, may have the potential for FLR hypertrophy.
Y-90 radioembolization is an established therapy for
locally advanced liver tumors, in which microspheres
loaded with Yttrium 90, a β-emitting isotope, are
delivered intra- arterially directly to the affected portion of the liver. [34] It has been shown to induce the
atrophy- hypertrophy complex, resulting in an atrophy
of the treated lobe and a hypertrophy of the untreated
lobe, [35] which could have the potential of local tumor
control while inducing a hypertrophy of the FLR. [36] A
systematic review of the literature on this topic demonstrated that 27%-47% FLR hypertrophy was seen after
Y-90 radioembolization; however, the rate of hypertrophy is slower than seen with PVE and may take several
months. [36] This may therefore limit the applicability of
Y-90 in inducing hypertrophy of the FLR, but may be
useful in cases where treatment response to the primary tumor is more desirable than an increase in FLR
volume.
In cases of metastatic disease to the liver where
there is a bilobar distribution of disease, a 2- stage
hepatectomy may be employed where the patient will
proceed to the operating room first to have the FLR
cleared from disease through nonanatomic resections,
followed at a later date by a complete resection of the
side with more tumor involvement (this usually
involves a right hepatectomy). [37] At the initial operation to clear the FLR of disease, a right portal vein
ligation can be performed in the operating room, which
obviates the need for an IR procedure and leads to a
reliable occlusion of the right portal vein to induce
hypertrophy of the FLR.

_Managing Inadequate FLR Growth After PVE_
Inadequate volume of growth, degree of hypertrophy, or
KGR of the FLR after PVE can be a challenging problem
to manage. Both a sense of urgency to intervene and treat
the disease coupled with managing the increased risks of
posthepatectomy complications and liver failure can be
daunting for the surgeon and the care team. Fortunately
there are some established techniques to assist in this difficult circumstance.
In patients where an extended right hepatectomy is
planned to remove segment 4 in addition to segments
5-8, volume increases in segments 2 and 3 are most
desired, as these will be the segments responsible for

most of the posthepatectomy physiologic function of
the liver. If there is inadequate growth of the left lobe
after a right PVE, and an extended right hepatectomy
is planned, 1 option is to consider embolization of the
segment 4 portal vein branches. Kishi et al evaluated
the effect that adding embolization of segment 4 to a
right PVE had on the volume changes in segments 2
and 3 prior to extended right hepatectomy. [38] Their
study included 73 patients, all of whom had normal
liver function and an FLR greater than 20%. Of the 73
patients, 15 patients underwent right PVE only, while
58 patients underwent a right PVE in addition to segment 4 PVE. The volume of segments 2 and 3 increased
significantly in both groups of patients. The patients
who underwent right PVE alone had a volume increase
of 106 mL (range: 10-178 mL). The patients who
underwent segment 4 PVE in combination with right
PVE had a significantly higher increase in volume
(141 mL (range: 22-335 mL), _P_ = .044). When
expressed as percentage change, there was a 26%
(range: 7%-70%) increase in the size of segment 2 and
3 when patients underwent a right PVE alone, when
compared to a 54% (range: 8%-135%) for right PVE
plus segment 4 PVE ( _P_ = .021). Furthermore, there
was no difference in complication rate for the right
PVE and the group with addition of segment 4 PVE,
with similar postoperative outcomes. Therefore, in
cases where an extended right hepatectomy is being
considered, segment 4 PVE can be considered in conjunction with right PVE, or to augment further growth
in the remnant liver if there has been inadequate
growth after right PVE alone. [38]
If an extended right hepatectomy is not planned,
adding segment 4 embolization is likely detrimental to
the overall growth of the FLR and other alternatives
must be considered. Embolization of the arterial
branches, in an effort to block even more of the inflow
of blood into the segment of liver that is to be resected,
may increase the risk of complications such as liver
abscess formation secondary to biliary ischemia. [39,40]
Hepatic vein embolization (HVE) has been investigated for its effects on FLR growth after the PVE
failed to induce adequate hypertrophy. Based on their
experience with living donor liver transplantation,
Hwang et al observed that occlusion of 1 graft hepatic
vein in a state of portal flow deprivation accelerated
atrophy of the right liver and resulted in further hypertrophy of the contralateral liver graft. [41] They hypothesized that subsequent right HVE would lead to further
growth of FLR volume in patients who had already
undergone right PVE in preparation for a right hepatectomy. For their cohort, the mean FLR prior to PVE
was 34.8% ± 1.6%. Two weeks after the PVE, the FLR
increased to 39.7% ± 0.6%. These patients then

_Dixon et al_ 283

underwent HVE, and no significant complications
occurred after HVE. FLR volumetry was determined 2
weeks after. This revealed a mean FLR of 44.2% ±
1.1%, which means an overall degree of hypertrophy
of 9.4%. Furthermore, immunohistochemistry studies
revealed that apoptosis occurred more in the area of
the liver affected by both PVE and HVE compared to
the area affected by PVE alone. [41]
The same authors examined this in a larger cohort
which was grouped by disease type. The largest of these
groups was patients with cholangiocarcinoma, which
included 34 patients. FLR volume prior to PVE was
33.9% ± 2.2%, which increased to 38.4% ± 1.5% after
PVE. HVE was then performed and FLR increased to
43.7 ± 2.1%. [42]
In an effort to reduce and optimize the phase of liver
preparation prior to hepatectomy, Guiu et al examined
the effects of performing PVE and HVE during the
same procedure. [43] No complications were observed
from the combined PVE- HVE procedure in a small
cohort of 7 patients. After a mean interval of 23 days
(range: 13-30 days) from the combined PVE- HVE to
repeat imaging, the FLR volume increased from 28.2%
(22.4%-33.3%) to 40.9% (33.6%-59.3%), resulting in a
mean degree of hypertrophy of 12.7%. [43] This demonstrates the feasibility of this technique producing sufficient hypertrophy of the FLR; however, it will need to
be further studied compared to PVE alone and to determine appropriate indications.
Associating liver partition and portal vein occlusion
for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) was initially described
by Schnitzbauer et al in 2012. [10] This initial description
of the ALPPS procedure triggered many responses and
comments, both positive and negative, from the liver
surgery community. [11,44–47] In an editorial about this initial paper, de Santibañes and Clavien reminded us of
the 5 stages of new surgical procedure development as
proposed by the Balliol group [48,49] using the IDEAL
acronym: innovation, development, exploration, assessment, and long- term study. [11] The initial publication by
Schnitzbauer et al fit within the “innovation” stage of
surgical procedure development as it involved highly
selected patients and very few surgeons. [11] Many subsequent studies have sought to push the ALPPS procedure
through the subsequent stages of surgical procedure
development. [50–57] Yet, it remains a controversial technique and its indications and applications have continued to be debated. The International ALPPS Registry
was established to add to the body of data on this technique. Enne et al published data on 20 patients who
underwent a salvage ALPPS procedure after PVE with
inadequate hypertrophy. [57] Median FLR after PVE and
prior to ALPPS procedure was 23%. Prior to the final
stage of the ALPPS procedure, FLR volumes were

calculated and the median FLR was 41%, representing
a degree of hypertrophy of 18%. Importantly, there
were no 90- day mortalities reported with the salvage
ALPPS. [57] While the rate of hypertrophy is impressive,
how ALPPS fits in to the picture remains to be seen. In
the presence of some promising minimally invasive
techniques, such as HVE to manage inadequate hypertrophy of the FLR after PVE, the applicability of
ALPPS is not well known and will require further study.

Title: The Future Liver Remnant: Definition, Evaluation, and Management
Author: Dixon
Content:
In summary, the boundaries of what is possible in terms
of aggressive liver surgery for malignancy have expanded
considerably thanks to a deeper understanding of minimum required liver volumes for adequate physiologic
function, as well as the ability to manipulate the volume
of the liver due to the increased use of PVE. A multidisciplinary and collaborative team, including surgeons,
radiologists, medical oncologists, and gastroenterologists
among others, is important in advancing the care of
patients with advance primary or metastatic liver tumors.
An understanding of the definition of FLR as well as
appropriate minimum cutoff values for FLR is a must for
the modern hepatobiliary surgeon. In addition to volume
cutoffs, degree of hypertrophy and KGR are both very
useful adjuncts in measuring the response to PVE and
cutoff values are well established to help minimize posthepatectomy liver failure and postoperative death due to

such as segment 4 embolization and HVE, are helpful in
producing even greater hypertrophy. It is unknown still
how salvage ALPPS fits into this picture, and more studies on this are necessary; however, this is another potential adjunctive procedure when PVE has not produced

with a cut-off point of abnormal CEA �2.5 ng/mL, when

When it comes to the bottom line—does the postoperative surveillance with serial CEA levels in patients with
colon cancer offer any survival advantage—several authors
agree that only small number of patients derive survival
benefit, ranging from 1% to 5% of all CEA-monitored
patients. [9–11] However, 40% to 50% of patients with recurrent colorectal cancer have liver metastases and when
diagnosed early half of them can be resected with 30%
5-year survival rates and low mortality rates. [5,6,12,13] This
subset of patients can be helped the most from CEA
monitoring, since patients with locoregional recurrence or
other distant metastases usually have much lower resectability and survival rates. [14] This was confirmed in a study
from Mayo clinic that demonstrated doubling of the 5-year
survival following liver resection when the metastases were
detected by an elevation in the CEA level compared with
symptoms and signs. [15]
The purpose of our 15-year period review of hepatic
resections for metastatic colorectal cancer was to attempt
to answer the following three questions: (1) Does the

Title: Is Carcino-Embryonic Antigen Useful in the Follow-up Management of Patients with Colorectal Liver Metastases?
Author: Bakalakos
Content:
Medical records and cancer data of all the patients who
underwent planned liver resection for metastatic colorectal
cancer, from January 1978 to December 1993 at the Ohio
State University were reviewed. Data collected included
the preoperative CEA level and the method of diagnosis of
liver metastases: persistent rise in CEA level as previously
described, [16] computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen
and pelvis, history and physical examination, and elevated
LFTs. Patients for whom the diagnosis of liver metastases
was prompted by rising CEA comprised group I. These
patients were followed up with serial CEA levels after their
primary colon resection, every 1 to 3 months the first 2
years and every 3 to 6 months thereafter. Patients for
whom the diagnosis was prompted by symptoms and signs,
elevated LFTs, or the diagnosis was made by CT of the
abdomen comprised group II. These patients were not
routinely monitored with serial CEA levels after their
primary resection. Patients who were diagnosed with liver
metastases at the time of the primary colon or rectal
resection (synchronous metastases) and underwent
planned hepatic resection at the same or at a later time
comprised group III. Several of these patients in each group
were referred to our Surgical Oncology Service. The follow-up that these patients had after their primary colon or
rectal resection was determined by the referring physician.

In our institution, the follow-up of patients with colon or
rectal carcinoma, after their primary resection, includes
history and physical examination, LFTs and CEA testing
every 3 months for the first 2 years, and every 6 months for
the following 3 years. A baseline CEA level is established
in the first postoperative visit, 4 to 6 weeks from the
primary resection. Every year endoscopy and chest radiography are performed. Patients with symptoms or signs of
metastatic cancer, or elevated LFTs, or persistent rise in
CEA level, undergo CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
and chest radiography.
Statistical analysis of patient groups was performed using
analysis of variance for continuous variables and chi-square
tests for categorical variables. Nonparametric test was used
to compare the levels of CEA in the three groups. Analysis
of survival was done with Kaplan-Meier log rank comparisons. Significance was defined as a _P_ value �0.05. Calculations were made with the help of SPSS computer software (Chicago, Illinois).

feel that they cannot deny the individual patient the small

advantage over those patients who had intermediate CEA
levels (5 to 200 ng/mL). [23] The resectability in patients
with normal preoperative CEA levels, can be assessed by
CT scan or magnetic resonance imaging, which may provide more accurate information than CT, about the extent
and relation of the tumor to the vessels. [24] Also, in these
patients staging laparoscopy may be utilized to decrease the
number of laparotomies when extrahepatic disease or more
diffuse metastases are found. This should be confirmed in
future prospective trials.
Routine liver function tests have not shown to lead in
diagnosis of colorectal liver metastases and increased resectability rate. LFTs should not be part of the routine
follow-up, but should only be utilized selectively.
We conclude that postoperative surveillance with CEA
levels is useful in the follow-up management of patients
with colorectal cancer who go on to develop liver metastases, for the following reasons: First, the higher the preoperative CEA level, the worse the prognosis is; and this
information can be used to advise the patient and family
accordingly. Second, if the CEA level is �30 ng/mL, it is
less likely that the liver metastases are going to be resectable, and that can be taken into account for planning
alternative treatment or using less invasive techniques like
laparoscopy and laparoscopic ultrasound to assess resectability. Third, CEA is complementary to history and physical examination, in the diagnosis of liver metastases from
colorectal cancer and in guiding the clinician in the treatment plan, even though its impact on survival has not been
shown.
