Content:
RESULTS

Using the described search strategy, 12 studies comprising 488
patients with a median of 42 patients per study underwent TSR [7–18].
This group of patients were a subgroup of the 4,940 total patient population with CLMs managed surgically (median ¼ 653 per study)
[7,8,12–18]. Hence, patients undergoing TSR comprised 6% of patients
with surgically managed CLMs (Table I). Ten studies reported a median of 90% (range: 61–100%) of patients undergoing preoperative chemotherapy prior to first-stage resection [7–10,12–14,16–18]. Three
studies mandated the use of preoperative chemotherapy in all patients
and excluded patients with disease progression whilst on chemotherapy
from first-stage resection [7,8,14]. From six studies, there was a median of 59% of patients having partial responses and 31% who had stable
disease after preoperative chemotherapy (Table II) [9,12–14,16,18].

First-Stage Resection

First-stage resection was combined with synchronous resection of
the primary tumor in a median of 30% of patients (range: 0–100%).

Journal of Surgical Oncology

First-stage resections were considered minor (<3 segments) in a median of 90% (range: 0–100%). Only a median of 4% (range: 0–25%)
had major resections (�3 segments) [7–16,18]. Radiofrequency ablation was used in seven institutions in a median of 23% of patients
(range: 3–100%) [7,9–11,13,16,18] as an adjunct to resection. A median of 1 (range: 0–3) unit of blood was required for transfusion
[7,9,11,13–15,18]. Postoperative complications after first-stage resection occurred in a median of 14% (range: 0–26%) of patients. The
median postoperative mortality was 0% (range: 0–4%; Table II)
[7,9–18].

Second-Stage Resection

Author: CHUA
Content:
Second-Stage Resection

The second-stage resection occurred a median of 99 (range: 32–
210) days after the first-stage resection [7–16,18]. During this interval period, portal vein embolization or ligation during the previous
surgery was performed in a median of 78% (range: 36–100%) of
patients [7,9–18]. Interval chemotherapy was used in a median of
61% (range: 0–100%) of patients [8–14,16–18]. The second-stage
resection was considered a major resection in a median of 78%
(range: 45–95%) of patients and minor in a median of 15% (range:
5–56%) of patients [7–16,18]. Radiofrequency ablation was used
during the second-stage resection in six institutions in a median of
12% (range: 2–18%) of patients. A median of 3 (range: 2–13) units
of blood was required for transfusion [7,9,11,13–15,18]. The median
rate of postoperative complication was 33% (range: 11–58%) and
postoperative mortality was 1% (range: 0–7%; Table III) [7–18].

Outcomes and Prediction of Failure the Two-Stage
Resection Strategy

Title: Summary Outcomes of Two-Stage Resection for Advanced Colorectal Liver Metastases
Author: CHUA
Content:
Outcomes and Prediction of Failure the Two-Stage
Resection Strategy

Of the 488 patients treated with an intent of TSR, a median of
77% (range: 64–100%) completed both stages and the median failure
rate was 23% (range: 0–36%) [7–10,12–18]. The causes of failure
included disease progression in a median of 100% (range: 56–
100%), poor performance status in a median of 0% (range: 0–11%),
death in a median of 0% (range: 0–20%) of patients, inadequate liver
regeneration in a median of 0% (range: 0–28%) of patients and other
reasons in a median of 0% (range: 0–16%; Table IV) [7–10,12–
14,16–18].
The median survival of patients with completed TSR was 37
(range: 18–66) months, median 3-year survival rate was 60% (range:
45–84%), and median 5-year survival rate was 48% (range: 32–70%)
[7,10–18]. The median disease-free survival after completion of TSR
was 11 (range: 8–18) months [10,12–14,17,18]. In patients who
failed to complete TSR, the median survival was 16 (range: 10–29)
months (Table V) [7,10,12–14,16–18].
Four studies reported univariate analysis examining clinicopathologic and treatment factors associated with failure to complete TSR
[7,13,16,18]. Understanding of these factors may improve the patient
selection process. Two studies reported having increased exposure to
chemotherapy prior to first-stage resection [16,18], two studies report
a high number of tumors [13,16] as predictor for failure to progress
to the second-stage. One study each reported the following factors as
predictor for failure to progress to the second-stage; major postoperative complication [7], older age [13], and a high CEA [13] (Tables VI
and VII).

Therefore, although the resection of liver metastases was not complete in these patients, the survival result remains still appeared fairly

In patients who completed TSR, the median survival was
37 months and 5-year survival was 48%. Therefore, the results of
this review suggests that the TSR is an effective option for patients
with initially unresectable and bilobar CLM and the survival results
are comparable to patients with initially resectable disease [21]. The
factors that impact on the ability to complete the intended treatment
include requiring more chemotherapy to achieve disease downsizing
for first-stage resection and the number of liver metastases. Requiring more chemotherapy may indicate features of emerging chemorefractory disease with high likelihood of progression during the
interval period. This differs from the clinical scenario of initially
resectable disease. Gallagher et al. [26] reported a series of 111
patients who underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy with synchronous
CLM and demonstrated that the median overall survival was similar
in patients with complete or partial response (58 months), stable disease (65 months), and progressive disease (61 months) after hepatectomy. It is likely that in the scenario of unresectable disease, the
influence of chemotherapy to achieve disease control within the liver
and systemically is a strong surrogate marker for postsurgical
outcome.
In conclusion, this study suggests that complete TSR is associated
with excellent survival outcomes in patients with advanced bilobar
CLM and is comparable to patients with initially resectable disease.
Disease response to chemotherapy is a strong surrogate marker for
outcomes after TSR and its application requires a multi-disciplinary
approach to carefully select appropriate patients for this surgical
strategy that is shown to be effective in expanding the criteria for
resection of CLM.

Background: Up to 50% of patients diagnosed with colorectal cancer develop metastases
during the course of their disease. Surgical resection remains the only curative treatment
option for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), frequently in conjunction with neoadjuvant
chemotherapy. This study sought to determine if the pathologic size of the largest CRLM
impacted disease-free survival (DFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) in the setting of
neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Methods: All patients diagnosed with CRLM who underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy for
liver resection at the Massachusetts General Hospital between 2004 and 2016 were
reviewed. The median size of the largest liver lesion was used as the cutoff for grouped
evaluation.
Results: A total of 214 patients were included. Median follow-up was 100.0 mo (interquartile
range 68.9-133.8 mo). The median size of the largest lesion was 21 mm. Patients with le
sions �21 mm exhibited significantly worse median DFS (12.5 mo versus 16.6 mo; P ¼ 0.033)
and median DSS (71.3 mo versus 103.5 mo; P ¼ 0.038). CRLM lesions �21 mm were asso
ciated with poorer DFS on univariate analysis (hazard ratio (HR) ¼ 1.42, 95% confidence
interval (CI) 1.03-1.95 P ¼ 0.033) and multivariable analysis (HR ¼ 1.58, 95% CI 1.07-2.35,
P ¼ 0.023). CRLM lesions �21 mm were also independently associated with poorer DSS after
liver resection on univariate analysis (HR ¼ 1.51, 95% CI 1.02-2.24; P ¼ 0.037) and multi
variable analysis (HR ¼ 1.98, 95% CI: 1.27-3.07; P ¼ 0.002).
Conclusions: The size of the largest CRLM is an important prognostic factor for both DFS and
DSS after neoadjuvant therapy and serves as a useful indicator of tumor biology.

Introduction

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Introduction

Up to 50% of patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) will develop
liver metastases over the course of their disease. [1][,][2] Hepatic
resection remains the standard of care when metastatic disease is confined to the liver, offering the best chance for cure. [3]
Previously, several scoring systems have been developed to
help predict long-term survival and are used as predictive
analytical tools for patients with colorectal liver metastases
(CRLM). [4-6] Among the reported risk scores, pathologic size of
the largest CRLM is often excluded as an independent risk
factor, [5-8] and those that included size of the largest CRLM
based on radiology have previously reported 50mm-80 mm as
prognostic discriminators. [6-8]
Recent advancements in surgical and perioperative treatment have continued to improve the survival of patients with
CRLM. [9-11] At the same time, wide application of neoadjuvant
therapy has altered the predictive ability of previously established clinical risk scores. [12] The downstaging effect of neoadjuvant treatment would lead to smaller CRLM at the time of
surgery. As a result, many more patients would be categorized
as having smaller CRLM compared to previously reported
cutoffs. [6-8] In the setting of neoadjuvant therapy, the pathologic size of the largest CRLM could be significantly altered,
and its predictive value is unknown. [13][,][14] In addition, few reports have focused findings on oncologic-specific outcomes,
such as disease-free survival (DFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS), rather than the more commonly reported overall
survival (OS).
The aim of this study was to evaluate whether the pathologic size of the largest CRLM after hepatectomy was associated with DFS and DSS, and specifically in the neoadjuvant
setting.

Methods

Patient population

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Methods

Patient population

All patients with CRLM who underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy for liver resection at the Massachusetts General
Hospital from March 2004 to March 2016 were retrospectively
analyzed from a prospectively maintained database. Exclusion criteria were distant metastatic disease, no receipt of
neoadjuvant systemic therapy, and incomplete information
on pathology or recurrence. Patients who never underwent
operative intervention were excluded from the study. This
study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of
Massachusetts General Hospital. This research involved
anonymous data and presented no risk to the participants,
therefore did not require informed consent. Institutional Review Board approval for this study waived the requirement to
obtain a signed consent from all participants.

Data collection

Clinicopathologic data were extracted and included age at
liver resection, sex, race, primary tumor location (left-sided
versus right-sided), whether the CRLM was synchronous with

the primary tumor, disease-free interval from CRC resection
to development of metastatic liver disease, primary nodal
stage in accordance with eighth revised edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer Staging Manual, the neoadjuvant chemotherapy regimen, preoperative use of
bevacizumab or cetuximab, radiologic tumor response in
accordance with response evaluation criteria in solid tumors
(RECIST) criteria, [15] preoperative portal vein embolization,
prehepatectomy serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level,
number of hepatic metastases, bilobar spread of hepatic disease, presence or absence of steatohepatitis in the background
liver, perioperative packed red blood cell transfusion, resection margin status, presence or absence of lymphovascular
invasion and perineural invasion, diameter of the largest liver
metastasis on the final pathologic analysis, and administration of adjuvant treatment after hepatectomy.

Outcomes

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Outcomes

The primary study outcomes were DFS and DSS. Follow-up
data were obtained from all patients and were updated until
March 1, 2019. Date of death was obtained either from the
electronic medical records or from the Social Security Death
Index. DFS was calculated from the date of liver resection to
the date of recurrence (event) or the date of the last follow-up
visit (censored). DSS was calculated from the date of liver
resection to the date of disease-specific death (event), or the
date of the last follow-up visit (censored), and is a more
powerful indicator of tumor biology than OS. Death was
considered nonedisease-specific if cause of death was otherwise indicated, or there was no sign of disease recurrence or
progression at the last follow-up that was within the month of
death to ensure disease-specific mortality.

Statistical analysis

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Statistical analysis

The patients were grouped based on the median of the largest
liver metastasis. If the data followed a normal distribution,
mean (standard deviation) was used, whereas medians
(interquartile range (IQR) or range) were reported if not. Data
were analyzed using Student’s t-test, the Wilcoxon signedrank test, Pearson’s chi-squared test, or Fisher’s exact test,
as appropriate. DFS and DSS were displayed using
KaplaneMeier (K-M) graphs. The log-rank test was used to
statistically compare survival curves.
Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess
prognostic risk factors. The assumption of proportionality
was tested by graphical methods (log-log graphs) and the
Schoenfeld test. Inclusion of variables into multivariable Cox
models was based on clinical relevance, irrespective of the Pvalue in univariable analyses. The multivariable models were
adjusted for the size of the largest liver metastasis, diseasefree interval greater than 12 mo, perioperative packed red
blood cell transfusion, sex, age, CEA (categorized as �200 ng/
mL, >200 ng/mL, or unknown), RECIST (progressive, stable,
partial response, or complete response), primary tumor
pathologic N-stage (0, 1a, 1b, 2a, or 2b), site of primary tumor
(left-sided or right-sided), lymphovascular invasion, perineural invasion, bilobar spread, �2 liver metastases, and

Results

Patient population

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Results

Patient population

Between March 2004 and March 2016, a total of 217 patients
underwent neoadjuvant chemotherapy and liver resection
for CRLM at the Massachusetts General Hospital. Three patients were excluded because they had insufficient clinical
data. A total of 214 patients were eligible for inclusion. There
were 110 men (51.4%) and 104 women (48.6%), and the majority were white (93.0%). Mean age at the time of resection
was 58.1 y. Primary tumors included 160 left-sided (75.2%)
and 54 right-sided tumors (25.2%). Preoperatively, 54 (25.2%)
underwent portal vein embolization. All patients underwent
FOLFOX, FOLFIRI, FOLFIRINOX � bevacizumab or cetuximab.
Overall, 185 (86.5%) patients received FOLFOX and 108 (50.5%)
received bevacizumab or cetuximab. All of these patients
subsequently underwent liver resection. The median size of
the largest liver metastasis was 21 mm (range 0-170 mm).
The median number of liver metastases per patient was 2
(range 1-21). After hepatectomy, 137 (64.0%) patients received
additional ‘adjuvant’ therapy. In the study population, median follow-up was 100.0 mo (IQR 68.9-133.8 mo) with 151
recurrences (70.6%) and 102 disease-specific deaths (47.7%).
Median DFS was 15.2 mo (IQR: 7.4-59.3), with a 5-year DFS
rate 24.6%. Median DSS was 92.6 mo (IQR: 39.1-NR), with a 5year DSS rate 58.2%.

Correlation between liver metastasis size and
clinicopathologic characteristics

Author: Ren
Content:
Correlation between liver metastasis size and
clinicopathologic characteristics

By using the median liver metastasis size of 21 mm as a cutoff,
the study cohort was divided into ‘large’ (�21 mm, n ¼ 112) and
‘small’ (<21 mm n ¼ 112) subgroups. Table 1 shows the comparison of clinicopathologic characteristics as stratified by the
size cutoff. There were no significant differences across the
demographic factors. The large liver metastasis group was
more likely to have >200 ng/mL preoperative CEA levels
(P ¼ 0.024) and have a stable RECIST response (P < 0.001). Patients in the large liver metastasis group were more likely to
have bilobar spread of metastases (P < 0.001), �2 liver metastases (P ¼ 0.014), and positive liver resection margins
(P ¼ 0.009). The large liver metastasis group showed significantly worse median DFS (12.5 mo versus 16.6 mo; P ¼ 0.033)
and median DSS (71.3 mo versus 103.5 mo; P ¼ 0.038) as shown
in Table 2.

Univariate and multivariable analyses of clinicopathologic
variables with respect to DFS after liver resection

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Univariate and multivariable analyses of clinicopathologic
variables with respect to DFS after liver resection

Table 3 lists the relationship between the clinical variables
and DFS after liver resection for CRLM in the current cohort.
On univariate analysis, in addition to larger size of liver
metastasis (hazard ratio (HR) ¼ 1.41, 95% confidence interval
(CI) 1.03-1.95, P ¼ 0.033), higher primary tumor N-stage
(P ¼ 0.002), presence of lymphovascular invasion (P < 0.001),
perineural invasion (P < 0.001), �2 liver metastases (P < 0.001),
and bilobar spread (P ¼ 0.009) were associated with poor DFS.
On multivariable analysis, larger liver metastasis size �21 mm
remained an independent and significant predictor of DFS
(HR ¼ 1.58, 95% CI 1.07-2.35, P ¼ 0.023). Other independent risk
factors include higher primary tumor N-stage, response to
neoadjuvant therapy, presence of lymphovascular invasion,
presence of perineural invasion, and �2 liver metastases. The
adjusted DFS K-M curves stratified by large versus small
metastasis groups are shown in Figure.

variables with respect to DSS after liver resection

Author: Ren

Univariate and multivariable analyses of clinicopathologic
variables with respect to DSS after liver resection

Table 4 lists the relationship between the clinical variables
and DSS after liver resection for CRLM in the current cohort.
On univariate analysis, in addition to large liver metastasis
(HR ¼ 1.51, 95% CI 1.02-2.24, P ¼ 0.037), higher primary tumor
N-stage (P ¼ 0.001), presence of lymphovascular invasion
(P ¼ 0.017), perineural invasion (P ¼ 0.003), and �2 liver metastases (P ¼ 0.018) were associated with poor DSS. On
multivariable analysis, larger liver metastasis size �21 mm
remained an independent and significant predictor of DSS
(HR ¼ 1.90, 95% CI: 1. 23-2.96, P ¼ 0.004). Other independent
risk factors included response to neoadjuvant therapy, higher
primary tumor N-stage, presence of perineural invasion, and
�2 liver metastases. The adjusted DSS K-M curves stratified by
large versus small liver metastasis size are shown in Figure.

Discussion

Title: Size of the Largest Colorectal Liver Metastasis Is an Independent Prognostic Factor in the Neoadjuvant Setting
Author: Ren
Content:
Discussion The present study included a group of patients with CRLM who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy for liver resection and evaluated the role of the pathologic size of the largest liver metastasis, specifically in the setting of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Our study identified a median size cutoff of 21 mm was independently associated with DFS and DSS. A higher primary tumor N-stage, presence of �2 liver metastases, and poor response to neoadjuvant therapy were also independently associated with poorer DFS and DSS. For patients with metastases from CRC confined to the liver, liver resection remains the treatment of choice, and various prognostic models for predicting outcomes after resection of CRLM have emerged. [5][,][19] Size of the largest liver metastasis size based on radiologic (not pathologic) evaluation has only occasionally been included. [5-8][,][19][,][20] Furthermore, several studies have disputed the prognostic value of size of liver metastases and failed to detect any association between size and subsequent oncologic outcomes such as recurrence or survival. This information contributes to prognostication and may aid in guiding additional postoperative decision-making with respect to administration of adjuvant therapy or targeted treatments. Despite only occasional reporting of size as a prognostic feature in CRLM, there has been no formal consensus on a size cutoff that predicts worse outcomes. A cutoff of 50 mm was previously reported as a potential discriminator of prognosis in some studies, [6][,][7] whereas another report used 80 mm as a suitable cutoff. [8] Importantly, however, with improvements in detection and diagnosis of CRLM, and especially in the setting of commonly used neoadjuvant therapy with anticipated tumor downsizing, smaller tumor sizes are more likely to be encountered during liver resection. [13][,][26] For example, in our cohort of 214 patients with CRLM, only 34 patients had tumors larger than 50 mm and 11 larger than 80 mm. It should be noted that in our data set, having smaller tumors was associated with better response to neoadjuvant treatment, but tumor size remained independently prognostic in multivariable analysis, indicating that its prognostic value was not dependent on response to neoadjuvant treatment. in the neoadjuvant setting that matters.
In keeping with previous reports, primary tumor nodal
disease stage was strongly and consistently associated with
prognosis, with a higher N-stage predicting a poorer DFS and
DSS. Similarly, the number of liver metastases is frequently
incorporated as a prognostic predictor, with previously reported cutoffs ranging from one to seven metastases. [6][,][14][,][16-18]
The median number of liver metastases in our cohort in the
setting of neoadjuvant systemic therapy was two, with 114
(50.9%) patients having two or more liver metastases. Using
the median of two metastases as a cutoff to dichotomize
these data, the number of metastases was found to be a
strong and independent predictor for poor prognosis, again
for both disease recurrence and survival (HR > 2 for both DFS
and DSS, P < 0.01). These findings confirm the reliability and
validity of the data. Importantly, the presence of perineural
invasion was associated with poorer DFS and DSS, which is
consistent with current knowledge from previous reports. [27-]
29 However, lymphovascular invasion was found to be associated with poorer DFS but not DSS after adjustment.

29 However, lymphovascular invasion was found to be associated with poorer DFS but not DSS after adjustment. Interestingly, preoperative CEA levels using a previously accepted
cutoff of 200 mg/mL [6] were not found to be associated with
neither poorer DFS nor DSS. Although this may have been
attributable in part due to a large proportion of missing variables in the cohort (63 patients; 29.4%), the cohort also
incorporated only patients who received neoadjuvant systemic therapy, which may have attenuated the effect of CEA
because of either reductions in serum levels and/or exclusion
of patients from liver resection in the event of rising values.
As we previously reported and has been shown in other
studies, [5][,][6] the impact of microscopic positive margin resections may be neutralized in the setting of neoadjuvant
systemic therapy. [30-32] Once again, a total of 16 (7.5%) patients
were found to be margin positive and without significant
impact on prognosis in either univariate or multivariable
analysis models. These findings are all reassuringly consistent with treatment of CRLM in the era of neoadjuvant systemic therapy.
The limitations of our study include its retrospective
design, thereby limiting conclusions to associations detected
over time. In addition, 93% of the patient population was
white, which could lead to lack of generalizability to nonwhite
populations. Finally, sample sizes are considered smaller than
sizes reported from national databases. Strengths of the present study were the strict inclusion of patients with CRLM who
received neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy, the ability to
report DSS, rather than OS, thereby excluding noncancer
deaths, and the aggregation of data from a reliable singleinstitution source with fewer missing data points.

Conclusion

In conclusion, using a median size cutoff of 21 mm, tumor size
on final pathologic was found to be a statistically significant
adverse prognostic factor for both DFS and DSS in patients
with CRLM who received neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed
by liver resection. Further prognostic factors were also

associated with oncologic outcomes, confirming the validity
and reliability of the data set.

**Introduction**

Colorectal cancer remains a major health problem in Europe, as in many areas of the world. It has

been estimated that in 2018 in France, approximately 44 000 individuals were newly diagnosed with
colorectal cancer, and 17 000 died of the disease. [1] In spite of mass screening programs deployed

since the 2000s, the proportion of patients diagnosed with a metastatic tumor has ranged from 20%
to 30% in European countries. [2,3] Although the liver is the main site for distant metastases in

colorectal cancer, little is known about the incidence of synchronous liver metastases.

Similarly, there have been few population-based studies describing the frequency of
metachronous liver metastases after resection of the primary colorectal tumor. [4-7] These

epidemiological figures can only be obtained from data covering the entire population of patients

with colon cancer in a given region. Such studies are rare because they require the accurate and

detailed collection of population-based data. In particular, the active participation of the entire

medical community is required, which is difficult to achieve for cancer registries that cover large

populations. For this reason, data on the management and prognosis of liver metastases have mostly

been provided by specialized hospital units; therefore, these data cannot be used as a reference due

to unavoidable selection bias. The aim of this cohort study was to investigate the incidence and

outcomes of synchronous and metachronous liver metastases using data from a population-based

series in France.

**Methods**

**Study Design**
This noninterventional population-based cohort study was approved by the French Data Protection

Authority (Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés). In accordance with French

legislation, there was no requirement for written informed consent because of the use of deidentified

**Proportion and Incidence of Synchronous Liver Metastases**
Of 26 813 patients (15 032 men [56.1%] and 11 781 women [43.9%]; median [IQR] age, 73 [64-81]

years) diagnosed with colorectal adenocarcinoma over the period of 1976 to 2018, 4546 patients

(17.0%) had synchronous liver metastases identified at diagnosis. The proportions of patients

The net survival of patients with synchronous liver metastases was 41.8% (95% CI, 40.3%-43.4%) at

metastases only increased from 4.0% (95% CI, 2.3%-6.9%) in the 1991 to 1995 period to 9.4% (95%

In patients with synchronous liver metastases, the outcomes for those with right colon cancer

metachronous metastases (eg, 3-year net survival: 26.0% [95% CI, 19.0%-35.4%] for right colon

After adjustment for sex, age, and metastases location, synchronous status was associated with

outcomes of synchronous and metachronous liver metastases according to tumor site and stage at

diagnosis of the primary colorectal cancer. There was no significant variation over time in the

greater improvement in outcomes for metachronous metastases than for synchronous metastases

through adapted treatment strategies. The reasons for the differences in net survival between

synchronous metastases from right-sided and left-sided colon cancers has been described previously

and was partly explained by older age and more comorbidities in patients with right-sided
colon cancer. [22]

The results of our population-based study suggest a gradual improvement in the therapeutic

management of colorectal cancer liver metastases. Patients with synchronous liver metastases from

colorectal cancer had worse outcomes than patients with metachronous liver metastases. These
results are consistent with those of a recent population-based study, [6] which found that overall

survival was still better in patients with late metachronous metastases detected more than 12

months after diagnosis of the primary tumor than in patients with early metastases detected within

12 months of the colorectal cancer diagnosis. The difference in prognosis between patients with
synchronous and metachronous liver metastases is controversial. Engstrand et al [23] suggested that

this difference in survival between those with synchronous vs metachronous metastases could be an

artifact of diagnosis and proposed using the diagnosis or resection of the primary tumor as the

standard cutoff point for defining synchronous and metachronous detection.

It is important to note that, in our study, the improvement in net survival in patients with

metachronous metastases was significant and was observed earlier than that in patients with

synchronous metastases, whereas the improvement in outcomes in patients with synchronous

metastases remained moderate. Before 1995, 5-year survival was not significantly different between

these 2 categories of patients. Five-year survival of patients with metachronous metastases

increased from 6.1% in the 1991 to 1995 period to 14.7% in the 1996 to 2000 period, then from 12.8%

in the 2001 to 2005 period to 26.1% in the 2006 to 2010 period. The performance of surgical

procedures for liver metastases may have been an early factor in improving prognosis during the
1990s. [24] However, only 20% to 30% of patients with liver metastases from colorectal cancer are
eligible for surgical treatment. [25]

In the second phase, at the end of the 1990s and in the 2000s, improved chemotherapy

outcomes may have led to increased survival in patients with either synchronous or metachronous

metastases. The improvement of molecular characterization of tumors has allowed personalization

of the use of monoclonal antibodies in protocols of chemotherapy. By adding targeted therapies,

such as anti–epidermal growth factor receptor or anti–vascular endothelial growth factor antibodies,

to the previous cytotoxic regimens, response rates higher than 50% and median survival of
approximately 30 months have been achieved. [26]

Some patients underwent major liver resection after downstaging with chemotherapy and

portal vein occlusion. However, this strategy has now been found to be associated with worse short
and long-term outcomes in patients with a slow response to chemotherapy and should be limited to
a selected subset of patients. [27] For slow responders to chemotherapy, more conservative strategies

are needed. The improvement in surgical strategies in the 2000s to include a liver-first approach for
some patients with multiple bilobar metastases [28] might be associated with the increase in survival.

The surgical strategy should now be decided according to the hepatic tumor burden, and all patients

with synchronous or metachronous liver metastases from colorectal cancer should be evaluated by
a multidisciplinary hepatobiliary team. [25] For those patients with tumors not considered suitable for
liver resection, radiofrequency ablation has been reported to be a safe and effective treatment. [29,30]

The prognosis has also improved in patients with synchronous liver metastases. A recent study

comparing 2 cohorts of patients with resected synchronous liver metastases (a 2012-2018 cohort

and a historical cohort [1992-2010]) reported that survival in the more recent cohort (71.7%) was
better than that in the historical cohort (44.3%). [31] However, these data were obtained at a tertiary

academic medical center and may have been subject to selection bias. The differences between

these results and those of our study suggest that population-based studies are important in

epidemiological research.

**Limitations**
This study has several limitations. The main limitation is related to its population-based design,

leading to a lack of detailed data on the characteristics of patients, liver metastases, and molecular

types, all of which might have had implications for the risk of metastases or the possibility of

receiving treatment. To estimate survival in patients with colorectal cancer who underwent resection
of liver metastases, biomarkers such as _BRAF_ or _KRAS_ variants should be included in future models. [32]

In our study, biomarkers were not available over the study period. This study is descriptive; thus, we

can only speculate about the mechanisms underlying the observed changes in cancer risk.

**Conclusions**

This population-based cohort study found that, in recent decades, improvement in survival was substan
tial in patients with metachronous liver metastases, whereas improvement remained modest in pa
tients with synchronous liver metastases. These findings suggest that the occurrence of synchronous

and metachronous liver metastases from colorectal cancer remains a substantial problem. The differ
ences observed in the incidence and survival of patients with colorectal cancer and synchronous or

metachronous liver metastases may be useful for the design of future clinical trials.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
The response rate of colorectal metastases to chemotherapy, ranging from 50 to
60%, has been shown to be a prognostic factor. Complete pathologic and radiological response
rates are approximately 4 and 7%, respectively. Hepatotoxic effects of oxaliplatin and irinotecan on the non-tumoral liver parenchyma have been reported and are incriminated in vascular
changes (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome [SOS]) and chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis
(CASH). Oxaliplatin-based regimens are associated with an increased risk of vascular lesions
and irinotecan-based regimens are associated with increased risks of steatosis and steatohepatitis. SOS increases morbidity after major liver resection, mostly after administration of more
than six cycles of neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy. CASH increases morbidity and mortality
rates after hepatectomy. Preliminary results have shown that the addition of targeted molecular therapy (bevacizumab or cetuximab) to conventional chemotherapy does not increase the
postoperative morbidity or mortality rates after hepatectomy and does not create additional
injury to the non-tumoral liver parenchyma. However, bevacizumab may impair regeneration
of the future remnant. Chemotherapy may reduce the sensitivity of CT scan and PET scan in
the detection of metastases.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
In Europe, as in the USA, colorectal cancer represents the second most common cause of
death by cancer. In France, it is the third most frequent cancer in men and the second in
women [1,2]. More than 50% of patients with colorectal cancer develop hepatic metastases.
At the time of diagnosis of colorectal cancer, hepatic metastases are found in 15 to 20%
of cases [3]. Hepatic metastases appear within 3 years of resection of primary colonic or
rectal cancer in 25 to 50% of cases [4].

Although there are no randomized studies on the topic,
comparative retrospective studies have shown that surgical resection of hepatic metastases represents the only
curative treatment capable of providing prolonged survival. Five-year survival after resection of hepatic colorectal
metastases is between 25 and 44% [5,6]. At the time
of diagnosis of hepatic metastases, approximately 20% of
patients have hepatic metastases initially amenable to
resection. Recent progress in hepatic surgery in terms of
morbi-mortality as well as the development of new parasurgical strategies (e.g. neoadjuvant chemotherapy associated
with targeted molecular therapies, portal embolization,
radiofrequency or cryotherapy modalities, or staged hepatectomy techniques) have led to larger and more complex
resections.
Management of liver metastases from colorectal cancer is an illustration of the necessity of a multidisciplinary
approach (surgeon, oncologist, radiologist, gastroenterologist), establishing a staged therapeutic strategy including
regular re-evaluations with the goal of achieving complete
resections (R0) for the majority of patients

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
There are two distinct situations. When metastases are
considered resectable from the start, chemotherapy is qualified as ‘‘neoadjuvant’’. When metastases are not initially
resectable, chemotherapy is necessary and is qualified as
‘‘induction’’ chemotherapy, the goal being to render the
metastases resectable.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
A European randomized controlled study from the EORTC
analyzed the efficacy of perioperative chemotherapy (four
to six preoperative and six postoperative cycles of FOLFOX) for immediately resectable metastases (≤ 4 lesions).
This study showed an 8.1% absolute increase in 3-year
progression-free survival for patients receiving perioperative chemotherapy (36.2% vs. 28.1%; _P_ = 0.04) [7]. Neither
the 5-year or overall results are yet known. Reversible postoperative complications, mostly biliary, occurred more often
after chemotherapy than after surgery alone (25.2% vs.

15.9%; _P_ = 0.04). This study leads to propose perioperative
chemotherapy as the standard treatment, routinely associated with resection of colorectal liver metastases.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
Once again, two different settings are possible: either the
metastases are potentially resectable or they are definitely
not. While this difference might seem subjective, in fact,
it depends on the expertise of the team that manages the
patient. Definitively nonresectable metastases usually correspond to situations when one or more metastases are
found in all the segments of the liver (Fig. 1) and/or to
extrahepatic disease. In both settings, chemotherapy is
administered but with different goals. In the first instance,
the goal is to render the lesion resectable, while in the
second, the goal is to increase survival with the least possible toxicity, i.e. privileging quality of life, starting with the
least harmful agents. The protocols call for three classes
of active cytotoxics: 5-FU, oxaliplatin, and irinotecan. Targeted molecular therapies can be associated secondarily.
A retrospective analysis of 11 randomized studies showed
a linear correlation between these three cytotoxic agents
and overall survival [8], correlation found irrespective of
the strategies used, and independently of whether first-line
treatment made use of one or two combined drugs.
Series in which metastases were rendered resectable
secondarily by induction chemotherapy resulting in survival
have been reported [9—19] (Table 1). In the first series published in 1996, Bismuth et al. [11] reported a 16% secondary
resectability rate in patients who were initially nonresectable, without any additional mortality or morbidity.
Three- and 5-year survival was 54 and 40% respectively, similar to survival in patients having undergone resection without chemotherapy. In phase II trials, these results were confirmed with secondary R0 resection rates reaching 43%. Folprecht et al. [20] showed a direct correlation between the
response rate to chemotherapy and secondary R0 resection
rate. Triple-therapies (FOLFIRINOX) seem to give the best
results with R0 resection rate between 35 and 43%, compared to 29 to 33% when biotherapy was used [19—21]. However, these therapeutic monoclonal antibody therapy strategies are fraught with high morbidity. Presently, the addition
of target directed therapies (bevacizumab, cetuximab) has
increased the objective response rate as well as progressionfree survival [22,23] with acceptable morbidity. The addition

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
The relationship between the response to chemotherapy and
survival has been shown by several studies [27—29]. Most
of these studies evaluated the response to chemotherapy
according the RECIST radiologic criteria based on CT scans
[30]. In one study in 131 patients, Adam et al. [28] reported
a 46% objective response rate, a 30% progression-free survival rate and 26% rate of disease progression with FOLFOX.
Five-year survival was 37% for responders versus 30 and
8% for stable patients and patients in progression, respectively. Five-year recurrence-free survival was 21, 17, and 3%,
respectively. A recent study [31] has shown that the response
to chemotherapy was a prognostic factor for survival and for
recurrence, and was more reliable than the clinicobiological
score devised by the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center [31]. Although the number of patients was small ( _n_ = 54),
this study suggests that traditional prognostic factors have
lost some of their value since the response to neoadjuvant
chemotherapy has become manifest. These results suggest
that in case of progression, surgery should be postponed and
that a new line of chemotherapy should be proposed.
The pathologic response to chemotherapy is variable and
has led to the description of a histological tumor regression
grading (TRG) system ranging from 1 to 5, founded on the
presence of residual tumor cells and the degree of fibrosis
(Fig. 2) [32]. Grade 1 corresponds to the absence of tumor
cells, replaced by abundant fibrosis; grade 2 corresponds to
rare residual tumor cells scattered throughout dense fibrosis; grade 3 to more residual tumor cells within predominant
fibrosis; grade 4 to large amounts of tumor cells predominating over fibrosis while grade 5 corresponds to almost
exclusively tumor cells without fibrosis and without signs of
tumor regression.
A correlation between the degrees of pathologic
response, the 5-year recurrence-free and overall survival
rates has been shown [32—34]. In the Paul Brousse series
of 767 patients, 5-year overall survival was 68% when the
response was complete, vs. 29% when the response was
partial ( _P_ = 0.004). In their series of 305 patients, the MD
Anderson group [34] reported a 5-year survival rate of 75%
when the response was complete vs. 33% when the response
was minor. The rate of complete pathologic response ranges
from 4 [32,33] to 9% [34]. Complete pathologic response
rates do not always correspond to radiological response
rates. For Adam et al., predictive factors for a complete
histological response rate included age less than 60, lesions

i

less or equal to 3 cm in diameter, ACE less than 30 ng/L,
and objective radiologic response [33]. For the MD Anderson team, independent predictive factors were complete
pathologic response, CEA less than 5 ng/L and lesions less or
equal to 3 cm in diameter as well as a therapeutic regimen
including oxaliplatin and bevacizumab [34,35].
However, the use of these chemotherapy drugs has a toxic
effect on non-tumoral parenchyma.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
Two histological consequences have been reported: the sinusoidal obstructive syndrome (SOS), associated with the use
of oxaliplatin, and chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis (CASH), associated with the use of irinotecan. These two
histological involvements have also been reported after the
use of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), but to a lesser degree [36]. The
incidence of these complications ranges between 37 and 79%
[37—43].

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
De Leve et al. [26,44] were the first to recognize anomalies
in the hepatic sinusoids and to give them the name of the
sinusoidal obstructive syndrome (SOS). The SOS has a characteristic macroscopic aspect, the ‘‘blue liver’’. Histological
characteristics include congestion and dilatation of the hepatic sinusoids, discontinuity in the sinusoidal membrane and
collagen deposits in the perisinusoidal spaces (Fig. 3).
Rubbia-Brandt et al. [37] reported the first cases of SOS
observed after administration of oxaliplatin. In their series,
SOS was found in 79% (34/43) of patients treated with oxaliplatin versus 23% (10/44) in patients treated with 5-FU. A
semi-quantitative classification, according to the degree of
dilatation, was formulated: grade 0 (absence of dilatation),
grade 1 or ‘‘mild’’ (centrilobular dilatation limited to 1/3
of the lobular surface), grade 2 or moderate (centrilobular
dilatation extending in 2/3 of the lobular surface), and grade
3 or severe (complete lobular involvement). These sinusoidal
dilatations can be associated with fibrosis. That oxaliplatin
has a role in the onset of SOS was confirmed by several
studies [37—42,45,46]. The number of cycles of oxaliplatin
(≥ 6 cycles) seems to be correlated with the onset of SOS
[40]. On the other hand, the cumulated dose of oxaliplatin
is not correlated with the severity of the SOS [41,42]. It has
not been shown that SOS regresses when oxaliplatin administration is discontinued. To the contrary, persistence or even
aggravation of the SOS 4 years after discontinuing oxaliplatin
has been reported [37,42]. At a later stage, regenera

Histological, steatohepatitis associates different degrees
of steatosis, lobular inflammation and hepatocellular ballooning (Figs. 5 and 6). Steatosis and steatohepatitis are
responsible for the characteristic macroscopic ‘‘yellow
liver’’ aspect. When these histological modifications are
present and in the absence of alcoholism, one speaks of
chronic hepatopathy called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
(NASH). To standardize the histological description of NASH,
Kleiner et al. [46] established a score including steatosis
(scored 0 to 3), lobular inflammation (scored 0 to 2), hepatocellular ballooning (scored 0 to 2). Most often, NASH
is associated with a dysmetabolic syndrome (obesity, noninsulin-dependent diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia).
After administration of chemotherapy, identical lesions have
been found and named, by analogy, CASH.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
Excepting the influence related to the type of the
chemotherapy molecule, factors responsible for the onset
of histological lesions in the hepatic parenchyma are not
well known. Brouquet et al. [49] looked at the independent predictive factors of histological involvement in
146 patients: the incidence of histologically proven hepatic involvement was 51% (SOS = 34%, steatosis = 22%, and
steatohepatitis = 10%). The independent risk factors were:
body mass index (BMI) greater than 27 Kg/m [2] ( _P_ = 0.002),
hyperglycemia greater than 7 mmol/L ( _P_ = 0.006), and an
interval between the last cycle of chemotherapy and operation less than 4 weeks ( _P_ = 0.011). Taking aspirin was found to
be a protective factor ( _P_ = 0.002). Only a BMI greater than
27 Kg/m [2] ( _P_ = 0.026) was found as an independent predictive factor for the onset of steatosis or steatohepatitis. As
concerns the onset of SOS, independent risk factors were
the synchronous character of liver metastasis ( _P_ = 0.015)
and nonresectability at the time of diagnosis of metastases

Data concerning the effect of anti-vascular endothelial
growth factor (VEGF) and anti-epidermal growth factor
receptor (EGFR) on non-tumoral hepatic parenchyma are
more limited [35,50,51]. In Ribero et al.’s series [35], SOS
occurred less often in patients receiving bevacizumab preoperatively (27% vs. 53% in patients receiving 5-FU and
oxaliplatin). In the series published by Klinger et al. [50],
severity of SOS was reduced by adjunctive use of bevacizumab. The incidence of grade 3 SOS was 23.9% in patients
not receiving bevacizumab and 1.9% in patients receiving
bevacizumab, while the overall rate of SOS was comparable
in both groups. Adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy does
not increase the insult in non-tumoral hepatic parenchyma.
Some authors have even stated that anti-VEGF has a protective effect, based on the fact that circulating VEGF is
correlated to the severity of SOS [52,53]. After administration of cetuximab, only one study has reported a regression
in the incidence of SOS and fibrosis [51].

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
After major hepatectomy, a higher rate of postoperative complications was found in patients with SOS (37.8%
vs. 13.6%), but without higher mortality rates [39]. The
morbidity rate was correlated to the number of cycles
of chemotherapy administered but not to the type of
chemotherapy regimen. Morbidity is increased when more
than six cycles are used. In one study by Nakano et al. [40],
the complication rate was 40% in patients with SOS versus
6.3% in patients without SOS. In the EORTC study [7], postoperative complication rates increased in patients receiving
preoperative chemotherapy (six cycles of oxaliplatin): 25%
versus 16% ( _P_ = 0.04). Higher perioperative transfusion rates
have been reported in patients receiving preoperative oxaliplatin, correlated with the presence of SOS [38] ( _P_ = 0.04).
The perioperative transfusion rate is a pejorative factor for
morbidity and mortality but also for long-term survival after
hepatic resection of colorectal cancer metastases [54]. To
date, nothing in the literature has shown that the postoperative mortality rate correlates to the presence and/or the
severity of SOS.
One potential consequence of SOS is portal hypertension
as attested by splenomegaly. After 6 months of administration, Angitapalli et al. [55] found that the splenic
diameter increased by 45.7% in patients treated with oxaliplatin versus 16.3% in patients treated with 5-FU ( _P_ = 0.0069)

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
The deleterious effect of steatosis on the postoperative
course after hepatectomy are known for many years [56,57].
Berhrns et al. [56] were the first to report increased morbidity and mortality after hepatectomy in patients with
moderate or severe steatosis. Fernandez et al. [48] found
that the incidence of hepatocellular insufficiency and postoperative mortality increased in patients with CASH when
BMI was greater than 35 Kg/m [2] . In the series published by
Vauthey et al. [43], postoperative mortality was 14.7% in
patients with steatohepatitis versus 1.6% in patients without: postoperative mortality was essentially related to the
development of hepatocellular insufficiency (5.8% vs. 0.8%).

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
There are few studies available to judge the influence of
cell-targeted therapy on the postoperative course and most
are retrospective.
In the study from the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center [58], 32 patients undergoing hepatectomy for
metastases and receiving bevacizumab (16 patients before
the operation and 16 patients at least after the operation)
were matched (according to age, gender, type of hepatectomy, the number, size and location of metastases) with
32 patients who did not receive bevacizumab. No significant
differences were found between the two groups concerning the rate or the severity of perioperative morbidity. In
the retrospective comparative study by Reddy et al. [59],
patients receiving bevacizumab had less blood loss and need
for transfusion after hepatectomy. Morbidity rates (abdominal wall and thromboembolic complications) did not differ
significantly between the two groups, although there was
a tendency toward higher overall morbidity in patients
operated on less than 8 weeks after the last course of bevacizumab. These data lead to the conclusion that elective
surgery for liver metastases is feasible and safe after treatment with bevacizumab without increasing the operative
risk, as long as treatment is discontinued 6 to 8 weeks before
surgery.
As concerns cetuximab, comparative data are sparse.
The initial results of the Crystal study [25] have not

shown increased postoperative morbidity. Adam et al.
[24] reported morbidity, hepatocellular insufficiency and
mortality rates of 52, 8, and 3.7% respectively after administration of cetuximab. In the case-matched prospective study
(according to age, gender, BMI, type of hepatectomy, the
number of cycles and the type of chemotherapy), adding
cetuximab to neoadjuvant chemotherapy did not increase
morbidity or mortality after hepatectomy [51].

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
A complete radiological response can be observed after
chemotherapy. Few studies have looked at the outcome
of ‘‘missing’’ metastases, and results are contradictory
[60—63].
In the study by Benoist et al. [60] including 586 patients
between 1998 and 2004, one or more metastases disappeared with chemotherapy in 38 patients (6.5%). In all, 66
of 183 initially visible metastases disappeared: 20 of these
(30%) were actually present, and resected during laparotomy, 15 scars were resected while 31 lesions were not
found and not resected. Tumor cells were found in 12 out
of 15 scars (80%). After 1-year follow-up, the local recurrence rate of lesions left behind was 74% (23/31). Last, of
the 66 preoperative radiological ‘‘missing’’ lesions, 55 (83%)
contained macroscopic or microscopic residual tumor tissue
or local recurrence. Similar results were found by Fiorentini et al. [61] who reported tumor cells in 63% of resected
scar tissue and 81% of macroscopic or microscopic residual tumor tissue or local recurrence after 2 years follow-up.
These ‘‘radiological complete’’ responses were obtained
after intra-arterial floxuridine-based chemotherapy.
In the study by Elias et al. [63], of 228 patients managed
between 1999 and 2004, one or more metastases had disappeared in 16 patients (7%) after chemotherapy. In all, 69
of 134 metastases initially present were ‘‘missing’’ and left
in the liver. After a median follow-up of 51 months, nonresected ‘‘missing’’ lesions reappeared in 10 patients (62%).
Three-year survival in these 16 patients was 94%. Hepatic
recurrence was significantly lower in patients having undergone postoperative intra-arterial chemotherapy (0% vs. 72%;
_P_ = 0.01). The authors attributed their good results to the
administration of adjuvant intra-arterial chemotherapy.
At the present time, in the absence of adjuvant intraarterial chemotherapy (which does not diffuse widely), most
authors propose either resection or destruction of scar tissue
from metastases whenever possible.

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
Helical CT scan is presently the most widely used imaging
technique for the detection of hepatic metastases. In two
recent meta-analyses, the sensitivity of CT scan ranged from
68 to 72% [64,65]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has
similar sensitivity [66] but CT scan is probably more reliable
in detecting small lesions. However, approximately 30% of
lesions are detected neither by CT nor by MRI [60,61,67]. For
this reason, a multimodal approach is recommended [68].
At the present time, the place of FDG PET scan remains
debated [65,69]; this modality has the advantage of analyzing the entire body and can therefore detect extrahepatic
lesions.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy decreases the detection rate
of metastases by CT scan, not only by increasing the falsenegative rate (missing lesions) but also by increasing the
false-positive rate by detecting a greater number of benign
lesions [70]; therefore in this study, the sensibility of CT
dropped from 69 to 54% after chemotherapy. Another study
[71] reported similar results with a reduction in CT sensitivity from 87.5 to 65.3% after chemotherapy. This study
analyzed the sensitivity of PET scan, which likewise plummeted from 93.3 to 49%. However, the sensitivity of helical
CT was higher than that of PET scan for the detection of
metastases after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Fig. 8).

Title: Consequences of chemotherapy on resection of colorectal liver metastases
Author: Pessaux
Content:
After portal embolization, chemotherapy can be continued with the goal of decreasing the risk of tumor
progression during the period of hepatic regeneration.
Two studies have reported contradictory results as to the
impact of chemotherapy on hepatic regeneration. Beal et
al. [72] showed that chemotherapy administered during
the hypertrophic phase impaired regeneration after portal
embolization. However, the number of cases in this report
was small as only five patients received chemotherapy. On
the other hand, Goéré et al. [73] reported that continuing chemotherapy after portal embolization neither altered
hypertrophy of the remnant liver nor increased postoperative morbidity.
After hepatic resection, VEGF receptor 1 is activated in
the hepatic sinusoids, leading to stimulation of mitogenic
factors (hepatocyte growth factor, HB-EGF, IL6) and hepatic regeneration [74]. Inhibition of VEGF could therefore
limit hepatic regeneration [75]. The effect of cetuximab on

hepatic regeneration has never been studied. As concerns
bevacizumab, there are two studies, with contradictory
results. Bevacizumab administered after portal embolization reduced hepatic regeneration essentially in patients
over 60 years old and when more than six cycles of bevacizumab had been delivered [76]. The MD Anderson Cancer
Center study [77] did not show any ill effects on hepatic
hypertrophy related to bevacizumab after portal embolization. Differences in the populations studied and in the
methodology used (in terms of volumetric evaluation and
number of cycles of chemotherapy administered before portal embolization) could explain the discordance of results.

Essential points
   - The objective response rate after chemotherapy,
shown to be a prognostic factor, ranges between
50 and 60%.
  - When metastases are not resectable initially,
induction chemotherapy can increase the
resectability rate to approximately 20%.
   - The complete histological and radiologic response
rates are approximately 4 and 7%, respectively.
  - Chemotherapy induces two histological
consequences: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
(SOS) associate with the use of oxaliplatin, and
chemotherapy-associated steatohepatitis (CASH),
associated with the use of irinotecan.
   - Adding cell-targeting therapies to chemotherapy
does not increase the rate of histological hepatic
lesions.
  - SOS increases postoperative morbidity after
major hepatectomy, especially when more than
six cycles of chemotherapy are administered.
Mortality is not increased.
   - CASH increases both postoperative morbidity and
mortality.
  - The new cell-targeting molecules do not modify
the postoperative course.
   - Chemotherapy decreases the detection rate of CT
and PET scan.

Content:

involving radiology (cross sectional, nuclear medicine and interventional),
Oncology, Liver surgery, Colorectal surgery, and Histopathology. Patient
management is based on assessment of sophisticated clinical, radiological and
biomarker information. Despite incomplete evidence in this very heterogeneous
patient group, maximising resection of CRLM using all available techniques
remains a key objective and provides the best chance of long-term survival and
cure. To this end, liver resection is maximised by the use of downsizing
chemotherapy, optimisation of liver remnant by portal vein embolization,
associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy, and
combining resection with ablation, in the context of improvements in the
functional assessment of the future remnant liver. Liver resection may safely be
carried out laparoscopically or open, and synchronously with, or before,
colorectal surgery in selected patients. For unresectable patients, treatment
options including systemic chemotherapy, targeted biological agents, intraarterial infusion or bead delivered chemotherapy, tumour ablation, stereotactic
radiotherapy, and selective internal radiotherapy contribute to improve survival
and may convert initially unresectable patients to operability. Currently evolving
areas include biomarker characterisation of tumours, the development of novel
systemic agents targeting specific oncogenic pathways, and the potential reemergence of radical surgical options such as liver transplantation.

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents a major worldwide health care burden, as the
second most common cancer diagnosed in women and third most common in men,
and accounting for 10% of all annually diagnosed cancers and cancer-related deaths
worldwide [[][1][]] .
As result of improvements in detection through screening [[][2][]], better referral
pathways [[][3][]], centralisation of services [[][4][]], effective primary surgery [[][5][]], development of
systemic chemotherapy [[][6][]], biological agents [[][7][]], and understanding of tumour biology [[][8][]],
survival rates following diagnosis have improved [[][9][]] .
Nevertheless, at least 25%-50% of patients with CRC develop colorectal liver
metastases (CRLM) during the course of their illness.
From a historical perspective, the surgical management approach to CRLM has
undergone a significant evolution. Starting from an era prior to the 1930s during
which liver surgery for malignancy presented insurmountable challenges for technical
and oncological reasons, tentative attempts at liver resection for malignancy were

WJCO https://www.wjgnet.com 762 October 24, 2020 Volume 11 Issue 10

Martin J _et al._ Colorectal liver metastase

made in the subsequent decades resulting in early reports establishing proof of
principle that long term survival following resection of CRLM was possible [[][10][,][11][]] . These
results were confirmed and emphasised by larger landmark studies firmly establishing
liver surgery as a potentially curative treatment for CRLM [[][12][,][13][]] .
The era since has been characterised by progress in understanding of tumour
biology as well as surgical and oncological developments. These overlapping and
interdependent factors have directed the modern management of CRLM to a
multidisciplinary approach involving radiology (cross sectional, nuclear medicine and
interventional), Oncology, Liver surgery, Colorectal surgery, Histopathology, and
Specialist nursing [[][14][]] . The paramount importance of the MDT cannot be
overemphasised as it represents the forum where key management decisions are made
after consideration of information spanning many different disciplines, with
demonstrable benefits in terms of significant treatment alterations [[][15][,][16][]], numbers of
patient offered resection [[][17][,][18][]], and ultimately translating into improved survival [[][19][,][20][]] .
In the following review, we present modern management of CRLM. In order to
assist the reader, section contents are provided below: (1) Diagnosis and staging of
CRLM post resection of CRC; (2) Tumour characterisation and biomarkers in CRC; (3)
Systemic and locoregional chemotherapy and targeted agents in CRLM management;
(4) Surgical management of resectable CRLM; and (5) Histopathological assessment of
resected CRLM.

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
The detection of CRLM is achieved during staging investigations in the case of
synchronous CRLM and by post CRC resection surveillance programmes in the case of
metachronous CRLM. The section below discusses the timing and epidemiology of
metachronous CRLM, an understanding of which is essential in judging the
effectiveness of post CRC resection surveillance practice. The section also describes
current optimal staging of CRLM, and finally current practice as it applies to
surveillance after resection of CRLM.

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
_
Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide and accounts for 10% of
all cancers. It is a major cause of morbidity and the second most common cause of
cancer related mortality [[][1][]] .
Although it is regularly reported that approximately 50% of patients with colorectal
cancer develop liver metastases, either as synchronous or metachronous disease [[][21][-][25][]],
this is likely an exaggeration of true incidence originating from an historic autopsy
study of patients who died with colorectal cancer [[][26][]] . Large epidemiological studies
from multiple European centres demonstrate the incidence of both synchronous and
metachronous liver metastases in patients with colorectal cancer to be lower, at
approximately 25% [[][27][-][31][]] . The incidence of synchronous liver metastases in
epidemiological studies ranges from 13.8%–17.1% [[][27][,][29][,][30][]] and the rate of metachronous
liver metastases in these studies ranges from 7.6%–15.1% [[][27][,][29][,][30][,][32][]] . The interval between
primary diagnosis and the detection of metastatic disease used in the literature ranges
from the time of primary resection [[][29][]], to 3 mo [[][29][,][33][]], or 6 mo after diagnosis, and this lack
of a consensus regarding the definition of metachronous metastases may partly
explain the reported variation [[][24][,][32][]] . Further confounders include evolution in the
sensitivity of pre-operative staging, and the reported increase in synchronous
disease [[][28][]] . CRLM occur more frequently in male patients and in patients with left sided
CRC, relating to embryological origin of the primary tumour [[][27][,][30][]] .
With regards to metachronous disease, most recurrences occur early in follow up:
76%-85.3% occur within a year and 83%-97.5% within 3 years, with 30%-40% of
patients having disease confined to the liver [[][33][,][34][]] . Approximately 2% of patients will
develop liver metastases between 5 and 10 years after resection of the primary
tumour [[][27][,][29][,][33][]] .

_

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
_
Surveillance programmes accompanied the widespread introduction of liver resection
for CRLM, to detect recurrent disease early, with a view to improve survival. A metaanalysis of five randomised controlled trials published in 2002 supported this
hypothesis by demonstrating a survival benefit associated with more intensive follow

WJCO https://www.wjgnet.com 763 October 24, 2020 Volume 11 Issue 10

Martin J _et al._ Colorectal liver metastase

up regimes [[][35][]] . This encouraged the introduction of more intensive surveillance
programmes, although a subsequent large multicentre randomised control trial
performed in the United Kingdom by Primrose _et al_ [[][36][]] failed to replicate these findings.
In this study, intensive surveillance regimes with computed tomography (CT) with or
without carcino-embryonic antigen (CEA) resulted in an increased rate of surgical
treatment with curative intent, but this failed to translate to improved survival when
compared to the minimal surveillance group [[][36][]] . Interestingly, the reported incidence of
metachronous disease in this study was markedly lower than that reported in the
previous meta-analysis (8.4% _vs_ 32%). The stage-specific case mix and risk of
recurrence within tumour stage across studies remained similar but one explanation
for this reported difference was possibly superior pre-operative staging. This would
provide an explanation for the previously reported improved benefit of more intensive
follow up programmes with early recurrence in these older studies representing
undetected residual disease [[][36][]] . A further meta-analysis published in 2016 of 15
randomised controlled trials came to a similar conclusion to that of Primrose _et al_ [[][36][]]
and demonstrated no overall survival benefit with more intensive follow up
regimes [[][36][,][37][]] .
In summary, surveillance programmes with either regular CEA or CT increase the
likelihood of detecting recurrent disease and result in an increased proportion of
patients undergoing surgical treatment with curative intent. This has not, however,
been shown to translate into improved patient survival in trials. This counter-intuitive
finding may partially be explained by the failure of randomised trials to detect small
differences: If 25% of patients develop CRLM post CRC resection, of which 25% are
operable, and of which 25% are 10 year survivors, the difference in overall survival in
a surveillance group may prove beyond detection. In practice, the real world
observation of lives saved following resection of metachronous CRLM has resulted in
the continued adoption of surveillance programmes using CT and serum CEA,
although the additional value of the latter has been difficult to demonstrate in trials [[][36][]] .

_

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
_
Imaging has an important role in defining optimal treatment of CRLM. Knowing the
size, location and vascular relationships of CLRM is essential prior to treatment
planning and assessment of neoadjuvant response. Imaging techniques include
ultrasound, CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and fluoro-18-deoxyglucose (FDG)
positron emission tomography (PET-CT).

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
Ultrasound has a limited role in pre-operative evaluation as it has a low
sensitivity (64%) for CRLM compared with other imaging modalities [[][38][]] . In recent years
contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) has become widely used to characterise liver
lesions based on dynamic assessment of tumour vascularity. CEUS has a reported
sensitivity of 80%–90%, comparable to CT and is significantly more sensitive than
grey-scale ultrasound for detecting small CRLM less than 10 mm [[][39][,][40][]] . Nevertheless,
CEUS does not offer comprehensive information needed for surgical planning as
compared to CT or MRI. Intra-operative ultrasound (IOUS) has an established role in
lesion detection and mapping of major hepatic vessels during surgery. IOUS has been
shown to identify new lesions in 16% of patients and alter clinical management in
9% [[][41][]] . Contrast enhanced IOUS has higher sensitivity and specificity than traditional
IOUS particularly for detection of “disappearing” lesions in the setting of neoadjuvant
therapy [[][42][,][43][]] .

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
CT is the modality of choice for detection of liver and
extrahepatic metastases. The high spatial resolution of CT combined with isotropic
pixel size enables reformatted images in various planes, which enables better
delineation of tumour and adjacent vascular structures for accurate segmental
localisation [[][44][]] . The portal venous phase (approximately 60-70 s after administration of
contrast agent) is the most reliable phase for detection of CRLM with a detection rate
of 85% and a positive predictive value of 96% [[][45][]] . CRLM are typically hypovascular
with variable heterogeneity depending on size and previous treatment. Since CRLM
are hypovascular, arterial phase imaging does not improve detection but is helpful for
pre-surgical or pre-embolisation planning [[][46][]] . The performance of CT is somewhat
limited in detecting CRLM < 10 mm which are interpreted as too small to
characterise [[][47][]] . In addition fatty liver is not uncommon post chemotherapy which can
further limit detection of liver metastases.

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
Compared to CT, MRI has superior soft tissue contrast
which makes it an invaluable tool for detection and characterisation of CRLM
particularly those below < 10 mm [[][48][]] . CRLM are typically T1-hypointense, mildly T2
WJCO https://www.wjgnet.com 764 October 24, 2020 Volume 11 Issue 10

Martin J _et al._ Colorectal liver metastase

hyperintense with heterogeneous but predominantly rim enhancement in the arterial
phase and hypo-enhancement in portal venous and delayed phases. Two advances
which have revolutionised the role of MRI in the last decade are diffusion weighted
imaging (DWI) and the use of hepatocyte-specific contrast agents. DWI measures the
mobility of water molecules in tissues. Apparent diffusion coefficient values are
quantitative estimates of diffusion restriction. CRLM show restricted diffusion of
water molecules due to their hypercellular nature which manifests as high signal
intensity lesions with low apparent diffusion coefficient values. Addition of DWI
improves sensitivity and specificity for lesion detection and characterisation [[][49][,][50][]] .
Hepatocyte-specific contrast agents are highly sensitive for detection of small lesions,
which may be virtually occult on other sequences [[][51][]] . This also allows for detection of
“disappearing” lesions which can mimic complete response to neoadjuvant therapy [[][52][]] .
Gadobenate dimeglumine (MultiHance, Bracco) and gadoxetate disodium (Eovist,
Bayer) are both hepatocyte-specific contrast agents which are preferentially taken up
by hepatocytes and excreted into the biliary tree. In the delayed hepatobiliary phase
(10–120 min after administration) normal hepatocytes are hyperintense compared to
liver metastases, which do not retain the contrast agent. DWI has similar sensitivity
and specificity as MRI with extracellular contrast agent but lower sensitivity than MRI
with hepatocyte-specific contrast agent [[][53][]] .

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
There is lack of clinical
evidence to show that Fluorine [18] labelled Positron Emission Tomography/Computed
Tomography ( [18] FDG PET-CT) has significant impact on the clinical management of
localised non-metastatic colorectal cancer preoperatively [[][54][]] . Its role in the initial
assessment colorectal cancer, therefore, is not yet established [[][55][]] . Most centres do not
carry out a routine [18] FDG PET-CT at this stage.
18FDG PET-CT is considered to be very accurate and sensitive in the detection of
CRLM, especially those greater than 10 mm [[][56][]] . However, small liver metastases (< 10
mm) and liver metastases from some mucinous adenocarcinomas can be missed [[][57][-][59][]] .
18FDG PET-CT has been found to be accurate in identifying extrahepatic metastasis.
Some studies suggest addition of [18] FDG PET-CT can lead to change in management in
over one-third of patients avoiding unnecessary metastasectomy [[][60][-][62][]], with a significant
impact on survival [[][63][]] . However, other studies have disputed this and found only a
modest 8% change in surgical management with 6% of false positive findings [[][64][,][65][]] . The
role of [18] FDG PET-CT in addition to standard imaging of CT chest, abdomen and
pelvis, and MR liver in presurgical patients remains uncertain. Some authors have
proposed it could be used as problem solving modality [[][66][]] to identify extrahepatic
metastases in high risk patients [[][48][]] . Despite its shortcomings, [18] FDG PET-CT remains
part of our imaging algorithm prior to hepatic metastasectomy.
There is insufficient evidence for the use [18] FDG PET-CT on routine surveillance,
however, it does have a supplementary role in the context of rising CEA if CT fails to
identify the site of disease [[][67][]] .

_

Title: Colorectal liver metastases: Current management and future perspectives
Author: Martin
Content:
_
Given that over half of patients undergoing liver resection for CRLM develop
recurrence [[][68][]], that approximately half of these are hepatic only [[][69][]], and in the light of
favourable outcomes after re-hepatectomy (see section 4) for intra hepatic recurrence,
there is an intuitive and logical justification for surveillance following resection of
CRLM. However, there is considerable heterogeneity in surveillance practice [[][70][]], and
concerns have been raised regarding the implications of irradiation [[][71][]] and health care
costs [[][72][]] .
Defining optimal surveillance requires a knowledge of when recurrence occurs, and
how best to detect it. In a retrospective multi-institution cohort study of 2320 patients
undergoing initial hepatectomy for CRLMs, Hallet _et al_ [[][73][]] reported that 89.1% of
recurrences developed within 3 years. Recurrence was intrahepatic in 46.2%,
extrahepatic in 31.8% and combined intra/extrahepatic in 22%.
Despite this concentration of recurrence in the early years, and many surveillance
protocols suggesting follow up for 5 years [[][69][,][74][]], there is consistent evidence of
recurrence occurring beyond 5 years in a significant minority of patients. Pulitanò
_et al_ [[][75][]] reported that whilst 93% of recurrences occurred within the first 5 years of
follow-up, 11% of patients who were disease-free at 5 years developed later
recurrence. Similarly, Tomlinson _et al_ [[][76][]] found that of patients who were found to be
disease free at 5 years, 23% had a documented first recurrence after 5 years, and
Viganò _et al_ [[][77][]] reported that 15% of the patients disease-free at 5 years developed later
recurrence.
