points were overall survival (OS), quality of life outcomes,
physical fitness, safety, programme adherence and eco­
nomic evaluations. The feasibility of change in exercise
behaviour was confirmed previously. [9]
At a median follow-up of 7.9 years, DFS was significantly
improved in the exercise group compared with the health
education group [hazard ratio (HR) 0.72, 95% confidence
interval (CI) 0.55-0.94, _P_ = 0.02]. [8] The 5-year DFS rate was
80.3% in the exercise group versus 73.9% in the health
education group. OS was also improved in the exercise
group versus the health education group (HR 0.63, 95% CI
0.43-0.94). [8] The exercise intervention achieved the goal of
increasing moderate-to-vigorous physical activity from
baseline by ∼10 MET-hours per week throughout the
entire 3-year programme, which is the equivalent of adding
∼45-60 minutes of brisk walking three or four times per
week or 25-30 minutes of jogging three or four times per
week. There were also meaningful improvements in
cardiorespiratory fitness and physical functioning. [8]
During the programme, adherence to mandatory
behavioural support sessions reduced from 83% to 63%,
and adherence to exercise sessions changed from 79% for
the mandatory supervised sessions (only applicable for
months 1-6) to 44% for the recommended supervised
sessions (during months 13-36). [8] The as-treated safety
analysis reported musculoskeletal adverse events (AEs) in
18.5% of patients in the exercise group versus 11.5% in the
health education group. These included arthritis as well as
joint, back, limb and muscle pain, and were grade ≥3 in
0.7% of patients ( _n_ = 3) in the exercise group and 0.2% of
patients ( _n_ = 1) in the health education group. Grade ≥3
AEs were reported in 15.4% of patients in the exercise
group versus 9.1% in the health education group. [8]
CHALLENGE provides the first high-level evidence of a
clinically meaningful and statistically significant DFS benefit
from a structured exercise programme in patients with
resected high-risk localised colon cancer after completion
of adjuvant ChT. Randomisation, stratification and a large

sample size likely ensured equal distribution of known and
unknown potential confounders between study arms. As
such, the trial provides key evidence that reinforces the
value of survivorship plans that integrate physical exercise
and other health-promoting measures. The study also es­
tablishes a new standard of care for selected patients in
specific clinical and socioeconomic contexts, and advocates
for the development of formal structured exercise pro­
grammes for patients with resected colon cancer after
completion of adjuvant ChT.
CHALLENGE is also associated with limitations related to
completeness or generalisability that necessitate clear
communication, shared decision making and investigation of
feasibility between health care professionals and patients.
Limitations include: (i) inclusion of selected relatively fit pa­
tients (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group PS score 0-1,
limited comorbidities, young age) completing adjuvant ChT,
(ii) insufficient information on distribution and nature of dropouts and censoring events, (iii) unknown implementability of
the exercise programme in the absence of required in­
frastructures (e.g. supervised sessions, health coaching) or
support (e.g. travelling, absence from work, financial toxicity
for patients), (iv) unknown impact of potential adaptations of
the exercise programme on clinical benefits (e.g. reduced
intensity or frequency for patients who are older, less fit or
less able to tolerate exercise, optimal initiation time),
(v) pending mature follow-up from CHALLENGE and the lack
of independent confirmation from other trials or high-quality
prospective observational studies, (vi) absence of results from
economic analyses on the cost effectiveness of the strategy
and on the biology-informed selection of patients who benefit
most.
Algorithms for the adjuvant treatment of stage II and
stage III colon cancer are provided in Figures 1 and 2.

Author: Hagen

_ A 65-year-old man underwent colonoscopy
to evaluate rectal bleeding and was found to have a low rectal
mass. Biopsy revealed moderately differentiated microsatellite
stable adenocarcinoma. The tumor was palpable at the
fingertip in the anterior rectum with the inferior border
5 cm from the anal verge by rigid proctoscopy. CEA was
0.8 ng/mL. CT imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis
showed no evidence of distant metastases. MRI confirmed
a 5-cm mass with one 8-mm mesorectal lymph node
metastasis and no extramural venous invasion. The tumor
penetrated the mesorectal fat to a depth of 4 mm, and the
circumferential margin was estimated to be 1 mm from the
tumor (Fig. 1). He was presented at the multidisciplinary
tumor board conference and interviewed and examined
at the multidisciplinary clinic. He was dismayed at the
prospect of his surgical options, a low anterior resection
versus abdominoperineal resection, and wished to keep the
options for organ preservation available. Standard longcourse chemoradiation was initiated, with resolution of his
bleeding after 2 weeks. He then completed 6 cycles of folinic
acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) chemotherapy
(consolidation total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT)). The
tumor was no longer palpable on office examination. A
complete clinical response (cCR) was confirmed by flexible
sigmoidoscopy (Fig. 2) and MRI (Fig. 3). He was entered
into the nonoperative management program with intense
surveillance scheduling and has no evidence of recurrent
disease almost 2 years after completion of TNT.

Title: Organ Preservation in the Treatment of Stage II and III Rectal Cancer
Author: Hagen
Content:
_

More than 40,000 Americans are diagnosed with rectal
cancer every year. Optimal management of rectal cancer
requires a multidisciplinary team to appropriately evaluate and treat a problem with a myriad of possible interventions. These options include variations of multimodality
treatment, including surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. The complexity of this topic is reflected in recent
related quality and patient safety projects, including the
American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons Best Practices Checklist and the National Accreditation Program
for Rectal Cancer. For the past few decades, stage II and
stage III rectal cancers have been treated with trimodality
therapy, including chemoradiation, surgery, and chemotherapy. Recently, a transition toward TNT has increased
the number of patients who have a pathologic complete
response after proctectomy. This has led patients and clinicians alike to wonder if there is a role for avoiding surgery if a cCR is seen after TNT. The terminology for this
approach has varied but includes nonoperative management, watch and wait, or organ preservation.

Title: Organ Preservation in the Treatment of Stage II and III Rectal Cancer
Author: Hagen
Content:
_

Until recently, standard treatment of stage II and stage III
rectal cancer was neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed
by TME 8 to 12 weeks after the last dose of radiation. This
was followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. Although local
recurrence with this treatment regimen is low, one quarter
or more of patients die from distant metastases, and one
third never receive postoperative chemotherapy because
of postoperative complications, frailty, or patient refusal. [2]
TNT was developed as an option to deliver all chemotherapy before surgery to allow early systemic treatment
of possible micrometastases at a time when the patient
is most apt to tolerate it. [2] Early studies exploring organ
preservation found that at least 20% to 40% of patients
receiving neoadjuvant therapy or TNT for rectal cancer
will have a cCR characterized by absence of tumor at digital rectal examination, endoscopy, and dedicated MRI. [3,4]
Radiological assessment by T2-weighted magnetic resonance sequences will provide relevant information regarding tumor response to treatment. Usually, the presence of
low-signal intensity is consistent with complete tumor
regression and replacement by fibrotic tissue. Diffusionweighted sequences may potentially provide additional
support of a complete response by showing absence of restriction to the movement of water molecules. Endoscopically, a white scar or even a completely normal shining
mucosa should be present among these patients. [5] The pioneering work of Habr-Gama in Brazil used 5-fluorouracil
(5-FU)–based chemotherapy, and additional data from a
multicenter US trial has shown high rates of pathologic
complete response using combination chemotherapy with
FOLFOX. [3,6] Patients with a cCR may not benefit from
TME, and the benefit of surgery needs to be weighed against the risk of TME, including the need for a perma

nent colostomy if sphincter salvage is not possible, and
low anterior resection syndrome (LARS) in those who do
have sphincter salvage. LARS is a condition characterized
by urgency, frequent bowel movements, bowel movement
fragmentation, and fecal incontinence. [7] For some patients
with a cCR, especially those with a high risk for LARS or
the need for a permanent colostomy, organ preservation
may be an attractive option if oncologic outcomes are not
compromised. [3] It must be mentioned, though, that there
is evidence of symptoms similar to LARS with chemoradiation as well. [8] Patients will certainly prefer better functional outcomes, but equally important are their oncologic
outcomes, and groups are starting to develop methods to
predict this. Jimenez et al have formulated a DNA Repair
Deregulation Score to identify those tumors that will have
a poor response to neoadjuvant therapy. [9] Unanswered
questions with attempted organ preservation strategy are [1]
whether recurrences can be salvaged by TME when the tumor is detected and [2] if regrowth or persistent disease will
seed metastases that could have been avoided with an upfront operation.
Neoadjuvant radiation for rectal cancer may be administered as long course or short course. Long-course
chemoradiotherapy consists of radiosensitizing infusional
5-FU or daily capecitabine (oral 5-FU) combined with 50
Gy of radiation in 25 to 28 fractions over 6 weeks. Shortcourse radiotherapy consists of 25 Gy in 5 fractions over
1 week, followed by an operation within 3 to 5 days or after a 4- to 8-week delay. Available data to support organ
preservation have been based on long-course treatment.
When choosing a TNT strategy, there are incomplete data
to support the choice to begin treatment with chemoradiation versus chemotherapy. Current National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines include a TNT option
that begins with chemotherapy but not chemoradiation.
Induction chemotherapy gives the most substantial systemic therapy at the earliest possible time, which may reduce distant failure. On the other hand, there is a theoretic

rates of 3-year disease-free survival and distant metastasisfree survival. [10]
The optimal surveillance strategy has not been established, and there is not yet a consistent standardized
practice model. A proposed algorithm for an organ preservation approach is shown in the algorithm. This strategy
uses endoscopic examination and MRI based on previous
trials that did not find utility in scar biopsies or endoscopic
ultrasound in assessing regrowth or persistent disease. At
this time there is no consensus on mandatory biopsies in
the area of treated tumor, and a biopsy is not required to
define a cCR in the OPRA trial. Future studies will define
the best way to predict a complete response, using molecular and tumor characteristics, and the best methods and
intervals to evaluate for regrowth or persistent disease.
Currently, available data suggest that the vast majority of regrowths (84%) detected in an intensive surveillance program are salvageable by surgery. [11] Observational
studies have shown that patients with local regrowth are

also at elevated risk for metastatic disease. [12] The functional benefits of organ preservation will need to be
weighed against emerging studies assessing the risk of
regrowths not salvageable by TME or regrowths seeding
distant metastases.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
# Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique

Dr CAROLINE BASTID [ a], Pr EMMANUEL CORON [ a], Dr JEREMY MEYER [ b], Pr FRÉDÉRIC RIS [ b], Pr GUILLAUME MEURETTE [ b] et Dr THIBAUD KOESSLER [ c]

_Rev Med Suisse 2023 ; 19 : 938-43  |  DOI : 10.53738/REVMED.2023.19.827.938_

Le cancer colorectal représente 4500 nouveaux cas par an en
Suisse. Son incidence chez les sujets de plus de 50 ans semble se
stabiliser, mais chez les plus jeunes elle est en augmentation. La
révolution technologique guide sa prise en charge. L’intelligence
artificielle en endoscopie optimise la détection de ­petites lésions
coliques. La dissection sous-muqueuse permet de traiter des
­lésions parfois étendues à un stade précoce de la maladie.
­L’amélioration des techniques chirurgicales, notamment par robot,
vise à limiter les complications et à ­optimiser la conservation
d’organes. Les outils moléculaires aboutissent au développement
de thérapies ciblées prometteuses pour les ­maladies localisées
ou celles avancées. Le ­développement des centres de référence
tend à rassembler cette expertise.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
_Colorectal cancer represents 4500 incidental cases in Switzerland_
_per year, with an incidence increasing among the youngest patients._
_Technological innovation guides the management of colorectal_
_­cancer. Artificial intelligence in endoscopy optimizes the detection_
_of small colonic lesions. Submucosal dissection allows treating_
_­extensive lesions at an early stage of the disease. The improvement_
_of surgical techniques, notably robotic surgery, allows limiting_
_­complications and optimizing organ preservation. Molecular tools_
_are leading to the development of promising targeted therapies for_
_localized or advanced disease. The development of reference_
_­centers tends to bring together this expertise._

INTRODUCTION

Le cancer colorectal (CCR) est le 2 [e] cancer chez l’homme et le
3 [e] chez la femme, il représente 4500 nouveaux cas par an et
entraîne 1700 décès par an en Suisse. On note, depuis
­plusieurs années, une tendance à une stabilisation, voire une
diminution progressive de l’incidence chez les sujets de plus
de 50 ans. Le dépistage organisé du CCR, depuis 2013,
­contribue largement à cette constatation. Malheureusement,
l’incidence augmente dans la population plus jeune (< 50 ans),
non concernée par le programme de dépistage. Cette observation a conduit les États-Unis à abaisser l’âge du début du
dépistage à 45 ans, ce qui n’est pas encore le cas en Suisse.

vous présente les avancées technologiques et thérapeutiques
qui y participent.

C. Bastid et E. Coron
L’intelligence artificielle ou la révolution diagnostique

Une révolution majeure concernant la prévention du CCR
vient de l’intelligence artificielle (IA) et de sa capacité à ­détecter
les lésions précancéreuses. En sachant que 25 % des polypes
sont manqués lors d’une coloscopie, il est difficile de ne pas se
pencher sur les nouvelles aides à la détection apportées par l’IA

2 groupes : coloscopie assistée par IA (n = 1519) et conven­

32,4 %), d’adénomes avancés (6,6 vs 4,9 %), d’adénomes détectés
par les endoscopistes experts (42,3 vs 32,8 %) étaient tous
­significativement améliorés par l’IA. Le message est donc que
l’IA n’est pas simplement intéressante pour pallier les carences
des « mauvais détecteurs » mais qu’elle est également une aide
pour les endoscopistes confirmés, au prix d’une légère augmentation du temps de retrait de la coloscopie (8,3 vs 7,8 min).
La deuxième étude par Repici et coll.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:

de 685 patients ayant eu des coloscopies de dépistage ou de
surveillance, des symptômes ou un test FIT positif dans
3 centres italiens. Le taux de détection des adénomes était
­significativement supérieur dans le groupe IA (55 %) par rapport
au groupe coloscopie conventionnelle (40 %). Cette différence
était particulièrement élevée pour des adénomes < 5 mm sans
augmentation du temps de retrait (environ 7 min).

En résumé, l’IA est un réel apport, que l’on soit débutant ou
­expert, pour détecter des petites lésions et enrôler les patients
dans des programmes de surveillance. Les perspectives du
­futur proche sont de combiner cette détection augmentée avec
une prédiction très fiable du type histologique de polype. Ceci
permettrait de déterminer l’intervalle de surveillance sans
­engendrer de coût ni de retard liés à l’analyse histologique, et
les premières études dans ce sens sont très encourageantes.

Author: Bastid
Content:
|17 mai 2023|

La laparoscopie est l’approche minimalement invasive la plus
pratiquée pour la chirurgie du CCR, mais présente des limitations inhérentes à la technique. La chirurgie robotique, quant
à elle, permet de dépasser les limites techniques de la laparo­
scopie en offrant notamment 7 degrés de liberté, des instruments dont l’angulation est plus significative, la démultipli­
cation et le lissage des mouvements, une vision 3D, et la
­possibilité de réalité augmentée. Cependant, l’approche robotique n’est toujours pas devenue le standard en chirurgie du
CCR, pour des raisons de coûts, de disponibilité et de manque
de preuves scientifiques de sa supériorité.

Cancer du côlon droit

Par conséquent, la laparoscopie reste l’approche préférentielle pour 90,5 % des colectomies droites minimalement
­invasives effectuées au Danemark et 96,2 % aux États-Unis.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Cependant, la laparoscopie ne permet pas de réaliser aisément
une anastomose intracorporelle, avec comme conséquences
une mobilisation du côlon droit intracorporelle, mais une
­réalisation de l’anastomose iléo-colique le plus souvent de
manière extracorporelle par incision médiane. Seuls 4,5 % des
patients bénéficient d’une anastomose intracorporelle durant
une colectomie droite minimalement invasive.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Comme
­corollaire, une incision médiane constitue le site d’extraction
préférentiel chez 81,6 % des patients.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Aux Hôpitaux universitaires de Genève, nous sommes
convaincus que la robotique permet de faciliter la réalisation
d’une anastomose intracorporelle lors d’une colectomie
droite, et d’extraire le spécimen opératoire plus simplement
par Pfannenstiel, et, dès lors, proposons une telle procédure à
des patients sélectionnés (

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
). Une anastomose intracorporelle présente plusieurs avantages par rapport à sa
­variante extracorporelle : durée de séjour plus courte, reprise
du transit plus rapide, plus faible incidence d’infection de site
opératoire et cicatrisation de plaies opératoires plus
courte.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
L’extraction du spécimen opératoire par incision
médiane présente un risque d’éventration de 10,6 % tandis
que ce risque n’est que de 0,9 % si le site d’extraction est une
incision de Pfannenstiel.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Finalement, l’approche robotique
permet aussi de réaliser de manière minimalement invasive
une CME (complete mesocolic excision) chez des patients
­sélectionnés,

Author: Bastid
Content:
Cancer du rectum

Sur le plan de la chirurgie oncologique du cancer du rectum,
la TME (total mesorectal excision)

Author: Bastid
Content:
peut se heurter à des
difficultés techniques importantes, notamment chez le
­patient masculin, avec pelvis étroit et en surpoids, nécessitant alors une conversion en chirurgie ouverte. De surcroît,
l’approche ­laparoscopique conduit parfois à des résections
incomplètes du mésorectum par rapport à la chirurgie
­ouverte.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Ces difficultés techniques ont conduit à développer une
­technique complémentaire de résection transanale dans le
plan de la TME, dénommée taTME (transanal total meso­
rectal excision).

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Par conséquent, la chirurgie robotique, qui
trouve son terrain de prédilection dans le pelvis, a constitué
une innovation bienvenue. En 2017, l’étude ROLARR ajoute à
la controverse en ne démontrant pas de diminution de
­l’incidence de conversion en chirurgie ouverte de l’approche
robotique par rapport à l’approche laparoscopique pour les
cancers du bas et moyen rectum.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Cette étude a été quelque
peu critiquée en raison de l’hétérogé­néité de l’expertise des
chirurgiens participants. Plus récemment, l’étude REAL a elle
confirmé que la chirurgie robotique permettait d’obtenir de
meilleurs résultats à court terme que la chirurgie laparoscopique pour les cancers du bas et moyen rectum.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
L’approche
robotique permet d’obtenir une meilleure préservation des
sphincters (+5,8 %), moins de conversion en chirurgie ouverte
(-2,2 %), de complications intra-opératoires (-3,3 %) ou post­
opératoires (-6,9 %), un temps plus court jusqu’au premier
passage de selles (-11,8 heures) et une durée de séjour moins
longue (-1 jour). Malgré ces avantages incontestables, reste la
question du coût plus élevé de l’approche robotique.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Nous
proposons cependant de pondérer ce surcoût par les meilleurs
résultats de cette approche, qui constituent autant d’économies indirectes.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
En conclusion, nous sommes convaincus que dans un avenir
proche, la chirurgie robotique deviendra le nouveau
­standard de soins pour la chirurgie minimalement invasive
du CCR.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
OUTILS MOLÉCULAIRES ET THÉRAPIES CIBLÉES
T. Koessler
Cancer colorectal localisé

Comme chaque année (ou presque) les recommandations
­européennes pour la prise en charge du CCR changent.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Cette année, la première thérapie ciblée a fait son apparition
dans le traitement des CCR localisés. Dans une étude de phase II
à un bras, une immunothérapie anti-PD-1, dostarlimab, a été
administrée à 12 patients atteints d’un cancer du rectum localisé porteur d’une instabilité microsatellitaire (MSI-H). Après
un suivi d’au moins 6 mois, les évaluations cliniques, radiologiques et endoscopique ont montré une disparition du cancer
chez 100 % des patients.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Une seconde étude prospective à un
bras a traité 112 patients ­atteints d’un cancer du côlon localisé
MSI-H. Après 6 semaines de traitement néoadjuvant (2 injections de nivolumab (anti-PD1) et une injection d’ipilimumab
(anti-CTLA-4)), tous les ­patients ont été opérés. L’examen
pathologique n’a pas retrouvé de tumeur dans 67 % et une
­réponse quasi-totale a été observée dans 95 % des cas. Pour
l’une ou l’autre de ces études, les données de suivi à long
terme sont encore attendues. Il est important de noter que
ces résultats ont été obtenus chez des patients dont la tumeur
était MSI-H, soit 0,5 à 1 % des cancers du rectum et 10‑15 % des
cancers du côlon. L’immunothérapie néoadjuvante ne fait
pas encore partie des recommandations pour les tumeurs
­localisées colorectales mais il apparaît évident qu’elle y sera
rapidement intégrée. Ces résultats extraordinaires avancent
l’idée que les traitements oncologiques du futur (proche) permettront de traiter la maladie oncologique tout en préservant
l’organe ­atteint, voire de la guérir sans opérer.

Cancer colorectal métastatique

Pour les CCR métastatiques, la prise en charge des patients
­nécessite la réalisation d’un profilage moléculaire de la tumeur
afin d’ajuster le traitement. Ces analyses séquencent un panel

de gènes (par exemple, _KRAS_, _NRAS_, _BRAF_ ), recherchent
­l’instabilité microsatellitaire (MSI-H) et l’amplification du
gène _HER-2_ (comme dans le cancer du sein). La présence ou
l’absence de ces altérations permet de donner un traitement
­ciblé. Pour les patients atteints d’un CCR métastatique MSI-H
(5 % des CCR métastatiques), une étude de phase III, a randomisé 307 patients à recevoir soit une chimiothérapie, soit une
immunothérapie (pembrolizumab – anti PD-1) en première
ligne. Les patients sous immunothérapie montrent une survie
sans progression significative de 16,5 mois versus 8,2 mois pour
ceux sous ­chimiothérapie. De plus, 43,8 % des patients traités
par immunothérapie ont vu leur tumeur diminuer de taille
contre 33,1 % pour ceux sous chimiothérapie.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Un bénéficie sur
la survie des patients n’a pas pu être montré car 60 % des
­patients du bras contrôle ont reçu de l’immunothérapie à leur
progression.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
L’immunothérapie est donc le meilleur traitement pour les 5 % des patients ­atteints d’un CCR métastatique
MSI-H et la première alternative thérapeutique sans chimiothérapie. Concernant les autres ­altérations moléculaires, elles
peuvent être prise en compte pour guider le traitement de
­deuxième (mutation _BRAF_ et MSI-H si pas utilisé en première
ligne) ou troisième ligne (amplification HER-2), tous avec des
régimes de traitements sans chimiothérapie.

Title: Cancer colorectal : révolution technologique
Author: Bastid
Content:
Après les lignes standards

Finalement, pour les patients en impasse thérapeutique, les
HUG et le CHUV proposent ensemble un profilage moléculaire des tumeurs qui est ensuite discuté conjointement dans
un nouveau tumor board, appelé tumor board moléculaire.
Après une série d’analyses moléculaires poussées – séquençage
de 400 gènes, recherche d’amplification dans le génome entier,
de translocation ou d’infiltration par des cellules immunitaires
­inflammatoires, les cas sont discutés par les pathologues,
­biologistes et spécialistes d’organes afin de tenter de trouver
des ­alternatives thérapeutiques. Bientôt, débutera en Suisse le
projet SPO (Swiss Personalised Oncology) ; ce projet national
vise à analyser les tumeurs de 300 patients dont 100 atteints

Author: Bastid
Content:

Ces ­prélèvements seront analysés avec les technologies les
plus avancées (par exemple, séquençage de cellule unique,
­organoïde, etc.). Les résultats biologiques corrélés aux données
­cliniques seront discutés au tumeur board moléculaire et
­permettront de proposer de nouvelles pistes thérapeutiques.
Ce projet national collaboratif est un bond technique, techno­
logique et conceptuel en oncologie ; même s’il doit encore
­démontrer son bénéfice pour le patient.

En conclusion, les nouvelles technologies apportent un bénéfice
quantifiable requérant cependant une courbe d’apprentissage
pour leur maîtrise et un certain volume de pratique. Le
­développement de centres d’excellence permet une prise en
charge experte des patients grâce à une actualisation et une
application des nouveaux traitements, un perfectionnement
de l’apprentissage de ces techniques innovantes et la connaissance du réseau médical de référence.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
# Prise en charge du cancer du rectum ­localisé en 2024

Dre NATHALIE BAUDOUX [ a], Dr JEREMY MEYER [ b], Dr ANDRÉ DURHAM [ c], Dre CLAUDIA CORRO [ d], Pr FREDERIC RIS [ b],
Dre ILINCA CONSTANTINESCU [ e], Dre CAROLINE BASTID [ f] et Dr THIBAUD KOESSLER [ a,d]

_Rev Med Suisse 2024 ; 20 : 962-7  |  DOI : 10.53738/REVMED.2024.20.874.962_

La prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé a beaucoup
­évolué ces deux dernières années. D’un côté, l’intensification des
traitements (radio-chimiothérapie, chimiothérapie, puis chirurgie) pour les tumeurs les plus avancées a montré une amélioration des résultats cliniques par rapport aux traitements moins
intenses. De l’autre côté, la possibilité, comme pour les cancers
de la prostate, d’opter pour une surveillance active sans chirurgie
chez les patients présentant une réponse clinique complète
après une phase de traitement est aujourd’hui acceptée. Plus
récemment, les recommandations suisses pour la surveillance du
cancer du rectum ont été modifiées et se différencient maintenant
de celles des cancers du côlon, en incorporant IRM pelvienne et
rectoscopie en sus, de même qu’un suivi spécial pour les tumeurs
en surveillance active.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
_The management of localized rectal cancer has evolved significantly_
_over the last two years. On one hand, intensification of treatments_
_(radio-chemotherapy, chemotherapy, then surgery) for the most_
_advanced tumors has shown an improvement in clinical results_
_compared to less intense regiments. On the other hand, the possi-_
_bility, as for prostate cancers, of opting for active surveillance_
_­without surgery in patients presenting a complete clinical response_
_after a treatment phase, is now accepted. More recently, the Swiss_
_recommendations for the surveillance of rectal cancer have been_
_modified and now differ from those of colon cancers, by incorporating_
_pelvic MRI and rectoscopy in addition, as well as special guidelines_
_for tumors under active surveillance._

INTRODUCTION

Le cancer colorectal se classe au troisième rang des cancers les
plus fréquents chez les hommes en Suisse et au deuxième rang
chez les femmes, avec environ 4 500 nouveaux cas par an, dont
environ un tiers sont des cancers du rectum. En ce qui
concerne la mortalité, il constitue la troisième cause de décès
par cancer dans les deux sexes.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
L’incidence est restée stable
ces trente dernières années chez les femmes, tandis qu’elle a
baissé chez les hommes au cours des dix dernières années.

Les taux de mortalité liés à ce cancer ont également diminué
au cours de la même période avec un baisse de 45 % chez les
hommes et de 41 % chez les femmes, grâce notamment aux
programmes de dépistage et aux progrès thérapeutiques.

La prise en charge d’un cancer du rectum localisé dépend de
facteurs intrinsèques à la tumeur, tels que la localisation, la
classification TNM, le statut microsatellitaire, et de facteurs
propres au patient, tels que les comorbidités, l’état général ou
encore le souhait d’éviter une chirurgie ou une chimiothérapie.
Les plans thérapeutiques, souvent multimodaux, sont discutés
de manière multidisciplinaire dans un « tumor board » impliquant au minimum radiologues, pathologues, radiothérapeutes,
chirurgiens, gastroentérologues et oncologues. Nous allons
détailler, ci-après, le bilan d’extension, les différentes stratégies
thérapeutiques en fonction des stades et le suivi des patients
après traitement du cancer du rectum.

DIAGNOSTIC
Endoscopique
En dehors des examens de dépistage recommandés, la
­présence de symptômes tels que des saignements rectaux, des
douleurs abdominales, des perturbations du transit ou une
anémie devrait évoquer une suspicion de cancer du rectum.
Une endoscopie par voie basse permet de confirmer la présence d’une lésion suspecte, d’en préciser les caractéristiques
(limites, aspect déprimé ou ulcéré ou à extension latérale
(Laterally Spreading Tumors (LST)) avec potentiel de dégénérescence), et d’éventuellement la biopsier.

Une coloscopie complète avec préparation préalable sera
­préférée lorsque la lésion est franchissable afin de ne pas
méconnaître une tumeur synchrone du reste du côlon (environ
5 % des cas).

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
En cas de tumeur infranchissable, seul le rectum
sera exploré par rectoscopie.

Si un traitement endoscopique est souhaité et s’il existe un
critère de dégénérescence, une échoendoscopie rectale doit être
effectuée afin de confirmer le caractère superficiel de la lésion
et de s’assurer de l’absence de l’envahissement en profondeur
de la musculeuse ou d’adénopathie, car ces éléments constituent des contre-indications au traitement endoscopique.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Radiologique

L’IRM, la coloscopie et la rectoscopie rigide constituent les
­examens clés du bilan d’extension local des cancers du rectum.
L’IRM permet de définir la classification TNM, c’est-à-dire la

avec les structures avoisinantes, comme l’appareil sphinctérien, l’atteinte du mésorectum et du péritoine, caractérisée
par la marge circonférentielle (CRM) (correspondant à la
­distance entre la tumeur et le fascia recti) et l’extension
­vasculaire (envahissement veineux extramural (EMVI)).

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
La
coloscopie permet le diagnostic histologique et s’assure de
l’absence de tumeur synchrone alors que la rectoscopie rigide
décrit précisément la distance exacte entre la marge anale et
la tumeur. Les facteurs de risque pour une récidive locale
sont : a) le stade T3 avec envahissement du mésorectum de plus
de 5 mm de profondeur ; b) le stade T4 ; c) l’envahis­sement du
fascia mesorectal (CRM positive) ; d) l’invasion vasculaire
extra-murale (EMVI) et e) l’atteinte de l’appareil sphinctérien
(

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
). L’IRM détermine si un traitement néoadjuvant est
nécessaire et, le cas échéant, oriente le choix du traitement
approprié. Le bilan d’extension est complété par un scanner
thoraco-abdomino-pelvien à la recherche de métastases. Il
n’y a pas d’indication à faire un PET/CT systématiquement.

TRAITEMENT
Stades précoces : stades I (cT1/cT2, cN0, cM0)
Résection endoscopique (stades cT1, cN0)
Seules les lésions uT1N0 peuvent être candidates à un traitement par résection endoscopique.

Auparavant, la mucosectomie (Endoscopic Mucosal Resection
(EMR)) représentait la technique de référence, mais permettait
une résection en monobloc des lésions de moins de 20 mm
uniquement. En cas de résection en plusieurs fragments, soit
_piece meal_, il existe un risque de récidive nécessitant une
­surveillance endoscopique rapprochée au minium, voire une
prise en charge chirurgicale.

Lésion tumorale du moyen rectum (étoile blanche) envahissant toute
l’épaisseur de la paroi et s’étendant au mésorectum avec une marge
de résection circonférentielle (trait bleu) à plus de 2 mm. Il s’agit de la plus
petite distance mesurée entre le fascia recti (flèches oranges) et la tumeur.
Présence d’un ganglion pathologique (flèche verte) au sein du mésorectum.
La tumeur est donc classée radiologiquement T3 CRM+ N1.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
La dissection sous-muqueuse (Endoscopic Submucosal
­Dissection (ESD)) permet la résection de lésions de plus de
20 mm (jusqu’à 10 cm) tout en préservant le rectum. Elle
consiste en une résection en monobloc avec un objectif
­d’exérèses en marges microscopiquement saines (R0) afin
d’éviter le risque de récidive local.

Le geste endoscopique commence par un marquage circon­
férentiel de la muqueuse autour de la lésion avec une marge
de sécurité de 1 à 2 mm. Une injection sous-muqueuse est
ensuite effectuée créant un espace de clivage entre la lésion et
le plan musculaire. La dernière étape consiste en une dissection sous-muqueuse détachant la lésion du plan profond en
utilisant des couteaux d’électrocoagulation (

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
). Ce
geste est réalisé par un opérateur expérimenté. Il existe un
risque hémorragique et de perforation variant de 4 à 13 %
selon les études, traité le plus souvent par voie endoscopique
(

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Les deux méthodes
s’avèrent efficaces et satisfaisantes sur le plan oncologique
pour traiter les lésions de dysplasie de haut grade ou les
­cancers superficiels. L’avantage de l’ESD repose sur le caractère
minimalement invasif et la possibilité de réaliser le geste en
ambulatoire.

Résection chirurgicale
Lorsque qu’une résection endoscopique n’est pas envisageable,
le traitement consiste en une chirurgie devant inclure une
exérèse complète ou partielle du rectum, de son mésorectum
selon le concept de Total Mesorectal Excision (excision totale
du rectum et de son mésorectum (TME)), ainsi qu’une
­lymphadénectomie d’au moins 12 ganglions. En Suisse,
l’OFSP a décrété que cette chirurgie (lorsque la tumeur est
située entre 0 et 12 cm de la marge anale) devait être effectuée dans un centre de médecine hautement spécialisée ; en
Suisse romande, les centres accrédités pour la chirurgie du
rectum sont les HUG et le CHUV.

En cas de cancer du haut rectum (situé de 10 à 15 cm de la
marge anale), une résection antérieure haute avec excision
partielle du mésorectum (PME) s’étendant 5 cm en-dessous
de la tumeur est suffisante, sans nécessité d’un traitement
néoadjuvant. En cas de cancer du moyen (situé de 5 à 10 cm
de la marge anale) ou du bas rectum (situé à moins de 5 cm
de la marge anale), une TME s’impose. Dans le cas de cancer
du bas rectum, il convient aussi d’évaluer si l’exérèse peut
être partielle (dissection intersphinctérienne préservant
le sphincter externe) ou doit être complète (amputation
abdomino-périnéale avec dissection extra-sphinctérienne) au
niveau de l’appareil sphinctérien, ceci afin d’obtenir des
marges distales et/ou circonférentielles sans tumeur.

Le choix de procéder ou non à une reconstruction avec rétablissement de la continuité colorectale dépend de nombreux
facteurs, dont la fonction sphinctérienne pré-opératoire, la
préservation ou non de l’appareil sphinctérien, ainsi que les
attentes du patient.

La voie d’abord chirurgicale préférentielle doit être minimalement invasive

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
La laparoscopie reste la technique majoritairement
pratiquée mais peut conduire, spécialement chez le patient de
sexe masculin et en surpoids, à un risque élevé de conversion
en chirurgie ouverte

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Afin de compenser les limites de la laparoscopie,
la résection transanale (taTME) a été développée comme
complément à la TME transabdominale. Cette technique
requière un haut degré d’expertise sous peine de conduire à
des résultats insuffisants.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Plus récemment, la robotique a
émergé comme une alternative intéressante à la laparoscopie
(associée ou non à la taTME) pour la chirurgie du moyen et
bas rectum et a montré une diminution de la conversion en
chirurgie ouverte ainsi qu’à de meilleurs résultats en matière
de qualité de résection.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Finalement, en cas de cancer du rectum précoce (défini
comme T1sm1, d’un diamètre < 4 cm, avec bonne différenciation et absence d’invasion lymphovasculaire) présentant un
risque de métastase ganglionnaire faible, une exérèse locale
par abord transanal (soit par Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery (TEM), soit par Transanal Minimally Invasive Surgery
(TAMIS)) peut constituer une alternative à l’exérèse du
­rectum avec PME/TME chez des patients soigneusement
sélectionnés et informés.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Dans le cas de figure d’une non-réponse complète au traitement néoadjuvant ou d’une recroissance de la tumeur, une
chirurgie d’exérèse doit être pratiquée. Elle suit les mêmes

principes que pour le cancer du rectum localisé, mais peut
parfois nécessiter une résection au-delà des plans de la TME,
que ce soit par une Extralevator Abdominoperineal Excision
(ELAPE) ou alors une exentération pelvienne incluant
d’autres organes pelviens.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
L’étendue de la résection doit être
dictée par l’obtention de marges chirurgicales négatives et
pondérée par sa morbidité potentielle.

Stades avancés : stades II et III (cT3/cT4 cN0, cTx, cN+)
Impact de la radiothérapie ou de la radiochimiothérapie
~~néoadjuvante avant la chirurgie~~
Le bénéfice de la radiothérapie avant chirurgie par rapport à la
chirurgie seule, que ce soit en termes de gain de survie globale
ou de diminution du taux de récidive locale, est clairement
établi depuis plusieurs décennies.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
L’ajout d’une chimio­
thérapie radio-sensibilisante à base de 5-fluorouracile (5-FU)
­permet également de diminuer le taux de récidive locale (16,5 vs
9,4 %) et d’obtenir une réponse pathologique complète (pCR)
dans 12 % des cas.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Ainsi, une RCT d’une durée de 5 semaines
suivie d’une chirurgie 8 à 12 semaines après est le traitement
de référence pour la plupart des patients (

Author: Baudoux
Content:
).

Impact du traitement néoadjuvant total avant la chirurgie
Avec la RCT classique, le risque de métastases à distance est
de 20 à 30 % dans les 3 à 5 ans, ce qui soulève la question
­d’intensifier le traitement. Le traitement néoadjuvant total
(TNT), qui intègre une chimiothérapie avant ou après la RCT
néoadjuvante avant une chirurgie radicale, a été développé

Author: Baudoux

|15 mai 2024|

pour diminuer le risque de métastases à distance ainsi que la
taille de la tumeur et accroître la possibilité d’une surveillance active. Deux études de phase 3 ont montré le bénéficie
d’une approche TNT versus le traitement classique par RCT
néoadjuvante. L’étude RAPIDO incluait une radiothérapie
courte (5 jours) suivie de 18 semaines de chimiothérapie
(CAPOX ou FOLFOX), puis d’une chirurgie versus une RCT
suivie d’une chirurgie suivie ou non d’une chimiothérapie
adjuvante (

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Le régime intensifié a montré : une
diminution de 6 % (24 vs 30 %) du taux de récidive, une
­diminution de 7 % du risque de développer des métastases et
un doublement du taux de pCR (28 vs 14 %) mais sans gain de
survie globale et avec un taux de récidive locorégionale plus
important dans le groupe expérimental (10 vs 6 %).

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
La
­deuxième étude, PRODIGE-23, incluait une chimiothérapie
de FOLFIRINOX pendant 12 semaines suivie d’une RCT puis
d’une chirurgie et d’une chimiothérapie adjuvante versus RCT
suivi d’une chirurgie et d’une chimiothérapie adjuvante.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024
Author: Baudoux
Content:
Ce
régime intensifié a aussi montré un gain de 7 % sur la survie
sans maladie, 7 % sur la survie globale, 10 % sur la survie sans
métastase, et une augmentation de 16 % du taux de pCR (28 vs
12 %). L’incidence des effets secondaires de grade 3 ou plus
était similaire dans les 2 groupes. En revanche, le taux de
­neuropathie durant la phase adjuvante était diminué de
­moitié dans le groupe expérimental.

Une stratégie d’épargne de radiothérapie, utile par exemple
chez les femmes en âge de procréer souhaitant éviter un
risque de stérilité, a été évaluée dans l’étude de phase 3 de
non-infériorité PROSPECT.

Title: Prise en charge du cancer du rectum localisé en 2024

Stratégie de surveillance active dans les tumeurs peu avancées
La prise en charge thérapeutique des tumeurs rectales est
complexe et peut entraîner des complications importantes.
La chirurgie, en particulier, peut être associée à des dysfonctionnements urinaires, sexuels ou à une incontinence fécale.
Dans 12 à 28 % des cas, la tumeur présente une réponse pathologique complète (pCR) après un traitement néoadjuvant. De
plus, il est établi que les patients dont la tumeur est en pCR
ont un meilleur pronostic à long terme que ceux dont la
tumeur n’a que partiellement répondu.

Author: Baudoux
Content:
La sélection des patients éligibles pour une
stratégie de surveillance active doit être discutée dans un
­colloque multidisciplinaire afin de sélectionner adéquatement patient et traitement.

Place de l’immunothérapie

L’immunothérapie, principalement les anti-PD1 ou anti-PD-L1,
a été testée en combinaison avec les traitements néoadjuvants (RCT ou chimiothérapie) sans grand effet, possiblement en raison de la population non moléculairement
sectionnée, d’un timing d’injection ou d’un fractionnement
de la radiothérapie sous optimal. Les HUG ont lancé une
étude, PEMREC (NCT04109755), combinant une immunothérapie à une radiothérapie courte pour les patients microsatellites stables et instables. Cette combinaison a montré
des résultats intéressants dans des modèles murins avec des
tumeurs sans instabilité microsatellitaire.

La radiothérapie – en tant que stimulateur du système immunitaire – n’est pas nécessaire chez les patients présentant une
instabilité microsatellitaire (MSI-H), représentant 2 % des
cancers du rectum.

Content:

atteints d’un cancer du côlon diffère de celui d’un cancer du
rectum. En plus du suivi classique, il comprend une recto­
scopie et une IRM pelvienne. Une autre nouveauté est un
suivi spécifique pour les cancers du rectum pour lesquels une
stratégie de surveillance active est proposée et comporte un
suivi clinique, endoscopique et radiologique très rapproché
pendant 3 ans, période durant laquelle le risque de récidive
locale et à distance est le plus important.

CONCLUSION

La prise en charge des cancers du rectum localisés se
­complexifie rapidement. Bien que la guérison reste l’objectif
principal, la qualité de vie des patients après les traitements
oriente désormais les choix thérapeutiques, étant donné la
­diversité des options thérapeutiques disponibles. Face à ces
enjeux, il est important que cette prise en charge soit faite dans
des centres offrant l’accès à l’éventail complet des possibilités
thérapeutiques et de manière multidisciplinaire, intégrant
médecins spécialistes, infirmiers référents, nutri­tion­nistes,
physiothérapeutes et stomathérapeutes notamment.

Title: Organ preservation for rectal cancer (GRECCAR 2): a prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial
Author: Rullier
Content:
The standard treatment for rectal cancer is total
mesorectal excision with or without neoadjuvant
chemoradiotherapy according to initial staging
definition. [1,2] Surgery is associated with complications,
including death during the operation for 2% of patients, [3]
and early or late morbidity in 25–50% of patients. [4–6]
However, neoadjuvant radiotherapy leads to tumour
sterilisation in 16% of patients and is associated with a
good prognosis for the disease. [7] These findings allow the
possibility of saving the rectum in the case of an
excellent response after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.
Saving the rectum would be revolutionary, especially in

locally advanced rectal cancer, where it would be
associated with a dramatic improvement of quality of
life, mainly because most postoperative complications
due to surgery will disappear, as well as later
complications, such as a definitive colostomy, urogenital
dysfunctions, or gastro­intestinal disorders. [5] Saving the
rectum would also be an opportunity to save costs for
health-care systems because smaller tumours, which are
good candidates for rectum preservation, are
increasingly found now because of national bowel
cancer screening programmes.
Organ preservation is a new concept for patients with
rectal cancer treated by neoadjuvant therapy. [8] For

Title: Organ preservation for rectal cancer (GRECCAR 2): a prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial
Author: Rullier
Content:
Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced rectal
cancer at tumour stages T3T4 induces 16% of tumour
sterilisation. Organ preservation, by use of observation or local
excision, is a new concept proposed for good clinical responders
to avoid morbidity and side-effects of rectal excision.
We searched PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov for English-language
articles published between January, 2000, and January, 2017,
using the terms “rectal cancer” and “organ preservation” or
“watch and wait” or “local excision”. We identified a few studies,
mostly about the “watch and wait” strategy, which were either
single institution (from a pioneering Brazilian team), or
multicentre trials (Danish, British, and Dutch studies), but
included only a few participants (55–109); one included a
comparative, retrospective analysis. Moreover, patient selection
criteria in these studies were unclear. Studies that investigated
local excision for organ preservation also included few
participants. Investigators from the ACOSOG Z6041 phase 2
trial reported a national experience with 5% local recurrence and
88% survival at 3 years; however, they only included patients
with T2, nodal stage (N) 0 tumours in their study and did not
report long-term side-effects. Finally, a systematic research
published in January, 2017, did not identify any phase 3,
randomised trials in the setting of organ preservation for rectal
cancer treated by neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy.

Author: Rullier
Content:
We reported the first phase 3, multicentre, national
randomised trial comparing local excision and rectal excision in
clinical good responders after chemoradiotherapy for patients

response, the strategies of observation (watch-and-wait)
or transanal local excision are available. Singleinstitution, [9] retro­spective, [10] and prospective cohort
studies [11,12] have reported findings from use of the
observation strategy (15% to 30% of local recurrence
usually controlled by curative radical surgery and 58% to
92% stoma-free with survival up to 80% in most studies
at 2 or 3 years of follow-up). [9–12] Local excision has been
assessed in single-institution [13] and multicentre studies [14–17]
(but not comparative studies), all of which included very
few patients. Only one phase 2 US trial has reported the
experience of organ preservation at a national level,
including low rectal cancer at stage T2N0 treated by local
excision after chemoradiotherapy. [18] Results were
promising with less than 5% local recurrence and
88% survival at 3 years; however, this study could not
change standard practice of total mesorectal excision
because there was no comparative group. Moreover, only
patients with stage I (T2N0) tumours were included.
We therefore did a randomised clinical trial comparing
local excision with total mesorectal excision in patients
who were good responders after chemoradiotherapy for

with T2T3N0–1 low rectal cancer, with the objective to assess
both oncological and non-oncological issues. Results from our
study confirmed those from the ACOSOG Z6041 trial by
showing 40% pathological response ypT0 and showed that
patients with rectal cancer tumour stage T2 and even T3, but
with tumours of no more than 4 cm, are good candidates for
organ preservation. By using a three-step strategy including
clinical staging, clinical response, and pathological response,
organ preservation could occur in 46% of patients without risk
of missing positive mesorectal lymph nodes. The strategy
seemed oncologically safe because 3-year local recurrence and
disease-free survival did not differ between the local excision
and total mesorectal excision groups. Globally, the strategy of
local excision was not superior to conventional surgery,
because of a high rate of completion surgeries, which increased
morbidity and side-effects at 2 years. The findings also showed
that few positive lymph nodes (8%) occurred in such small
irradiated tumours, indicating that completion surgery should
be limited to less than 10% of patients (at stages ypT2/N1
and ypT3).

rectal tumours are the best candidates for this strategy.
Completion surgery could even be restricted further to patients
with high-risk ypT2-3 tumours after local excision. Using our
three-step strategy is oncologically secure and offers a
promising new standard in patients treated by
chemoradiotherapy for rectal cancer.

Patients were included before or after neoadjuvant

Title: Organ preservation for rectal cancer (GRECCAR 2): a prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial
Author: Rullier
Content:
We hypothesised that the incidence of each event of the
composite endpoint after local excision versus total
mesorectal excision for downstaged rectal cancer would
be the following: operative death 0 versus 2%, major
morbidity 5% versus 20%, severe complications 5%
versus 25–50%, and we expected local recurrence (5%)
and metastatic recurrence (10%) to be similar in both
groups, assuming that local excision would be as
successful as total mesorectal excision on those
oncological endpoints. [26] The proportion of patients
having at least one event was therefore expected to
be 25% versus 60% (for superiority); 46 patients per
group were required (α=0·05, power=90%, two-sided
χ² test). Assuming 10% of patients in the local excision
group would have a poor pathological response and
require a completion total mesorectal excision,
120 patients (60 in each group) were required. After

inclusion of 60 patients, the independent data monitoring
committee recommended to increase inclusions up to
72 per group due to an estimate of 20% of patients having
a poor pathological response after local excision.
Qualitative variables were compared at 2 years with the
χ² test or Fisher’s exact test when appropriate. The
composite endpoint and each of its components were
compared at 2 years after surgery between groups using
logistic mixed models adjusted on centres, tumour, and
nodal stages, in a modified intent-to-treat analysis (some
patients were excluded from analysis for eligibility
criteria or consent withdrawal). Missing data were
replaced by occurrence of the event. We also did a
sensitivity analysis excluding patients with missing
outcome data. Kaplan-Meier method or adapted KaplanMeier method handling deaths as a competing risk were
used for the estimation of 3-year disease-free and overall
survival, 3-year local, uncontrolled local, and metastatic
cumulative incidence rates. Patients were all censored at

(three were missing data), there were five at stage ypT0,
eight at ypT1, 14 at ypT2, and six at ypT3; five were ypN1
(five [18%] of 28 were from a total mesorectal excision)
and one had an R1 resection. 13 (39%) of 33 had a good
pathologic response of ypT0-1.
The sensitivity analyses excluding missing data
presented similar results to those obtained for the
primary endpoint. However, the exploratory analysis
showed variability in morbidity and severity of
complications according to type of surgery: the more
aggressive the surgery, the higher the complication rates
(table 4). The severity of complications was also
influenced by surgery; patients with local excision had
minor complications requiring medical or endoscopic
treatment mainly for rectal bleeding, whereas patients
with total mesorectal excision or completion total
mesorectal excision had severe complications requiring
reoperation for pelvic abscess, peritonitis, small bowel
obstruction, or colonic ischaemia. Three (6%) of
53 patients had early complications specifically related to
local excision alone, and one (2%) of 53 had late
complications related to local excision alone; all were
minor. The major complications occurring after local
excision alone (two pelvic abscess of 53) were due to
salvage total mesorectal excision for local recurrence.
Exploratory analyses according to the type of surgery
showed that cumulative 3-year local recurrence occurred
in five (9%) of 53 patients after local excision alone, two
(3%) of 61 patients after total mesorectal excision, and in
no patients after local excision plus completion total
mesorectal excision; metastatic recurrence was noted in
eight (15%) of 53, eight (13%) of 61, and four (14%) of 28
in the local excision, total mesorectal excision, and local
excision plus completion total mesorectal excision
groups, respectively. At 3 years, 37 (70%), 50 (82%), and
24 (86%) in these groups, respectively, were alive and free
from disease.

Author: Rullier
Content:
however, we considered it important to assess the
procedure overall with a measure combining all clinical
outcomes.
Our study showed that patients favoured the organ
preservation approach because they valued a possible
better quality of life associated with less invasive surgery,
as underlined by the lower compliance to the allocated
surgery in the total mesorectal excision group than in the
local excision group in case of good clinical response.
Furthermore, some patients in the local excision group
refused to undergo a completion total mesorectal
excision. The originality of our study is the three-step
strategy, which included three criteria for patient
selection for organ preservation: clinical staging, good
clinical response to chemoradiotherapy, and pathological
response. One of our main findings was that after
chemoradiotherapy for small T2T3 rectal carcinomas
(≤4 cm), 75% of patients had a good clinical response
(carcinoma ≤2 cm), which was associated with 61% of
good pathological tumour response (ypT0-1) that
correlated with a low risk of positive lymph nodes
(100% ypN0). This strategy theoretically translates to

organ preservation in 46% of patients without the risk of
positive mesorectal lymph nodes being missed in an
assessment. The advantage of our strategy is therefore to
propose and predict the chance of organ preservation in
selected patients with a low oncological risk.
The number of patients with morbidity and compli­
cations was similar in both groups, which did not enable
us to show an advantage of the local excision strategy.
This high morbidity is due to the higher than anticipated
number of completion total mesorectal excisions, and to
that the morbidity of completion total mesorectal
excisions was twice as high after a primary total
mesorectal excision. An exploratory analysis according to
the type of surgery undertaken suggested that local
excision was associated with less morbidity than total
mesorectal excision, which in turn was less morbid than
local excision plus completion total mesorectal excisions.
Additionally, the types of complications after local
excision appeared to be less severe than after total
mesorectal excisions or completion total mesorectal
excisions, although they were considered as a major
morbidity according to Dindo’s classification. Thus,
although we were not able to show a difference between
the groups, we hope for a potential advantage of local
excision in the future, if modifying the screening and
surgical indication criteria enables inclusion of a
population with a lower risk of requiring completion
total mesorectal excisions.
Pathological data showed a low rate of positive lymph
nodes, 8% for the overall population, suggesting that
completion total mesorectal excision was overused in our
study. Positive lymph nodes occurred in 0, 0, 8%, and
40% of patients with ypT0, ypT1, ypT2, and ypT3
tumours, respectively, after chemoradiotherapy for small
T2T3 rectal cancer. These numbers are lower than the
5%, 8%, 26% and 55% usually reported after chemo­
radiotherapy for more advanced T3T4 disease, [27] and
might be attributed to the smaller size of the tumours in
our trial (maximum diameter 4 cm). Indeed, tumour and
nodal responses are correlated with the clinical tumour
stage and tumour size. [28] In our study, the lower number
of positive pathological lymph nodes in patients clinically
staged N0 than in those staged N1 suggests that patients
with ypT2 and cN0 tumours, conventionally treated with
completion total mesorectal excision, might not require
completion total mesorectal excisions in the future. This
finding is in accordance with the results of the ACOSOG
Z6041 trial. [18]
Results from the non-randomly assigned patients
(ie, those considered as clinically inadequate responders),
showed that 39% had a good pathological response
(ypT0-1), suggesting that the method of assessment of
the response in our study was not optimum and that
some clinically inadequate responders could have
benefited from organ preservation. Improved imaging,
particularly pelvic MRI, [29] and a delay before making a
decision, might improve the diagnosis of response.

Title: Organ preservation for rectal cancer (GRECCAR 2): a prospective, randomised, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial
Author: Rullier
Content:
The American ACOSOG Z6041 phase 2 trial included
79 patients with T2N0 lower rectal cancer treated with
chemoradiotherapy (54 Gy, capecitabine and oxaliplatine)
followed by local excision. [18] 4% of patients had local
recurrence and 88% were alive and free from disease at
3 years, and the investigators concluded that local
excision after chemoradiotherapy was an alternative to
major surgery in unfit patients. Our finding of 5% local
recurrence occurring in the local excision group confirms
the results of ACOSOG Z6041. Although we included
more patients with advanced tumours (T3 and N1), we
believe that local recurrence remained low in our trial
because only good clinical responders were considered
for local excision and completion total mesorectal
excision was recommended for patients with ypT2-3
tumours. The proportion of patients alive and diseasefree at 3 years was lower in our study compared with the
ACOSOG Z6041 (78% _vs_ 88%) probably because we
included patients with stages II and III disease, as well as
those with stage I disease. Therefore, metastatic disease
could be a problem if patients with more locally advanced
tumours are considered for organ preservation
programmes. Indeed, after local excision or watch-andwait strategies, adjuvant chemotherapy is not con­
ventionally used. [11,12,18]
A Dutch observational study [12] reported results from
100 patients with T1-4/N0-2 rectal tumours located
between 0 and 15 cm from the anal verge, treated with
chemoradiotherapy (50 Gy) or radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy):
61 had an immediate complete clinical response, 24 had
delayed complete clinical response 3 months later, and
15 had local excision for near complete clinical response. [12]
Most patients had no surgery at all, and at 3 years,
85% were recurrence-free and 81% were alive and
disease-free. This study supported the previous results of
a Brazilian team (Gama and colleagues [9] ), and was able to
improve the diagnostic performance of complete clinical
response after neoadjuvant therapy by using high quality
MRI. [29] Findings from a Danish trial proposed high dose
chemoradiotherapy alone (external beam 60 Gy plus
brachytherapy 5 Gy) in patients with T2-3/N0-1 lower
rectal tumours. [11] The trial stopped after the first
55 patients because of accrual difficulties. Of 40 patients
with complete clinical response, 26% had local recurrence
at 2 years; all local recurrences were treated by curative
radical surgery.
The OnCoRe Manchester registry study [10] compared
retrospectively 109 patients with T2-4 rectal cancers treated
by chemoradiotherapy and observation (watch-and-wait)
with 109 matched patients treated by chemoradiotherapy
and total mesorectal excision. Although survival was not
compromised in the observation group, 38% of patients
had local recurrence at 3 years, and most patients
(24 [65%] of 37) treated for local recurrence received
abdomino­perineal resection or Hartmann’s.
In the future, there is no doubt that observation, as
proposed in previous studies, will become a standard in

good clinical responders after chemoradiotherapy for
rectal cancer, especially for patients with a complete
clinical response. Indeed, observation alone is less
invasive than surgery, even local excision. However,
given the findings from our trial, especially the high
morbidity and number of complications at 2 years in the
less invasive local excision group with no advantage
compared with standard surgery, it seems necessary to
investigate long-term non-oncological outcomes in any
type of organ preservation programme. In particular,
investigations should include the effect of salvage total
mesorectal excision, and to compare this in intention-totreat populations with standard of care.
Organ preservation after neoadjuvant chemo­
radiotherapy for rectal cancer includes a risk of
overtreatment, where total mesorectal excision alone
would be a safe possibility. The response is stagedependent with 58% of T1, 28% of T2, 16% of T3, and
12% of T4 tumours reaching stage ypT0. [7] Big tumours
theoretically are exposed to a high risk of overtreatment
if organ preservation is anticipated, because the chance
of sterilisation is low. Conversely, small tumours can be
overtreated, especially for patients who will require a
completion total mesorectal excision. Our study reporting
40% of patients with ypT0 tumours, similar to the 44% of
patients with ypT0 tumours in ACOSOG Z6041, [18]
suggests that small T2T3 tumours less than 4 cm are
good candidates for organ preservation because of the
high chance of complete or subcomplete pathological
response. Furthermore, our data suggest that most
completion total mesorectal excisions could be avoided.
Finally, close follow-up with MRI to detect lymph node
recurrences could also be an alternative to completion
total mesorectal excisions.
Our clinical trial had several limitations. First, the
sample size was small—however, our study included
ultra-selected patients with small T2T3 low rectal
tumours, which represents 20% of rectal cancers. The
anticipated number of patients required to test our
hypothesis was obtained and we do not think that
inclusion of more patients would have changed the
conclusions.
Second, we used a non-usual composite primary
endpoint. This strategy might have induced difficulties
for interpretation of the results because no weighting
was used for each component. However, we believe that
the composite outcome was representative of what is
expected from a patient with rectal cancer and good
clinical response, because it included oncological,
toxicity, and functional issues. Also this study was not
masked, because of the different surgical procedures in
the two groups.
Third, we did not show the superiority of local excision
over total mesorectal excision, and furthermore the width
of the CIs of the comparative analysis showed the limited
precision of the estimates, preventing any argument that
the local excision approach was non-inferior (or equivalent)

results needs caution because of the protocol deviation of
nine of 71 patients assigned to total mesorectal excision not
receiving total mesorectal excision. This protocol deviation
might have produced less morbidity in the total mesorectal
excision group, suggesting underestimation of morbidity
occurred in this group; however, this possibility was
explored in the per-protocol analysis, and the conclusions
were not affected. By contrast, the choice of Dindo
stages III–V to define surgical morbidity suggests
overestimation of morbidity in the local excision group
because severity of complications was higher after total
mesorectal excision than after local excision. Indeed, rectal
bleeding after local excision treated by endoscopy was
defined as grade 3, similar to that noted with laparotomy
for peritonitis after total mesorectal excision. Thus, there is
a potential for overestimation of morbidity after local
excision alone and in the local excision group, although
this was not shown in the study.
In conclusion, local excision was not superior to total
mesorectal excision in patients with T2T3 small rectal
cancers with good response after chemoradiotherapy;
however, 3-year local recurrence and disease-free survival
did not differ significantly between groups (although the
study was not powered to test formally whether local
excision was oncologically safe). The absence of
superiority of local excision might have been due to a
high occurrence of completion total mesorectal excisions
that probably increased morbidity and complications.
However, pathological data showed a low occurrence of
positive lymph nodes in such small, irradiated tumours,
suggesting that most completion total mesorectal
excisions were not necessary. We hypothesise that,
similar to ypT0-1/Nx tumours, the subgroup of ypT2/N0
tumours might not require completion total mesorectal
excisions either, and only high-risk patients with ypT2N1
and pT3 tumours will require this surgery. A new trial,
GRECCAR 12, will test this hypothesis and will serve
to optimise the response by using neoadjuvant
chemotherapy plus chemoradiotherapy. In the future,
watch-and-wait studies, as well as local excision studies,
will contribute together to study the efficacy and safety of
strategies aimed at increasing the chances of organ
preservation in complete or subcomplete responders

after neoadjuvant therapy for rectal cancer. By using such
strategies, we expect around 20% of patients with rectal
cancer could avoid radical surgery.

A B S T R A C T

Purpose
A pathologic complete response (pCR; ypT0N0) of a rectal tumor after neoadjuvant radiochemotherapy (RCT) is associated with an excellent prognosis. Several retrospective studies have
investigated the effect of increasing the delay after RCT. The aim of this study was to evaluate the
effect of increasing the interval between the end of RCT and surgery on the pCR rate.

Methods
GRECCAR6 was a phase III, multicenter, randomized, open-label, parallel-group controlled trial. Patients
with cT3/T4 or Tx N+ tumors of the mid or lower rectum who had received RCT (45 to 50 Gy with
fluorouracil or capecitabine) were included. Patients were randomly included in the 7-week or the 11week (11w) group. Primary end point was the pCR rate defined as a ypT0N0 specimen (NCT01648894).

Title: Effect of Interval (7 or 11 weeks) Between Neoadjuvant Radiochemotherapy and Surgery on Complete Pathologic Response in Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial (GRECCAR-6)
Author: Lefevre
Content:
Results
A total of 265 patients from 24 centers were enrolled between October 2012 and February 2015. The
majority of the tumors were cT3 (82%). After RCT, surgery was not performed in nine patients (3.4%)
because of the occurrence of distant metastasis (n = 5) or other reasons. Two patients underwent local
resection of the tumor scar. A total of 47 (18.6%) specimens were classified as ypT0 (four had invaded
lymph nodes [8.5%]). The primary end point (ypT0N0) was not different (7 weeks: 20 of 133, 15.0% v
11w: 23 of 132, 17.4%; P = .5983). Morbidity was significantly increased in the 11w group (44.5% v
32%; P = .0404) as a result of increased medical complications (32.8% v 19.2%; P = .0137). The 11w
group had a worse quality of mesorectal resection (complete mesorectum [I] 78.7% v 90%; P = .0156).

Conclusion
Waiting 11 weeks after RCT did not increase the rate of pCR after surgical resection. A longer waiting
period may be associated with higher morbidity and more difficult surgical resection.

Current guidelines recommend neoadjuvant radiotherapy or radiochemotherapy (RCT) for T3/T4
or N+ cancer of the mid or lower rectum. This
treatment has been associated with a significant
reduction in the local recurrence rate without any
improvement in overall survival. [1][,][2]
RCT allows frequent (. 70%) tumor downsizing or downstaging and, more rarely (, 25%),

Several retrospective studies have studied the effect of increasing

Title: Effect of Interval (7 or 11 weeks) Between Neoadjuvant Radiochemotherapy and Surgery on Complete Pathologic Response in Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial (GRECCAR-6)
Author: Lefevre
Content:
In 2008,
Tulchinsky et al [8] showed that the only independent factor associated
with a good response was the delay between the end of RCT and
surgery (17% in the group that underwent surgery at, 7 weeks v
35% in the group that underwent surgery after 7 weeks; P = .03). The
same conclusion was drawn by Kalady et al [9] after examining a series
of 306 patients with rectal cancer. The pCR rate increased from
16.3% (14 of 86) in the group that underwent surgery at, 8 weeks
to 30.8% (28 of 91) in the other group (P = .03). The waiting period
was also the sole predictive factor of pCR. A recent meta-analysis that
included 13 retrospective studies and 3,584 patients confirmed this
favorable impact on the pCR rate and the absence of morbidity
associated with these delayed surgical procedures. [10]
Despite this evidence, the actual effect of increasing the
waiting period is unknown. All of these studies have inevitable
biases. For example, the choice of surgical timing was made by the
attending surgeon and was likely influenced by the tumor size or
response to RCT. [11] Moreover, the type of RCT and the cutoff for
the waiting period differed among these studies. [12]

The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of a longer
interval between the end of RCTand rectal cancer surgery (7 weeks
v 11 weeks) on the pCR rate in a randomized trial.

METHODS

Title: Effect of Interval (7 or 11 weeks) Between Neoadjuvant Radiochemotherapy and Surgery on Complete Pathologic Response in Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial (GRECCAR-6)
Author: Lefevre
Content:
The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of a longer
interval between the end of RCTand rectal cancer surgery (7 weeks
v 11 weeks) on the pCR rate in a randomized trial.

METHODS

Study Design and Participants
The design and rationale of this trial were previously published. [13] The
GRECCAR6 trial was a phase III, multicenter, randomized, open-label,
parallel-group, controlled trial. Patients with cT3 or T4 or TxN+ tumors
assessed by radiologic examination (magnetic resonance imaging and/or
endo-ultrasound) of the mid or lower rectum who had received RCT (45 to
50 Gy with intravenous fluorouracil or capecitabine) were included. The
exclusion criteria consisted of patients younger than 18 years of age,
patients with upper-third rectal cancer, rectal cancer with synchronous
metastasis, patients who had not received the complete RCT regimen,
a previous history of neoplasia (except cutaneous cancer) during the last
5 years, and patients under guardianship or subject to legal protection. After
completing the preintervention assessments, the patients were randomly
assigned to groups (ratio, 1:1) by using CleanWEB software (Telemedecine
Technologies S.A.S., Boulogne-billancourt, France). Blocked, centralized
randomization with stratification by center was prepared by Unit´e de
Recherche Clinique de l’Est Parisien. The GRECCAR6 trial was approved by
the National Institutional Review Board (the Regional Committee of Patient
Protection of South-West I, No. 1-12-19:30/08/12) and by the National
Agency of Medicine and Medical Products (ANSM: B111580-10). The research was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and
[was referenced on clinicaltrials.gov: NCT01648894.](http://clinicaltrials.gov)

Outcomes
The primary end point of the GRECCAR6 trial was the pCR
rate defined as a ypT0N0 specimen confirmed by the two pathologic examinations. The secondary outcomes included postoperative morbidity
according to the Clavien-Dindo scale, [17][,][18] the sphincter-saving procedure rate, overall survival, and disease-free survival. Postoperative death
was defined as death that occurred within 30 postoperative days or during
the first hospitalization. Postoperative complications were defined by the
occurrence of medical or surgical complications within 90 postoperative
days or during the first hospitalization.

In this article, we report the primary end point and the morbidity. An
analysis of survival will be performed after at least 3 years of follow-up.

Statistical Analysis
The required sample size was calculated according to the hypothesis
that the pCR rate of the 7w group would be similar to the typical rate after
6 to 8 weeks (12%) [7][,][9][,][19][,][20] and the expectation that the pCR rate in the 11w

test with a significance level of .05, and a 10% drop-out rate, at least 264
patients were needed for this analysis. A futility analysis was performed
after random assignment of 132 patients using a Bayesian statistical interference, which showed no impact on the type 1 error. [23] Of the 265
patients enrolled, only 253 patients underwent surgery for oncological
rectal resection with mesorectal excision.

DISCUSSION

We showed in this study that a 4-week increase between the
completion of RCTand surgery was not associated with an increase
in the pCR rate. However, the delay was associated with a higher
postoperative morbidity rate and a worse quality of mesorectal
excision.
These results are inconsistent with those of previously
published retrospective studies with smaller sample sizes. This
discrepancy may be explained by several factors. First, our
17% pCR rate was higher than the rate reported in previous
publications. [7][,][11][,][22][,][24] In the largest study published by Probst
et al, [25] which examined 17,255 rectal cancers, the pCR rate was
8.7% before 6 weeks and 13.2% after 8 weeks (P, .001). Because
of such low pCR rates, a longer waiting period may be of interest.
Regarding the pT stage, a “glass ceiling” exists for a pCR rate of
approximately 17% to 20%. Waiting longer does not change the
intrinsic characteristics of the tumor and its ability to be eliminated. Some previous publications have shown no difference in the
pCR rate when comparing different waiting periods. [26][,][27]
The higher pCR rate observed after longer waiting periods in
retrospective studies may be due to the selection of patients.

The higher pCR rate observed after longer waiting periods in
retrospective studies may be due to the selection of patients. Indeed, our pCR rate was consistent with all previous randomized
studies that have assessed RCT using fluorouracil or capecitabine.
R¨odel et al [28] observed a 14% pCR rate, Sauer et al [2] observed a 9%
pCR rate, G´erard et al [29] observed a 14% pCR rate, Roh et al [30]
