Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
The UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23 trial is a multicentre,
open-label, phase 3, randomised, controlled trial done at
35 French hospitals (comprehensive cancer centres,
university hospitals, private hospitals, and public
hospitals; appendix p 1). The trial was designed under the
auspices of the Partenariat de Recherche en Oncologie
Digestive (PRODIGE) intergroup. Participating gastro­
intestinal surgeons had been trained to do total
mesorectal excision and worked in centres in which
more than 30 gastro­intestinal cancer operations a year
take place.
Eligible patients were aged 18–75 years, had a
pathologically confirmed rectal adenocarcinoma within
15 cm of the anal verge, with a WHO performance status
of 0 or 1, and staged cT3 (at risk of local recurrence and for
which a multi­disciplinary tumour board recommended
preoperative chemoradio­therapy) or cT4. [17] Additionally,
the following laboratory results were required: a neutrophil
count of 1·5 × 10⁹ cells per L or higher, a platelet count of
100 × 10⁹ per L or higher, a haemoglobin concentration of
10 g/dL or higher, a renal clearance rate higher than
50 mL/min, and a normal bilirubin concentration.
Comorbid­ities were permitted except for ischaemic
coronary disease, peripheral neuropathy of grade 2 or
worse, and symptomatic inflammatory bowel disease.
Patients with distant meta­stases and non-resectable
cancer were ineligible, as were those who had received
previous pelvic radiotherapy or chemotherapy. A full list of
[inclusion and exclusion criteria is available in the protocol.](http://gofile.me/2FMlw/CaZYbUeoa)
The extent of the primary tumour was assessed by MRI
in all patients. Endorectal ultrasound was mandatory
for patients with mrT3N0 or cT3N0 staging to further
exclude cT2 tumours. High-resolution, three-dimensional,
T2-weighted MRI was mandatory before and after
preoperative chemotherapy and before surgery. MRI
reports included the following details: tumour height
from the anorectal junction; craniocaudal length of
tumour; circumferential location of the tumour; depth of
extramural spread; shortest distance to mesorectal fascia;
invasion to other structures, sphincter complex, or
peritoneum; percentage of circumferential extension;
TNM staging; distance of the tumour to anal levators; and,
at restaging, the response to preoperative treatment.
Extramural venous invasion was not specifically identified
in accordance with 2012 available guidelines. Regional
lymph nodes with a short-axis diameter of more than
9 mm and those with a short-axis diameter of 5–9 mm
that met at least two morphological criteria (ie, irregular
borders, heterogeneous signal intensity, or round shape)
on MRI were considered as metastatic. Baseline thoraco­
abdominopelvic CT scans were done as part of the initial
investigations before inclusion in the trial to exclude
metastases, then after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, after
chemoradiotherapy before surgery, postoperatively, and
after the last cycle of adjuvant chemotherapy.

The trial was done in accordance with the Declaration
of Helsinki, International Harmonization Conference
Good Clinical Practice guidelines and relevant French
and European laws and directives, and reported according
to CONSORT guidelines. [18] The trial protocol and all
subsequent amendments were approved by an
independent ethics committee (Comité de Protection des
Personnes Est III) and the French National Agency for
the Safety of Medicines. An independent Data Safety
Monitoring Board was established to ensure ethical
conduct, especially on three criteria: toxic death
rate (<2%), rate of patients not having had any rectal
surgery, and rate of postoperative re-hospitalisations. All
patients gave written informed consent.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
Patients were recruited at the participating centres after
recommended tumour staging and patient’s assessment,
discussion in tumour board meetings, and before starting
any treatment. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1)
to either the neoadjuvant chemotherapy group (six cycles
of FOLFIRINOX, followed by chemoradiotherapy, surgery,
and adjuvant chemotherapy) or the standard-of-care group
(chemo­radiotherapy, surgery, and adjuvant chemotherapy)
within 14 days of enrolment. Randomisation was done
online by investigator representatives with the NKI
software (TenAlea, Amsterdam, Netherlands) using a
minimisation technique that included a random element
of 80%, with stratification according to centre, extramural
extension of tumour into the perirectal fat assessed by
MRI (≥5 mm _vs_ <5 mm), tumour location (≤5 cm _vs_
5·1–10 cm _vs_ 10·1–15 cm, from anal verge on rigid
proctoscopy), and stage (cT3 _vs_ cT4; cN0 _vs_ cN+).
Investigators and participants were not masked to
treatment allocation.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
Patients in the neoadjuvant chemotherapy group received
FOLFIRINOX, which consisted of oxaliplatin (85 mg/m²)
and leucovorin (400 mg/m²), delivered as a 2-h intravenous
infusion, followed by irinotecan (180 mg/m²) as a 90-min
intravenous infusion, and fluorouracil (2400 mg/m²) by
continuous intravenous infusion over 46 h. FOLFIRINOX
was given every 14 days for six cycles. Prescription of
prophylactic granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF)
was considered on a case-by-case basis whenever a cycle
had been postponed for a week or longer because of
neutropenia. G-CSF was mandatory after febrile neutro­
penia, grade 4 neutropenia lasting more than a week, or
infection occurring during grade 3–4 neutro­penia.
Chemoradiotherapy was planned 1–3 weeks after the last
FOLFIRINOX cycle.
Chemoradiotherapy in both groups consisted of 50 Gy
over 5 weeks (2 Gy five times per week, with a reduction in
fields after 44 Gy) and concurrent oral capecitabine
(800 mg/m²) twice daily for 5 days per week. Capecitabine
was to be stopped in case of myocardial ischaemia.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
Surgery was mandatory and was planned 6–8 weeks after
chemoradiotherapy. Total mesorectal excision was strongly
recommended. Low anterior resection was advised for
high-rectal, mid-rectal, and low-rectal cancers with distal
margins of more than 1 cm. For very low-lying tumours,
intersphincteric resection with coloanal anastomosis or
abdominoperineal resection was done by the surgeon. A
watch-and-wait policy was considered a protocol violation.
Adjuvant chemotherapy was started 5–12 weeks
following surgery in both groups, regardless of patho­
logical response stage, and consisted of modified
FOLFOX6 (mFOLFOX6) or capecitabine according to
centre choice throughout the study. mFOLFOX6 consisted
of oxaliplatin (85 mg/m²) given as a 2-h intravenous
infusion, followed by leucovorin (400 mg/m²) given as a
2-h intravenous infusion, followed by fluorouracil
(400 mg/m²) given as an intravenous bolus then as
continuous intravenous infusion (2400 mg/m²) over 46 h
every 14 days. Capecitabine (1250 mg/m²) twice daily was
given orally on days 1–14 every 21 days. Adjuvant
chemotherapy was given for 3 months in the neoadjuvant
chemotherapy group and 6 months in the standard-ofcare group. As such, patients in the standard-of-care group
received 12 cycles of mFOLFOX6 or eight cycles of
capecitabine, and patients in the neoadjuvant chemo­
therapy group received six cycles of mFOLFOX6 or
four cycles of capecitabine. Adjuvant chemotherapy was
stopped in cases of myocardial ischaemia.
Laboratory and adverse event monitoring during
preoperative therapy were done before all cycles of
neoadjuvant chemotherapy, weekly during chemoradio­
therapy, before and after surgery, and before all cycles of
adjuvant chemotherapy. Laboratory tests included serum
total bilirubin concentrations during neoadjuvant
chemotherapy. The full list of laboratory tests is provided
in the protocol. Adverse events related to preoperative
and adjuvant therapy were assessed and graded by the
investigators using Common Terminology Criteria for
Adverse Events, version 4. A serious adverse event was
defined as any event, whether or not a causal relationship
has been established with the study, that results in death,
persistent or substantial temporary disability or
incapacity, a congenital anomaly, birth defect, or abortion;
is life-threatening; requires admission to hospital or
prolongation of ongoing hospital stay; or any clinically
significant event affecting the safety of the participants.
The Unicancer pharmacovigilance unit was notified of
any serious adverse events and, from these reports,
surgical complications were classified according to the
Clavien-Dindo grading system.
In case of toxic effects, FOLFIRINOX and mFOLFOX6
cycles were delayed until the neutrophil count was
1·5 × 10⁹ cells per L or higher and the platelet count was
100 × 10⁹ per L or higher. Briefly, dose reductions were
recommended in patients who developed febrile
neutropenia, grade 4 neutropenia lasting more than a
week, grade 3–4 thrombocytopenia, or any toxicity worse

than grade 2. The oxaliplatin dose was reduced when
grade 2 peripheral neuropathy was painful or persistent
between cycles and oxaliplatin was stopped in case of
motor impairment. Leucovorin was delivered at fixed
doses. Capecitabine dose was adapted to blood counts
and renal clearance. Dose reduction or discontinuation
of capecitabine was considered in case of grade 2 toxicity.
Full dose adaptations are described in the protocol.
MRI scans were done at enrolment, after neoadjuvant
chemotherapy, and before surgery. The resection rate,
type of surgical procedure, stoma (temporary or
permanent), and resection (curative or palliative),
peroperative detection of metastases, and number of red
blood cell units transfused were described for each
allocation group. A standardised pathological examination
was done after surgery; the quality of mesorectal excision
was assessed by pathologists using Quirke’s method [19]
and tumour regression was assessed by the modified
Dworak system. [20] Post-treatment follow-up assessments,
including CT scans, carcino­embryonic antigen measure­
ment, physical examination, and digital rectal examination
after sphincter-sparing surgery, were done every 4 months
for the first 3 years, then every 6 months for the next
2 years, then once after 6 years and 7 years. Total
colonoscopy was mandatory 6 months after surgery if no
preoperative total colonoscopy was performed because of
an obstructive tumour, after 3 years, then every 5 years.
Patients with disease progression were monitored for
survival. All reports of imaging, surgical, and pathology
results were assessed by independent masked central
review.
Disease-free events were centrally reviewed, with
outcome assessors masked to treatment allocation. Data
collection continued after the first event for separate
analyses of locoregional recurrences and distant
metastases.
Quality of life was assessed using the European
Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer
Quality of Life Questionnaire Core-30 (EORTC QLQ-C30),
version 3.0, [21] and the colorectal cancer module (QLQ-CR29;
appendix p 2). [22] Questionnaires were completed by patients
in both groups at baseline, on the last day of chemo­
radiotherapy, before and after surgery, after the last cycle of
adjuvant chemotherapy, at each visit for 3 years or until
progression, and, in the neoadjuvant chemo­therapy group,
after cycles two and six of neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
The primary endpoint was disease-free survival at 3 years,
defined as the time from randomisation until the first
cancer-related event, second cancer, or death from any
cause. Secondary endpoints were overall survival,
metastasis-free survival, cancer-specific survival, loco­
regional recurrence rate, metastatic recurrence rate,
ypT0N0 rate, R0 resection rate, surgical morbidity, safety,
and patient-reported quality of life (appendix p 7). Qualityof-life outcomes will be reported in detail separately.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
To show a 10% increase in 3-year disease-free survival
(from 75% to 85%), corresponding to a hazard ratio (HR)
of 0·56, a total of 460 patients (230 in each group) were
required to observe 136 events with 90% power and a
two-sided significance level of 5%.
Efficacy analyses were based on the intention-to-treat
principle, and safety analyses were done separately on
treated patients at each stage; the neoadjuvant safety
population included all patients who received at least
one administration of FOLFIRINOX, the preoperative
chemoradiotherapy safety population included all
patients who received at least one administration of
radiotherapy or cape­citabine, and the adjuvant
chemotherapy safety population included all patients
who received at least one administration of FOLFOX6
or capecitabine. The type of surgical procedure, type of
stoma and stoma rate, and the resection rate were
analysed in each group. The neoadjuvant rectal score,
which is a post-hoc analysis, was calculated using
the following equation: (5ypN–3 × [cT–ypT] + 12)² ÷ 9·61. [23]
We also did preplanned analyses to compare
compliance, dose intensity, and toxic effects for the whole
duration of adjuvant therapy and neoadjuvant plus
adjuvant therapy, whereas comparison of dose intensity
of adjuvant chemotherapy between the two groups in the
first 3 months was a post-hoc analysis.
Survival rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier
method [24] and compared using a stratified log-rank test.
A stratified Cox proportional hazards model according
to stratification factor (but not according to centre
because of the high number of centres, since 60% of
centres had enrolled less than ten patients) was used to
estimate HRs with 95% CIs. The proportional hazards
assumption was verified by the Schoenfeld residual
method. [25] HRs indicating the effects of prognostic
factors (ie, sex, age, WHO performance status, tobacco
use, localisation of tumour, carcinoembryonic antigen,
mrT, cT, N stage, TNM staging, predicted lateral
margin, tumour size, extramural spread of the tumour
to the perirectal fat, ypT0N0, perinervous infiltration,
and lymphovacular invasion) on treatment effect for
disease-free survival were also calculated in accordance
with the protocol. A Cox proportional hazards model
was used to evaluate the effects of prognostic factors in
univariate analyses. Clinically relevant factors or
variables with p values of less than 0·2 were explored in
a multivariate analysis. Categorical variables were
compared using the χ² or Fisher’s exact test, and
continuous variables were compared using the
Wilcoxon test. All statistical tests are two-sided and the
significance threshold is set at 5%. No interim analysis
was planned.
All analyses were done using Stata version 16.0 and
SAS version 9.3 software. This study is registered with
EudraCT (2011-004406-25) and ClinicalTrials.gov
(NCT01804790).

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
From June 5, 2012, to June 26, 2017, 461 patients were
randomly assigned to the neoadjuvant chemotherapy
group (n=231) or the standard-of-care group (n=230;
figure 1; appendix p 3). All patients were included in
the efficacy analyses. Baseline patient characteristics
were well matched in both groups (table 1). Overall,
457 (99%) of 461 patients had cT3 or cT4 tumours, and
415 (90%) of 461 had clinical lymph-node involvement.
34 (7%) of 461 patients had no high-risk factors (cN+,
lateral lymph nodes, or predicted involved radial margin),
two of them (1%) with cT2N0 and 32 (7%) with cT3N0
(15 [6%] in the neoadjuvant chemotherapy group
and 17 [7%] in the standard-of-care group).
At data cutoff (Jan 14, 2020), the overall median follow-up
was 46·5 months (IQR 35·4–61·6); median follow-up for
the neoadjuvant chemotherapy group was 47·7 months
(IQR 35·0–60·9) and for the standard-of-care group it was
45·7 months (35·9–61·7). Disease-free survival events
were reported in 58 (25%) of 231 patients in the neoadjuvant
chemotherapy group and 78 (34%) of 230 in the standardof-care group (appendix p 17). 3-year disease-free survival
rates were 76% (95% CI 69–81) in the neoadjuvant
chemotherapy group and 69% (95% CI 62–74) in the
standard-of-care group (stratified HR 0·69, 95% CI
0·49–0·97; p=0·034; figure 2A). The subgroup analysis of
disease-free survival according to baseline characteristics
showed no evidence for heterogeneity of treatment effect
size (appendix p 4). Standard-of-care group, low tumour
localisation, T4 stage, and TNM stage IV were identified as
adverse prognostic factors for disease-free survival in the
univariate analysis (appendix p 18). Neoadjuvant chemo­
therapy group and lower TNM stage were identified as
favourable prognostic factors in the stratified multivariate
analysis (appendix p 20).
At the time of database lock, 68 patients had died,
including 27 (12%) of 231 patients in the neoadjuvant
chemotherapy group and 41 (18%) of 230 patients in the
standard-of-care group (appendix p 17). 3-year overall
survival rates were 91% (95% CI 86–94) in the neoadjuvant
chemo­therapy group and 88% (95% CI 83–91) in the
standard-of-care group (figure 2B). 3-year cancer-specific
survival rates were 92% (95% CI 87–95) in the neoadjuvant
chemotherapy group and 89% (95% CI 84–93) in the

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
Standard management for locally advanced rectal
cancer—namely, chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery
and adjuvant chemotherapy—provides excellent control
of local disease but has not been shown to reduce the risk
of distant metastases. In this trial, including patients with
stage T3 or T4 rectal cancers, neoadjuvant chemotherapy
with FOLFIRINOX followed by chemoradiotherapy
signifi­cantly prolonged disease-free survival compared
with preoperative chemoradiotherapy only and did not
alter quality of life. Our 3-year disease-free survival results
in both groups were worse than predicted, probably due
to patients’ tumour characteristics (92% had a staging
greater than T3a). However, the 3-year disease-free
survival rate in the standard-of-care group (69%) is
consistent with the 3-year disease-free survival rate in the
previous PRODIGE-02 trial (68%). [2] Pathology findings
after surgery showed significant improvements in
pathological complete response rate, tumour regression,
and the number of metastatic regional lymph nodes with
neoadjuvant chemotherapy compared with the standard
of care. The neoadjuvant rectal score, a strong surrogate

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX and preoperative chemoradiotherapy for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (UNICANCER-PRODIGE 23): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
Author: Conroy
Content:
endpoint for disease-free survival, [23] was also significantly
lower in the neoadjuvant chemotherapy group. There was
also a significant improvement in metastasis-free survival
with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, providing evidence that
shifting systemic chemotherapy to earlier in the treatment
sequence might improve control of distant metastases
without increasing the likelihood of locoregional failure.
This effect might be associated with improved overall
survival with longer follow-up, and an updated analysis is
planned at a median of 5 years of follow-up. To our
knowledge, this is the first study to provide evidence of
improved long-term disease-related outcomes with
neoadjuvant chemotherapy in patients with locally
advanced rectal cancer.
Compliance with FOLFIRINOX in our study was very
high, with more than 90% of patients completing six cycles
of treatment, thus avoiding one of the major shortfalls of
adjuvant chemotherapy. [1,6–8] Importantly, upfront use of
FOLFIRINOX did not compromise the uptake of surgery,
increase surgical morbidity, or adversely affect compliance
with adjuvant chemotherapy. However, discontinuation
of capecitabine during chemoradiotherapy was slightly
increased after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, an observation
that has also been reported in another study. [9] Grade 3–4
adverse events with FOLFIRINOX, mainly neutropenia
and diarrhoea, occurred in 46% of patients. Despite the
higher cumulative oxaliplatin dose, patients in the
neoadjuvant chemotherapy group had significantly less
neurotoxicity, probably due to the long interval between
neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy because of
chemoradiotherapy and surgery treatments. We have
endeavoured to improve the safety of FOLFIRINOX
through restriction of eligibility to patients younger than
76 years, removal of bolus fluorouracil, and targeted use of
G-CSF. The notable reduction in the incidence of
grade 3–4 neutropenia (17%) in the present trial compared
with the initial study on this regimen (85%) [13] provides
support for these initiatives.
No postoperative deaths within 30 days occurred in the
neoadjuvant chemotherapy group, whereas five deaths
occurred in the standard-of-care group (four from cardiac
or vascular events and one from suicide after R1 resection).
We have no data to suggest that patients undergoing
neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX might have been better
assessed for risk of ischaemic disease or better prepared
for surgery (due to the longer time between diagnosis and
surgery), but it is a possible hypothesis. Another possibility
is that maximised reduction of primary tumour size due
to the neoadjuvant chemotherapy strategy might facilitate
surgery.
One limitation of our trial is that the accrual rate was
lower than initially planned probably due to concurrent
competition from three other academic randomised trials
for rectal preservation during the PRODIGE 23 inclusion
period. This fact probably resulted in selected patients in
our trial having high-risk lower tumours. However,
hospitals that included patients in this trial were

university hospitals, comprehensive cancer centres,
general hospitals, and private institutions, which is
representative of the French health-care system.
Two aspects of treatment were changed in the
experimental group of PRODIGE 23 compared with
the control group: chemotherapy was moved from the
adjuvant to the perioperative setting, and 3 months of
adjuvant chemotherapy (mFOLFOX6 or capecitabine) was
replaced with the FOLFIRINOX regimen. We selected
the FOLFIRINOX triplet, rather than FOLFOX, as the
neoadjuvant regimen for two key reasons. First, the
regimen has substantial efficacy in metastatic disease. [13,14]
Second, four phase 2 randomised, controlled trials of
neoadjuvant chemotherapy with fluoropyrimidine–
oxaliplatin doublets before chemoradiotherapy showed no
increase in pathological complete response rate (the
primary endpoint) despite increased chemotherapy
exposure. [9–12] Among these trials, the Spanish Grupo
Cáncer de Recto-3 trial randomly assigned 108 patients
with locally advanced rectal cancer to four cycles of
neoadjuvant capecitabine plus oxaliplatin (CAPOX)
followed by chemoradiotherapy or to chemo­radiotherapy
followed by four cycles of adjuvant CAPOX. [9] Grade 3–4
toxicity was significantly reduced in the neoadjuvant
chemotherapy group; however, there were no reductions
in metastases after 69 months’ median follow-up. [16] In the
more recent RAPIDO trial, [26,27] patients were randomly
assigned to preoperative chemo­radio­therapy, surgery,
and optional adjuvant chemo­therapy (standard-of-care
group) or to short-course radiotherapy and 18 weeks
of fluoropyrimidine–oxaliplatin before surgery. 58% of
patients in the standard-of-care group did not receive
adjuvant chemotherapy. A significant reduction in 3-year
disease-related treatment failures (24% _vs_ 30%) was
observed, with no benefit in 3-year overall survival
(89% _vs_ 89%). In the experimental group, surgery was
scheduled approximately 24 weeks after the start of radio­
therapy. Despite no significant differences in surgical
procedures, significantly higher perioperative blood loss,
lower rate of intact mesorectal plane, and more ClavienDindo grade IV and V complications were observed, [26,27]
confirming that a longer delay between radiotherapy and
surgery might be associated with more difficult surgical
resection. [28] Until now, the addition of a third drug to
six cycles of a neoadjuvant fluoropyrimidine–oxaliplatin
combination has not shown superior efficacy (eg, the
addition of bevacizumab or aflibercept substantially
increased surgical compli­cations in two trials [12,15] ). The
addition of cetuximab to neoadjuvant CAPOX followed
by chemoradiotherapy did not increase pathological
complete response or 5-year progression-free survival. [11–29]
From these observations, we suggest that both the addition
of irinotecan to FOLFOX and the neoadjuvant treatment
approach had a crucial role in our results.
Central review of all major prognostic factors was done
to minimise the risk of staging errors and to better analyse
benefit in subgroups. This central review identified ten

Content:

inclusion. Some patients had cT3N0 tumours without
predicted involved radial margin and might have been
overtreated. The absence of extramural venous invasion
reporting on preoperative MRI in PRODIGE 23 is also a
limitation. However, major prognostic determinants
for disease-free survival (ie, age, T stage, lymph-node
invasion, low location, tumour differentiation, and lateral
lymph nodes) were equally distributed in each group.
There were also no differences in quality of the
mesorectum, circumferential margin, neural invasion,
and vascular invasion in histopathological specimens.
Moreover, we included the neoadjuvant rectal score in
analyses. The ability of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX to
improve ypN0 rate and the median neoadjuvant rectal
score further supports the positive effect of this strategy
on tumour parameters related to the risk of death.
A strength of our study was that it included clear
guidelines for the provision of adjuvant chemotherapy.
These guidelines ensured that the total duration of
chemotherapy was identical in both groups (6 months),
thus minimising an important methodological bias.
Despite the study requirements for adjuvant therapy,
22% of patients who were eligible for adjuvant chemo­
therapy did not receive it, mainly because of investigator
decision or because they developed postoperative
complications, with no difference in the causes of
non-compliance between groups; this rate is similar to
that observed in the CAO/ARO/AIO-04 study (22·3%). [5]
Both groups in our trial received adjuvant therapy with
low dose intensity, mainly due to treatment delays,
suppression of bolus fluorouracil, or oxaliplatin
dose reduction or discontinuation with mFOLFOX6,
which suggests that future trials should test delivery of
all chemotherapy before surgery. Because of the high
rate of pathological complete response in the neo­
adjuvant chemotherapy group, future studies should
also logically address the possibility of risk-adapted
therapy, including further evaluation of non-operative
manage­ment and organ-preserving strategies in selected
patients following neoadjuvant chemotherapy (such as
the GRECCAR12 trial, NCT02514278).
In conclusion, neoadjuvant chemotherapy with
FOLFIRINOX followed by chemoradiotherapy, surgery,
and adjuvant chemotherapy significantly improved
outcomes in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer
compared with patients who received standard chemo­
radiotherapy, surgery, and adjuvant chemotherapy.
The significantly improved disease-free survival in the
neoadjuvant chemotherapy group and the reduced
toxicity indicate that the perioperative approach is more
efficient and better tolerated than adjuvant chemotherapy
is. Therefore, these results could change clinical practice.
